articles.title: Kim pro quo: North Korea is emerging from international isolation by backing Russia’s war in Ukraine
articles.body:
In early September, Russia and North Korea opened a road bridge across the border river Tumen. Analysts note that the structure could become a key gateway for transporting North Korean troops and weapons for the war against Ukraine. Since 2023, military aid deliveries to Russia have become a key source of revenue for North Korea’s budget, fueling unprecedented economic growth. As Pyongyang has drawn closer to Moscow, China has also entered the competition for influence over North Korea — even though it backed sanctions against the country together with Russia back in 2017. Combined, these factors have strengthened Pyongyang’s position enough that it no longer needs to seek a thaw with the United States. At the same time, Donald Trump has shown readiness for talks, which, should they take place, could cement North Korea’s status as a nuclear power.
In July, South Korea’s central bank estimated that North Korea’s economy had grown by more than 3% for a third consecutive year, its best results since a comprehensive sanctions package took effect in 2017. The turnaround would have seemed improbable only a few years ago. North Korea emerged from the COVID-19 pandemic impoverished and more isolated than ever after sealing its borders, while international restrictions continued to limit trade as its nuclear program deepened the country’s estrangement not only from the West, but even from its traditional Chinese and Russian allies. Yet renewed trade with China, ambitious state-led development programs and, increasingly, military cooperation with Russia have produced North Korea’s strongest sustained growth in years. At the same time, Moscow has turned Pyongyang from an international liability into a useful military partner, while Donald Trump’s return has revived the possibility of direct diplomacy at the leader level. The Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) represents perhaps the most striking example of a state rejecting the post-Cold War world, and its sudden breakout from isolation serves as a signal that the order which once marginalized North Korea is beginning to unravel.
An unlikely recovery
North Korea’s recovery began, in part, by simply reopening the country. Trade with China had collapsed from nearly $2.8 billion in 2019 to $539 million in 2020— and it was just $318 million in 2021 after Pyongyang responded to COVID-19 by virtually sealing its borders. However, freight traffic gradually resumed in 2022, and by 2023 bilateral trade had recovered to around $2.3 billion. That reopening restored supplies of fuel, fertilizer, machinery, and consumer goods while allowing North Korean exports back onto the Chinese market. At the same time, the state poured resources into construction and industry, and improvements in agricultural production also helped pull the economy out of its pandemic slump. Russia would soon add an entirely new source of demand and foreign revenue, but North Korea’s recovery was already far from dependent on the wartime relationship with Moscow alone.
The domestic component of North Korea’s sudden relative prosperity has been remarkably visible. Since 2021, Kim Jong Un has made construction and regional development a central priority for the government, combining a five-year program to build 50,000 new apartments in Pyongyang with an extensive rural housing drive. With even grander ambition, in 2024 the DPRK’s Supreme Leader launched the “Regional Development 20x10 Policy,” calling for the modernization of factories in 20 cities and counties every year for a decade, with an emphasis on food processing, clothing, and everyday consumer goods. This represents a notable turn away from the focus on heavy industry traditionally favored by the state. Even more worrying for its neighbor to the south (and for the power of UNSC sanctions more broadly), however, is the fact that these programs are difficult to dismiss as propaganda. Satellite imagery has shown construction beginning within weeks of its announcement, and factories were installed in all 20 communities targeted during its first year. Building on its initial success, in 2025 the 20x10 program expanded into hospitals, leisure facilities, farming infrastructure, and other local projects, again opening all of its intended projects before the end of the year.
This headline policy represents a significant shift for a nation that has historically experienced extremely uneven economic development, with the capital, Pyongyang, and strategic heavy industries absorbing a disproportionate share of state investment while much of the country’s provincial economy remained dependent on Cold War-era factories or the nation’s growing informal economy. The 20x10 program, by contrast, is an explicit attempt to narrow that divide and invest in creating local provincial centers capable of processing regional materials into basic consumer products. It also seeks improvements in food production, agricultural mechanization, and housing. Whether these new industries can survive the country’s harsh shortages of electricity, machinery, and several raw inputs remains to be seen, but its focus on provincial economies and light industry is a significant departure from traditional party doctrine and seems to have borne early fruit.
That shift in emphasis, however, has not come at Pyongyang’s expense. At the same time the government has redirected investment toward provincial cities, it has continued an enormous reconstruction of the capital. In February, the government announced the completion of the aforementioned program to construct 50,000 new housing units, much of it concentrated in the brand new Hwasong district, where the program transformed former agricultural land into dense high-rise neighborhoods. The more striking changes, however, are taking place at the street level rather than on Pyongyang’s prominent skyline (which itself has long been a Kim family prestige project). Foreign visitors returning after the pandemic described the city as shockingly different from its pre-COVID self, with app-based taxis, QR-code payments, food and medicine delivery services, new storefronts and restaurants, and a far more visible smartphone economy. For the first time, the city’s wide streets and parking lots have been tested to capacity as the country experiences an influx of largely Chinese vehicles, imported despite UN sanctions. The most important new source of resources behind this expansion, however, came from outside the country.
Beginning in the summer of 2023, Pyongyang became a major supplier of artillery ammunition and ballistic missiles to Russia, eventually providing more than 15 million artillery rounds, according to South Korean intelligence estimates.
The resources for North Korea’s economic upturn largely came from military cooperation with Moscow
The Institute for National Security Strategy (INSS), a think tank affiliated with South Korea’s intelligence service, estimates that weapons exports alone earned North Korea more than $10 billion between mid-2023 and the end of 2025 — an extraordinary sum for a country whose entire annual GDP is estimated at only around $27 billion. The subsequent deployment of roughly 15,000 North Korean soldiers to Russia added hundreds of millions more, even if INSS says only a fraction of the proceeds has been confirmed as payment in kind, while much of the remainder may consist of sensitive military technology, components or materials, or may still be owed.
More consequential than the scale of the payments themselves, however, is the extent to which the relationship has begun to dismantle the economic constraints imposed on North Korea over the previous decade. The sanctions adopted after 2016 derived much of their force from the unusual willingness of both Russia and China to participate in isolating Pyongyang — restricting its access to fuel, machinery, foreign currency, overseas labor, and many of the export markets on which it had previously depended. Russia has now reversed that situation by becoming a major customer for the same military-industrial complex that the sanctions were intended to constrain while simultaneously supplying North Korea with many of the resources those measures sought to keep out. In short, the DPRK’s recent recovery is not simply a rebound from the extraordinary deprivation of the pandemic years, but the result of a much larger change in the country’s international position.
Pyongyang’s place in the new world
North Korea’s problem was never a lack of powerful backers. When it was nearly destroyed by the U.S.-led coalition during the Korean War, Communist China intervened in large part out of fear of having an American-aligned state and military presence on its border, and to this day the DPRK-PRC alliance remains China’s only mutual-defense commitment. What it couldn’t secure were powerful friends that truly needed anything it could provide. For most of the post-Cold War era, Pyongyang had little to offer in exchange for its dependence on Chinese and Russian trade and diplomatic protection — a meagre workforce, a domestic market too poor to absorb high-end imports, and an endless stream of diplomatic liabilities generated by its nuclear program and recurring foreign provocations. However, the war in Ukraine has begun to reverse that imbalance, turning qualities that had made North Korea a diplomatic liability into assets that its allies increasingly covet.
The shift is clearest in relations with Moscow. In 2017, Putin insisted that Russia “unequivocally condemned” North Korea’s nuclear tests and pledged “fully complied with the UN Security Council resolutions” imposed on the DPRK. And yet, by 2024 he was in Pyongyang signing a mutual-defense treaty as Russia purchased billions of dollars’ worth of North Korean munitions. The change soon reverberated to international institutions that had been designed to constrain the DPRK. In March of that year, Russia vetoed the renewal of the UN Panel of Experts responsible for monitoring sanctions on North Korea, dismantling one of the central mechanisms through which the Security Council could apply pressure on the country.
In March 2024, Russia vetoed one of the central mechanisms through which the UN Security Council could apply pressure on the DPRK
Of course, for Pyongyang the benefits go far beyond munitions export revenue and diplomatic protection. North Korea also receives access to fuel, materials, and advanced military equipment. According to some South Korean and Western assessments, the partnership also includes transfers of military technology in areas ranging from air defense to missile and satellite development. For the Korean People’s Army (KPA), which is still overwhelmingly reliant on Cold War-era Soviet designs and indigenous attempts at their modernization, such cooperation offers one of the few plausible routes toward modernizing the capabilities that North Korea cannot readily develop on its own.
The benefits of friendship with Russia also affect North Korea’s other international relationships. If anything, Pyongyang’s growing independence from Beijing appears to have made China more attentive when it comes to preserving its own influence. After starting to cool off during the pandemic, relations with Beijing grew dramatically closer starting in late 2025. As a result, in June 2026, Xi Jinping made his first visit to Pyongyang in seven years, pledging that China would not waver in its support for North Korea and agreeing to deepen cooperation in various fields. Rather than displacing Beijing, Russia’s entry has made North Korea more valuable to China by giving Pyongyang a realistic alternative source of support. Kim is now in a position to draw economic backing from Beijing and military and diplomatic benefits from Moscow while reducing the degree to which either power can take its influence over the DPRK for granted.
By the time Trump returned to office, he found the conditions that had enabled his famous first negotiations with North Korea largely absent. Back then, the DPRK was largely isolated from the rest of the world, and Western offers of sanctions relief and moves toward normalization were actually enticing. Now, Pyongyang has retained its nuclear arsenal, expanded its missile program, rebuilt much of its foreign trade, and secured relationships with Moscow and Beijing that are far more economically valuable than the recognition America once promised. While none of this removes negotiations or even potential steps to rapprochement from the table, it has shifted the starting point decisively in Kim’s favor. Trump’s America is still interested in talking to North Korea, but Kim’s North Korea has less of an incentive to reciprocate.
Trump’s gambit
Trump’s most consequential move toward Pyongyang so far took place on August 16. Only hours before the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises were scheduled to begin, the president ordered the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” America’s participation, arguing that the drills were costly and that they sent a “totally inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea, a country he described as having been “unthreatening and respectful” during his first term. The eleven-day exercise was subsequently cut to five days and its field component reduced; Washington later cancelled a separate upcoming joint Marine Corps exercise. For Pyongyang, which has spent decades portraying the exercises as rehearsals for an invasion and demanding their termination — along with the end of America’s presence in South Korea — Trump demonstrated immense goodwill without even requiring Kim to meet him.
Trump has shown readiness to engage with Pyongyang since returning to the White House
While it’s unclear how much Trump’s apparent frustration with South Korea’s lack of backing for American action in Iran contributed to the cancellation, the move itself isn’t entirely unprecedented. Days after his first summit with Kim in Singapore in 2018, Trump announced the suspension of Ulchi Freedom Guardian and several smaller exercises, similarly adopting Pyongyang’s description of the drills as “provocative” while arguing that their cancellation would save the U.S. money. However, the circumstances surrounding the two decisions could hardly be more different. In 2018, Trump’s suspension came amid perhaps the most dramatic thaw in inter-Korean relations since the division of the peninsula, with Moon Jae-in and Kim Jong Un having already met at Panmunjom, where they declared that “there will be no more war” between the two Koreas and that reconciliation, economic cooperation, and even the eventual reunification of the peninsula were desirable.
Today, nearly every condition that made such a gesture logical in 2018 has disappeared. The inter-Korean rapprochement surrounding Singapore has given way to Pyongyang’s formal abandonment of reunification, its designation of the ROK as a hostile state, and even the destruction of sections of the road and railway links that Moon and Kim had once promised to reconnect. At the same time, North Korea would enter any renewed negotiations with a growing nuclear arsenal, a mutual-defense treaty with Russia, and considerably less dependence on the sanctions relief that once formed Washington’s principal bargaining chip.
Despite offering little in return, Pyongyang does not appear to have ruled out renewed talks. Following Trump’s move, South Korean intelligence assessed that another Trump-Kim summit could be arranged “at any time.” However, unlike in 2018, North Korea now treats its nuclear arsenal as a permanent component of the state and the ultimate guarantor of its sovereignty. Analysts argue that, from Pyongyang’s perspective, America’s war against Iran vindicated a lesson already drawn from Libya and earlier attacks on Tehran: a credible nuclear deterrent is a necessary guarantee against potential American attack. This leaves any renewed summit with a much narrower window for discussion, particularly given Washington’s enduring policy calling for the complete denuclearization of North Korea (which is mirrored by South Korea).
Regardless of whether Trump’s gambit produces another summit, the larger reversal has already taken place. Less than a decade ago, North Korea faced a sanctions regime endorsed by Washington, Beijing, and Moscow, and the country depended almost entirely on China for its economic survival while remaining a liability even to the powers most interested in keeping it alive. Today, Pyongyang has already hosted two of the three most powerful leaders on Earth and is within reach of another meeting with the third. For the beleaguered hermit kingdom, it is a break in the storm clouds perhaps unmatched at any point this millennium.
A shrinking peninsula
For all of North Korea’s vast newfound advantages, the peninsula clearly leans in South Korea’s favor. For the DPRK, the enormous Korean People’s Army KPA remains central to the state, but the South Korean armed forces are still judged to hold the conventional advantage, as they are built around cutting-edge technology as opposed to the North’s heavily aged stockpiles. The economic imbalance is even more lopsided, with South Korea’s nominal GNI coming in at 56 times that of the North’s in 2025. Seoul’s annual defense budget alone now exceeds the estimated value of North Korea’s entire economy, giving the South a capacity to modernize, replace losses, and sustain high-end weapons systems on a scale Pyongyang cannot realistically match.
The one area where this overwhelming disparity is beginning to matter less, however, is manpower. South Korea’s fertility rate stood at just 0.80 children per woman in 2025, and the demographic collapse which for decades loomed as a distant economic problem has now reached the pool from which the ROK draws its soldiers. Between 2019 and 2025, the number of 20-year-old men fell by roughly 30%, while the active-duty military shrank by a fifth (to around 450,000 personnel), leaving a manpower shortfall estimated at roughly 50,000 troops. Seoul has been able to soften the consequences through force restructuring, expanded recruitment of women and career personnel, and a growing reliance on technology, but none of these measures change the arithmetic behind a conscription system which is drawing each successive intake from a substantially smaller generation than the last.
From 2019 to 2025, the number of young men in South Korea fell by 30%, and the size of the active-duty military by 20%
North Korea has also struggled demographically, though not as severely as its neighbor. The UN estimates its fertility rate at 1.8 children per woman in 2025, far above the South’s but still below replacement level. As the much smaller generation born during and after the famine of the 1990s reached enlistment age, the government reportedly loosened physical requirements for military service and also drew increasingly heavily on women. The country’s working-age population is estimated to have begun shrinking by almost 1% annually after 2020, and similar shortages have appeared outside the military, leading the state to increasingly direct young people toward mines and farms and mobilizing married women into factories and other production sites where the supply of workers has begun to thin.
The demographic balance between the Koreas is consequently moving in two directions at once. In the near term, South Korea is losing military-age manpower far faster, allowing Pyongyang to preserve one of the few quantitative advantages which Seoul’s economic ascent never completely eliminated. Over a longer horizon, however, the North is facing the same problem, only with much less room to absorb it. A smaller South Korean generation still enters an economy capable of sustaining increasingly capital-intensive production and defense, whereas a smaller North Korean generation has to be divided between an oversized military and a civilian economy in which agriculture, mining, construction, and large parts of manufacturing remain unusually dependent on labor. What currently looks like a durable Northern advantage is therefore better understood as a delayed disadvantage, albeit one which may matter considerably for the military balance during the decades before the DPRK’s own demographic contraction fully catches up with it.
Over a longer horizon, however, the North is also facing a demographic decline, only with much less room to absorb it
That reversal extends far beyond the demographic balance. North Korea’s reinvigorated economic growth, wartime partnership with Russia, renewed importance to China, and reduced dependence on what Washington can offer have together placed Pyongyang in perhaps its strongest international position since before the end of the Cold War. The country remains vastly poorer and conventionally weaker than the South, and its own demographic decline may ultimately prove more difficult to absorb, but it no longer approaches the outside world from the position of near-total dependence which shaped Trump’s first negotiations with Kim. If the two return to the negotiating table, Trump will therefore confront not the isolated North Korea he encountered in Singapore, but a state which has found in the unraveling of the post-Cold War order considerably more room to survive on its own terms.

articles.title: Ukraine wants homegrown missiles capable of striking deep inside Russia, including Moscow, but its existing ‘Flamingos’ show how hard mass production can be
articles.body:
Ukraine wants homegrown missiles capable of striking deep inside Russia, including Moscow, but its existing ‘Flamingos’ show how hard mass production can be
On September 11, Fire Point, Ukraine’s leading manufacturer of long-range strike weapons, said it was ready to supply the military with the FP-7 short-range ballistic missile. The FP-7 is intended to replace — or supplement — the well-known ATACMS. Fire Point is also continuing to test the medium-range FP-9, a type of missile Ukraine does not currently possess. The company says that “with adequate funding,” it will be able to produce up to three FP-9s a day within the next few months. If it delivers on that promise, Ukraine could substantially expand its ability to strike deep inside Russia and put new targets within reach that it currently lacks the weapons to hit. However, not all of Fire Point’s projects have gone according to plan. Suspected corruption is not the only issue: The company has also faced practical difficulties organizing production, particularly securing engines. Nor is it clear how the new ballistic missiles will perform in combat against Russian air defenses. Here, we examine the prospects and problems facing Ukraine’s missile program.
Why does Ukraine need missiles at all? Can’t drones strike Russia?
Compared with missiles, UAVs have obvious advantages — they are inexpensive and can be produced in enormous quantities — but they also have drawbacks.
- Low speed: This makes drones vulnerable to air defenses, including mobile units armed with nothing more than machine guns. The standard way to overcome these defenses is to launch drones en masse, overwhelming the enemy’s air defenses so that some reach their targets. But this partly negates their cost advantage: Many UAVs must be expended against a target that requires only one hit. Once losses are factored in, destroying a target may not be cheap at all. Meanwhile, both Ukraine and Russia face financial problems as the cost of the war rises. Ukraine has a $27 billion hole in its military budget that only its Western partners can fill. Russia’s military spending reached 10% of GDP in the first half of the year, causing its budget deficit to soar. A significant share of this spending is tied specifically to expanding drone production and making costly modifications to drones.
- Low speed and a small payload: Unlike cruise and ballistic missiles, drones carry relatively modest warheads weighing less than 100 kilograms, while missile warheads weigh hundreds of kilograms and can reach a metric ton. Because they strike at speeds of less than 200 kilometers per hour, drones cannot penetrate any reasonably sturdy barrier. Missiles have far greater penetrating power because their kinetic energy increases with the square of their speed. As Russian and Ukrainian strikes have shown, drones therefore cannot be used effectively against reinforced-concrete structures such as industrial buildings. This has forced Ukraine to focus its attacks on “soft” targets such as oil-refinery equipment and retailers’ warehouses. Attempts to disable military factories with drones have had little success, though there have been exceptions. Several large-scale attacks on a Geran-type UAV production facility in Tatarstan, for example, neither shut it down for long nor prevented its expansion. Russia’s strikes show that missiles are much better suited to such tasks, though Ukraine has sometimes restored some power generation at plants even after large-scale missile attacks.
- Low-cost countermeasures: Air-defense systems designed to counter drones can be produced quickly and at relatively low cost. It is hard to imagine anti-drone defenses running out of ammunition entirely. By contrast, missiles — especially ballistic missiles — require sophisticated, high-speed interceptors, which are often in critically short supply.
Ukraine therefore needs large numbers of missiles with different capabilities to hit military targets in Russia, including production facilities and newly built aircraft hangars at airfields.
What kinds of missiles does Ukraine need? And why doesn’t the West simply supply them to Kyiv?
Kyiv is developing — or seeking from its Western partners — a full range of cruise and ballistic missiles with varying ranges and payloads. Today, only Russia, the United States, China, and Israel possess such an arsenal. Strategic intercontinental ballistic missiles are the only weapons in this arsenal that Ukraine is not currently seeking.
Nor does Ukraine currently plan to develop hypersonic missiles, meaning missiles that can travel at speeds of up to Mach 10 and maneuver within the atmosphere.
Missiles can be broadly categorized by their range and payload, as well as by the type of engine that determines their flight profile.
- Cruise missiles of various ranges can fly and maneuver at low or extremely low altitudes at roughly the speed of sound or, less commonly, several times faster. This gives them an advantage against air-defense systems, which struggle to detect low-flying targets at long distances.
- Ballistic missiles typically travel at several times the speed of sound and follow elliptical trajectories. At the highest point in their flight, they can rise tens or even hundreds of kilometers above the Earth’s surface. Destroying them requires high-speed interceptor missiles. The most effective interceptors, such as the Patriot system’s PAC-3, use kinetic energy to destroy missiles with a direct hit.
By range, the cruise and ballistic missiles Ukraine is seeking can be divided into short- and medium-range weapons. Short-range missiles can travel up to 300 kilometers and strike targets behind Russian lines and in occupied territories. Medium-range missiles can travel 500–1,000 kilometers and strike targets far behind enemy lines.
The Ukrainian military already has Western-made short-range weapons: British Storm Shadow and French SCALP cruise missiles, as well as U.S.-made ATACMS ballistic missiles. Each carries a warhead weighing hundreds of kilograms but has a range of no more than 300 kilometers. Suppliers restrict their use, with U.S. rules tighter than those imposed by Britain and France, which allow regular Ukrainian strikes on Russian border regions. Supplies are also limited.
Several years ago, the United States also committed to begin supplying Ukraine with specially developed air-launched ERAM cruise missiles or glide bombs in the fall of 2026, with a range of up to 450 kilometers. The program’s current status is unknown.
Ukraine faces greater difficulties with long-range missiles. The United States refused to provide Kyiv with Tomahawk missiles, which have a range of more than 1,000 kilometers. Ukraine lacks sufficient ground-based launchers for them anyway; the United States launches Tomahawks from ships and submarines. Ukraine’s Fire Point developed the FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile and began using it in August 2025. But the program has yet to meet the manufacturer’s stated targets. Instead of producing the promised dozens or hundreds of missiles a month, Ukraine launches salvos of only a few missiles every few weeks.
Why is Ukraine’s missile program struggling? And can the Russian military shoot down Flamingos?
There are no definitive answers, but it is clear that Ukraine’s programs to develop and mass-produce cruise and ballistic missiles remain stalled at various stages.
Consider the most advanced program: production of the FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile. Fire Point was expected to produce hundreds of Flamingos a year, allowing Ukraine to strike targets thousands of kilometers inside Russia with a powerful warhead. The Ukrainian military carried out its first test strike in August 2025, targeting buildings at an FSB border post on the boundary between Russian-annexed Crimea and the Russian-occupied part of Ukraine’s Kherson region. Since then, about 10 more hits have been documented in video footage and satellite imagery. Salvos of three to six missiles have typically been launched every three to eight weeks.
Flamingos were last used on September 11, after a long hiatus. The target was the Volgogradpromproekt plant, which produces solid rocket fuel, among other products. The strike was not particularly successful. One missile exploded in an empty lot near the plant, while a second damaged one of its buildings. Once again, the damage fell short of what the missile’s stated specifications would suggest: Reports have said it carries a warhead weighing more than 1,000 kilograms.
Only a few of the 10 Flamingo strikes have been confirmed to have caused serious damage to their targets. One such target was the Skif-M plant in Belgorod, which Ukraine said was part of the supply chain for Russian military aircraft production. Four missiles hit the facility, just 60 kilometers from Kharkiv, causing extensive damage. Strikes on the ballistic-missile plant in Votkinsk, the VNIIR Progress military-navigation systems facility in Cheboksary and the Titan-Barrikady strategic-missile transport systems plant in Volgograd were also successful. A Flamingo strike also damaged an ammunition depot in Kotluban, in the Volgograd region.
Notably, strikes on targets closest to Ukraine were the most successful. This probably means the missiles can evade Russian air defenses more easily over shorter distances. The Flamingos may also be equipped with powerful warheads only when targeting nearby targets; the farther the target, the more fuel the missile must carry, at the expense of warhead weight.
Western and Ukrainian media have already suggested that the Russian military quickly learned to shoot down almost every Flamingo. According to this theory, Russia’s Aerospace Forces use A-50 airborne early-warning and control aircraft to detect the missiles from long range, then deploy combat aircraft to destroy them. Standard ground-based air-defense radar is known to struggle with the same task because Flamingos and similar missiles fly at low altitudes.
The theory is plausible because the Soviet Air Force planned to use precisely this method against U.S. long-range Tomahawk cruise missiles. Flamingos are also almost certainly far more visible to A-50 radar than Tomahawks because of their enormous size and lack of stealth features.
There is no evidence, however, that Russia regularly uses A-50 aircraft to hunt Ukrainian missiles. Although Russia’s Defense Ministry frequently says it has destroyed Flamingos, photographs of wreckage only occasionally support these claims. No statistics exist on how air defenses have actually performed against these missiles in combat.
The main problem is probably the extremely limited number of Flamingos. The small number of missiles in each salvo makes it harder to overwhelm air defenses, and the salvos themselves are exceedingly rare.
Fire Point executives say the main obstacle to mass production is securing engines for the Flamingo. This is a common problem for most countries starting their own missile programs.
The Flamingo uses the AI-25 aircraft turbojet engine, developed during the Soviet era at the Motor Sich plant in Zaporizhzhia. The Czechoslovak L-39 Albatros trainer aircraft, for example, used the same engine. Russian bombing has destroyed most of Motor Sich’s production facilities during the current war.
Fire Point acknowledges that it had to “collect engines from around the world.” The choice of a Motor Sich engine determined the missile’s size — it is twice as long as a Tomahawk, with three times the wingspan — and probably also limited production. Other Ukrainian projects have likewise failed to reach mass production. One example is the effort to adapt the Neptune anti-ship missile, which also uses a Motor Sich engine, to strike ground targets hundreds or thousands of kilometers from its launch site.
Fire Point executives say the company is developing new engines for the Flamingo and plans to begin mass-producing them in 2027.
Another problem is that European countries do not produce small turbojet engines for long-range cruise missiles. Safran makes these engines for the Storm Shadow/SCALP. The company also adapts its TR50 engines for use in the European Union’s only long-range cruise missile, France’s sea-launched Missile de Croisière Naval, or MdCN. The MdCN’s range and payload capacity are one-third lower than those of the Tomahawk.
The U.S. company Williams makes engines for the Tomahawk and supplies engines for European missiles, including Germany’s Taurus cruise missile, which has a considerably longer range than the Storm Shadow/SCALP. Germany, however, continues to refuse to supply Ukraine with these missiles. The United States clearly has no plans to expand exports of Williams engines because it intends to sharply increase its own production of Tomahawks and similar weapons.
European Union countries recognize the problem. Safran and Rolls-Royce plan to develop new engines for the Stratus cruise missile, which will have a range of 1,000 kilometers, and to begin producing them by 2028.
Kyiv will almost certainly face — or may already be facing — similar problems obtaining rocket engines for ballistic missiles. Ukraine’s ballistic missile development has traditionally been handled by Dnipro-based Pivdenmash, which the Russian military has struck dozens of times. Even before Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, the plant had failed to bring its Sapsan/Hrim tactical ballistic missile system, whose missiles have a range of up to 150 kilometers, into mass production. Nor is Europe likely to help: It does not produce engines for short- and medium-range ballistic missiles. Germany, for example, purchases Israeli missile systems.
Fire Point executives say the company is preparing to produce its own engines for the FP-7, its counterpart to ATACMS, and the FP-9, its counterpart to Russia’s Iskander. Engines are not the only foreseeable difficulty. Unlike cruise missile engines, which run on kerosene, Fire Point’s ballistic missiles require solid rocket fuel. The long-range FP-9s, which Ukraine plans to use against targets deep inside Russia, including Moscow, require particularly large amounts of fuel. A plant intended to produce it was being built in Denmark, but its opening has been postponed until 2027.
Long-range ballistic missiles, however, probably pose a greater threat than Flamingo cruise missiles even in small numbers. In theory, the Russian military has counterparts to the Patriot system — the already-deployed S-400 and the S-500, which is still entering service — along with specialized anti-ballistic missile interceptors. The interceptors are said to have capabilities similar to those of the American PAC-3, which has been used successfully against Iskanders and heavy Iranian ballistic missiles. But the Russian equivalents are new weapons that have not been tested in combat and are probably produced in extremely small quantities.
Fire Point has nevertheless managed to supply Ukraine with its most widely used long-range drones, the FP-1/FP-2 series, despite production-scaling problems, corruption allegations, and claims that the company was funded at the expense of other, potentially more advanced projects. The drones have proved effective in attacks on Russian oil refineries and warehouses.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: Intel Reveals 19 Russian Missile, Drone Firms Still Outside International Sanctions
articles.body:
Nineteen Russian companies involved in producing components for missiles, drones, and military aircraft remain untouched by sanctions from any country in the international sanctions coalition, Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) said on Monday.
The companies are among 54 enterprises belonging to or managed by KRET, Russia’s largest radio-electronics holding, and part of the state-owned defense conglomerate Rostec, according to data published by HUR, on its War&Sanctions portal.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The agency said the KRET companies develop and manufacture electronic warfare systems, friend-or-foe identification technology, and onboard electronics for Russian fighter jets and helicopters. Their products also include electric motors, drone navigation and control systems, counterdrone equipment, and remotely operated machine-gun platforms.
The intelligence agency identified several KRET enterprises that it said contribute directly to Russia’s ballistic and hypersonic missile programs.
The Stavropol Signal Plant produces compact S200A1 jamming stations for Russia’s 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles. HUR said the Kaluga Scientific Research Radio Engineering Institute supplies components for the 3B228 electronic protection system used in Russia’s 3M22 Zircon hypersonic missiles.
KRET’s parent organization also covers funding shortages under Russian state defense contracts carried out by companies within the holding, the agency said.
Ukraine Strikes Russian Refinery, Aircraft Plant and Ozon Facility in Massive Overnight Attack
Ukraine has repeatedly called on its partners to impose sanctions not only on major Russian weapons manufacturers, but also on the network of factories producing navigation equipment, electronics, and other specialized components used in Russian weapons.
Among the 19 companies that HUR said remain unsanctioned is Inertial Technologies of Technocomplex, which produces inertial navigation systems for Kh-59M2 and Kh-59M2A guided air-launched missiles and Orion drones.
Another company, the Tambov Elektropribor plant, supplies gyroscopes used in 9M727 cruise missiles launched by the Iskander system, according to the agency.
The Ulan-Ude Instrument-Making Production Association manufactures aircraft automation components, radio navigation equipment, and electric motors for drones, HUR said.
KRET is the 10th Rostec holding whose corporate network Ukraine has published through the War&Sanctions database. The portal now contains information on 764 Rostec-linked enterprises, including identifying details, their functions within Russia’s defense-industrial structure, corporate relationships, and existing sanctions.
HUR called for the remaining companies to be added to international sanctions lists and for governments to strengthen enforcement of existing restrictions.
The agency said sanctions would be effective only if accompanied by controls preventing companies from obtaining foreign technology through intermediaries and by penalties for those helping Russia circumvent restrictions.
You can also highlight the text and press Ctrl + Enter

articles.title: Iran War Has Cost U.S. Nearly $40 Billion and Fueled Inflation, CBO Finds
articles.body:
The war with Iran has cost the U.S. government around $38 billion and contributed to growing inflation, according to a new analysis by the Congressional Budget Office, the nonpartisan agency that provides economic and budget estimates to Congress.
The estimate, which covers the war’s direct costs through Aug. 1, is in line with the Pentagon’s most recent public accounting from July, when Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Congress that the war had cost $37.5 billion. A later report from the Defense Department's inspector general determined that conflict cost an estimated $33.4 billion between February 28 and June 30.
But the new CBO analysis finds that the price of the war is continuing to rise, estimating that the government will spend another $2 billion to $3 billion each month the conflict continues. It also notes that the war has significantly depleted U.S. munitions, including air-defense interceptors, potentially reducing the military’s capacity to respond to another major conflict.
Taken together, the reports are a mixed bag for an Administration that has faced mounting questions over the consequences of a war President Donald Trump initially said would be over in a few weeks. Nearly $40 billion is a substantial sum, Democrats say, particularly at a time when the federal government is carrying more than $40 trillion in gross debt and most Americans consider affordability their top issue heading in the midterms. However, the estimate is considerably lower than some early projections of what the conflict could cost, giving the Administration an argument that the direct military price of the war has so far been more limited than some critics had feared.
The bulk of the spending—$21.7 billion—comes from replacing munitions expenditures, the CBO found, including $13.1 billion for missile defense interceptors and $7.3 billion for land-attack cruise missiles. Other costs include repairing or replacing equipment, increased flying hours for air operations and transportation, and increased fuel costs. However, it does not factor in the cost of damage to U.S. bases and facilities in the Middle East.
The separate report from the Defense Department's inspector general, released a day before the CBO’s, estimated the cost of repairing "physical damage from Iranian strikes" to U.S. diplomatic facilities in Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE at approximately $184 million. It also determined that throughout Operation Epic Fury the U.S. military has spent $22.3 billion on munitions and has lost around $3.7 billion in aircraft and equipment, including four destroyed F-15 fighter jets, seven KC-135 tanker aircraft, a dozen damaged or destroyed KC-135 refueling aircraft, and the loss of up to 30 MQ-9 Reaper drones.
The CBO estimates that replenishing the stockpiles depleted by the war could take five years or longer, suggesting the true cost of the conflict could not be known until the Pentagon spends money to rebuild inventories and restore capabilities that existed before the war. Top Administration officials have repeatedly denied claims of U.S. munitions shortages ahead of the two reports, though the Defense Department urged the defense industry to increase weapons manufacturing last month.
The CBO’s accounting gives members of Congress an independent assessment against which to judge the Trump Administration’s requests to continue funding its military campaign in Iran. As Congress’s nonpartisan fiscal scorekeeper, the CBO’s findings frequently become the benchmark lawmakers use to debate the consequences of tax and spending decisions. However, the CBO report notes that its own estimates “are subject to considerable uncertainty” because it relied on government databases and public reports as the Defense Department did not respond to the CBO’s requests for information.
Democrats are using the findings to argue that the money could have been better spent easing the cost of living. “Donald Trump and Republicans have spent years telling Americans that we cannot afford to help families here at home, but apparently they can find tens of billions of dollars, and potentially much more, for a reckless war that is leaving Americans to pay the price,” Rep. Brendan Boyle, the ranking member of the House Budget Committee, said in a statement. In March, Boyle asked the agency to examine the costs of military operations and the conflict’s effects on prices at home.
Democrats were expecting the cost estimate to be higher than the CBO reached in its report, in part because they believed it would account for the cost of borrowing to finance the war. The $40 billion figure does not include debt service, or additional interest the government could pay over time.
As a result, the CBO estimate is not a final accounting. Much of the information needed to assess the military’s expenditures remains classified or undisclosed, and the eventual bill will also depend on decisions still ahead about troop deployments, replenishing weapons, and rebuilding damaged American bases.
Earlier this summer, the White House requested an additional $67.1 billion for the Pentagon, while House Republicans later advanced a spending framework containing roughly $73 billion in additional funding for defense and intelligence as Democrats pushed back, saying that they lack a clear picture of the war’s duration and ultimate requirements.
Outside Washington, the costs are less abstract. The national average price of regular gasoline reached $4.33 a gallon on Tuesday, up from $4.01 a month earlier. Diesel surpassed $6 a gallon, increasing the expense of moving goods across the country. An Energy Department forecast released last Wednesday projected that gasoline would remain near $4 for the rest of the year.
The CBO expects the war to add roughly 0.5 percentage points to inflation in the price index for personal consumption expenditures in the first quarter of 2027, driven largely by higher energy prices resulting from supply disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.
Inflation reached an annual rate of 3.4% in August, according to figures released Friday, compared with 2.4% in February.
The pace of the war has ebbed and flowed in recent months, with sporadic bursts of fighting and attacks across the region. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted, renewed attacks have threatened commercial vessels, and Houthi strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure have complicated efforts to move oil through alternative routes. The uncertainty has helped push oil prices back above $100 a barrel.
Trump has more recently asked Americans to accept higher prices as the cost of preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. His assurances about the duration of that sacrifice, however, have changed. In March, he described the war as a “short-term excursion” that would end “soon.” Last week, speaking at a Republican convention in Dallas, he said the war would end “immediately after” the midterm elections.

articles.title: Space wars: What 'weapons' does the US have in orbit?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Space wars: What 'weapons' does the US have in orbit?
The US has acknowledged that it has weapons deployed in orbit, offering a rare glimpse into a rapidly developing military competition that could transform space into a new battlefield.
US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said this week that Washington possesses "on-orbit space control weapons", but declined to reveal what the systems are or precisely what they can do.
The disclosure does not mean the US has missiles or bombs circling the Earth ready to strike targets below. "Space control" encompasses capabilities designed to protect American satellites or disrupt, disable and potentially destroy those belonging to an adversary.
But it comes amid an accelerating military competition involving the US, China and Russia - and growing interest from other powers in technologies once largely confined to science fiction.
Israel, meanwhile, has gone further in publicly describing its ambitions. Defence Minister Israel Katz has called for the country to become the first capable of attacking targets on Earth directly from space.
What are space weapons?
Modern militaries are deeply dependent on satellites for communications, navigation, missile warnings, surveillance and targeting.
Destroying or disrupting those systems could therefore blind or severely hamper an adversary without directly attacking its forces.
Space weapons can range from electronic jamming and cyberattacks to lasers, anti-satellite missiles and spacecraft potentially capable of physically disabling other satellites.
China and Russia have invested heavily in counter-space capabilities, while India demonstrated an anti-satellite missile in 2019.
The US and China have also developed manoeuvrable satellites capable of approaching other objects in orbit. Such rendezvous technology has legitimate uses but could theoretically allow one spacecraft to interfere with another.
Is an arms race in space legal?
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibits countries from placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit.
It does not, however, comprehensively ban conventional weapons there, leaving considerable room for technologies barely conceivable when the treaty was written.
Once one major power openly acknowledges deploying military systems in orbit, rivals have an obvious incentive to develop ways of destroying them - and protecting their own.
Who could follow the US into orbit?
China and Russia are Washington's principal competitors, but the technology is no longer solely the preserve of the world's largest powers.
Israel has already made clear that it wants to take the next and potentially more consequential step: attacking Earth from above.
"We also need to operate from up there toward the earth: by disrupting systems, which will happen sooner, and also with kinetic attacks," Katz recently told a conference in Israel.
"Today, no country has the capability for a space-based attack, so I've declared for the defence establishment the need to be first in attack."
Israel already possesses an advanced military space programme, including reconnaissance satellites, while its Arrow 3 missile defence system has intercepted ballistic missiles outside the Earth's atmosphere.
But firing a weapon from Earth into space is fundamentally different from stationing a weapon in orbit capable of striking Earth. Katz's proposal would cross that threshold.
The prospect carries particular significance following Israel's genocidal war on Gaza and its expansion of military operations across the Middle East, including attacks on Lebanon, Syria, Yemen and Iran.
The Israeli defence establishment is reportedly developing a wider programme to strengthen its space capabilities, with around 16 billion shekels ($5.4 billion) in investment contemplated over the next decade.
Could countries really bomb Earth from space?
The concept has existed for decades.
One of the most notorious proposals is nicknamed "Rods from God": placing enormous tungsten projectiles in orbit and releasing them towards targets on Earth, deriving their destructive power from the immense velocity reached during descent.
Versions have been studied in the US, but huge launch costs and engineering difficulties have prevented such a weapon becoming operational.
Reusable rockets and the dramatic fall in the cost of reaching orbit have nevertheless changed calculations about what might eventually be feasible.
Other concepts are closer to existing technology. Satellites could carry interceptors designed to destroy missiles during flight, while lasers, electronic warfare and manoeuvrable spacecraft could attack or disable other space systems.
For now, an important boundary remains. Space can dramatically change the nature of warfare on Earth, but there is no publicly confirmed operational system raining conventional firepower from above.
The significance of Washington's disclosure is not that science-fiction warfare has suddenly arrived. It is that some of the architecture required for a battlefield in orbit is already being assembled.
As the US, China, Russia and increasingly countries such as Israel compete for military advantage above the atmosphere, the question may be shifting from whether space will be weaponised to how far that weaponisation will go.

articles.title: Pentagon inspector general says Iran war has caused weapons shortages
articles.body:
Pentagon inspector general says $22.3B spent on Iran war munitions has caused "strategic inventory shortfalls"
The Defense Department's inspector general revealed Monday that the United States is facing a shortfall in ammunition as a result of its costly war in Iran.
In a first-of-its-kind mandatory report to Congress, the inspector said that between Feb. 28 and June 30, Operation Epic Fury (OEF) had an estimated cost of $33.4 billion, with $22.3 billion of that spent on munitions alone.
"The munitions expenditure on OEF has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply," the report states.
It also lists American military assets lost in the war, including four F-15s destroyed, one F-35 damaged, seven KC-135 tanker aircraft damaged and up to 30 MQ-9 Reaper drones destroyed.
U.S. military ready "for any contingency"?
President Trump has repeatedly brushed off concerns of depleted weapons supplies during the six months of war in the Middle East, saying just two weeks ago that the U.S. has "virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use for this, or for any other War (which is highly unlikely!), that could improbably take place. In addition, we are producing Munitions at levels never seen before. We are stockpiling and preparing for any contingency that could happen."
Mark Cancian of the Center for Strategic and International Studies, when asked if the U.S. has enough weapons to see the Iran war through, told CBS News, "for a war against Iran, the answer is yes. The problem is a war against China. We might be able to provide enough munitions for a month, but getting on to month two or month three or four, that's a great challenge."
Top Pentagon officials had also denied claims of U.S. munition shortages ahead of the inspector general's report dropping on Monday, but Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has been urging the defense industry to increase weapons manufacturing, which Lockheed Martin's Tim Cahill, the head of the company's missile division, describes as "controlled chaos."
"CBS Sunday Morning" was recently granted access to Lockheed Martin's production facility in Arkansas to see work on the latest model of the Patriot air defense missile. The weapon is designed to shoot down incoming ballistic missiles, but each one costs around $4 million, and Lockheed Martin is currently producing 750 of them a year.
Non military Iran-war related costs for U.S. taxpayers
Additionally, the inspector general's report says the U.S. State Department spent $79.2 million responding to "contingencies stemming from the Iran conflict, such as evacuation-related expenses for State personnel and their family members, U.S. citizens, and eligible third-country nationals."
The report put the price tag to repair "physical damage from Iranian strikes" to U.S. diplomatic facilities in Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the UAE at approximately $184 million.
The report notes also that "Iranian strikes damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan," but it does not include costs estimates and says it's not yet clear if all the bases will be repaired, or who would foot the bill.
In April, a Pentagon official estimated in testimony on Capitol Hill the cost of Operation Epic Fury at about $25 billion, but U.S. officials familiar with internal assessments told CBS News soon after that the true price tag of the Iran war at the time was closer to $50 billion.

articles.title: China finally acknowledges its massive missile silo fields
articles.body:
- A CCTV documentary marking the PLA's 99th anniversary gave China's first semi-official acknowledgment of its western missile silo fields, first discovered by satellite imagery in 2021.
- Analyst Robert Rust wrote that the documentary frames the rushed construction as driven by concerns over U.S. missile defense, not a shift from China's no-first-use policy.
Chinese state television has aired the first semi-official acknowledgment of the country’s massive intercontinental ballistic missile silo fields in a documentary marking the 99th anniversary of the People’s Liberation Army.
The program, produced by China’s national broadcaster CCTV, features an army engineer describing years of work building what he calls “houses for missiles” in the country’s western deserts.
The engineer, identified as First Master Sergeant Cui Daohu of an unspecified People’s Liberation Army Rocket Force brigade, says the project came under intense pressure from senior leadership in Beijing to finish on schedule. His account, first reported by the South China Morning Post, marks the first time a state-linked source in China has openly discussed the silo project since satellite images exposed it in 2021.
Those images, analyzed by open-source researchers, showed roughly 320 silos under construction across three fields in western China, plus a related training site at Jilantai. The discovery prompted years of speculation among Western governments and analysts about whether China was abandoning its long-standing “no first use” nuclear policy in favor of a more aggressive posture. Chinese officials have consistently avoided commenting on the silos directly, even as the government reissued a 2025 white paper insisting its arsenal remains sized at “the minimum level necessary for national security.”
The documentary’s framing suggests a different explanation for the rapid construction than a doctrinal shift. Cui describes the urgency as driven by a need to secure China’s ability to strike back after absorbing a nuclear attack, its so-called second-strike capability, rather than by any intent to use nuclear weapons more aggressively. Robert Rust, a China analyst with the Global Security Program at the Union of Concerned Scientists, wrote in an analysis published by the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists that the framing points to concern in Beijing over American missile defense programs, including the Trump administration’s Golden Dome initiative, as a driver of China’s nuclear expansion.
Cui says he was repeatedly pressed on the same question by colleagues at China’s National People’s Congress, where he has served as a military delegate since 2023.
“Will the project be finished on time?”
He describes developing a faster construction method to meet the deadline, including a change to how a core structural component is installed, and says the pressure came from an understanding that the silos needed to “ensure the country can play its strategic trump card,” a phrase commonly used in China to refer to its strategic nuclear missiles.
Rust noted that Cui had appeared in Chinese military media before, in a 2025 series honoring soldiers selected by the Central Military Commission, but that earlier appearance focused on his engineering inventions and made no mention of the silos or their role in national deterrence. The new documentary’s willingness to connect his work explicitly to strategic missiles, he wrote, suggests the silo project itself may now be complete.
The acknowledgment comes as outside researchers continue to debate how large China’s nuclear arsenal could eventually grow. The U.S. Department of War and some independent researchers have projected China could field 1,000 or more warheads by 2030, partly by diverting plutonium from civilian fast-breeder reactors. But those reactors have faced delays, and a 2025 Pentagon report on Chinese military power assessed that the first such unit likely still was not operating. Separate estimates cited by Rust suggest China may already possess enough plutonium to reach 800 to 1,000 warheads without relying on the delayed reactors, raising questions about how the reactor-based growth projections align with the documentary’s portrayal of a leadership in a hurry.
China has continued to display its newer missile systems publicly, including the DF-61 and DF-31BJ intercontinental ballistic missiles shown at a Victory Day parade in Beijing last year. Rust wrote that the shift from total silence to this kind of semi-official signaling could open space for more direct dialogue between Washington and Beijing on reducing nuclear risk, though no such talks have been announced.

articles.title: Hunting down Kalibr missile carriers: how Ukraine has lured Russian frigates into a trap and is gradually taking them out
articles.body:
Hunting down Kalibr missile carriers: how Ukraine has lured Russian frigates into a trap and is gradually taking them out
It was a few years ago that Ukraine's defence forces forced the Russian Navy to flee occupied Sevastopol for the safer port of Novorossiysk. Yet Russian warships have found no sanctuary there either: Ukrainian drones, missiles and uncrewed surface vessels continue to strike terror into the Russian fleet.
On the night of 8-9 September, the defence forces launched another strike on Novorossiysk using drones and domestically-produced Neptune missiles. It is there that the Russian frigates Admiral Essen and Admiral Makarov are based, along with a number of other warships that launch Kalibr missiles on Ukrainian cities.
This remarkable operation is just one part of a major naval campaign Ukraine launched in 2026, bringing together forces from several key security agencies. The goal is to destroy what remains of the Black Sea Fleet and leave it incapable of launching cruise missiles.
Analysts from the Plitka Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT) community have examined the recent strikes on Russian frigates exclusively for Ukrainska Pravda, detailing how Ukraine's defence forces are gradually disarming the Russian Black Sea Fleet in Novorossiysk.
The retreat from Sevastopol
Sevastopol is a strategically important base for Russia's Black Sea Fleet. The Kremlin once cited the need to control Sevastopol, which it described as the "key to control of the Black Sea", as a justification for its occupation of Crimea. Ironically, just a year and a half into the full-scale war, the city began to rapidly lose that strategic importance.
On 13 September 2023, Storm Shadow cruise missiles struck the Sevmorzavod shipyard in Sevastopol. The strike damaged the dock, and the resulting fire destroyed the large landing ship Minsk and the submarine Rostov-on-Don. Nine days later, another strike hit the Black Sea Fleet headquarters.
Satellite imagery from early October showed that Russia's main surface ships armed with cruise missiles had been moved to Novorossiysk, farther away from Ukraine's reach. The frigates Admiral Essen and Admiral Makarov were the most significant examples, as they are two of the Black Sea Fleet's most important warships. The Admiral Makarov has served as the fleet's flagship since the cruiser Moskva was sunk.
The logic behind the redeployment was simple: to move the ships out of range of Ukrainian weapons. Novorossiysk lies more than 300 km from the front line, has a naval base in the Geoport area and is protected by coastal air defence systems.
Geography, however, puts these warships at a disadvantage. Sevastopol Bay is narrow, with an entrance that can easily be blocked by booms. Novorossiysk Bay, by contrast, is wider, and Ukrainian aerial and naval weapons can reach its military harbour and the oil terminal's jetties.
The Admiral Essen and the Admiral Makarov are two of the few Black Sea Fleet ships capable of firing Kalibr cruise missiles. Each is equipped with an eight-cell universal vertical launcher.
Ukraine's defence forces were not going to leave them untouched. In 2026, things took a truly petrifying turn for the two ships.
How Ukraine has attacked Novorossiysk in 2026
In March, the Ukrainian military carried out its first combined strike, sending up to 200 drones into the attack alongside missiles. The Admiral Essen was hit in the middle of the superstructure, and the resulting fire raged for around 18 hours.
Satellite imagery analysis showed that the section housing the ship's defensive and threat-detection systems had been burnt out. The damage affected the PK-10 launchers for passive countermeasures, the TK-25 electronic warfare system, the Fregat-M2M detection radar and the MP-90 Orekh target illumination stations. Without the Orekh stations, the ship's air defence system cannot guide missiles against incoming targets. Ukraine's General Staff officially confirmed that both frigates, the Admiral Essen and the Admiral Makarov, had been damaged.
In April, attack drones from Ukraine's 1st Separate Drone Centre struck the Sheshkharis oil terminal in an operation supported by long-range strike capabilities. The Russian frigates were also hit during the strikes.
Satellite analysis by the OSINT community CyberBoroshno showed that the Essen had taken a hit to the bow that night, around the A-190 100mm gun mount, directly above the MGK-335M Platina hull-mounted sonar system. Its distinctive white radar domes made it possible to identify the ship in satellite images. The Makarov, meanwhile, was recorded as having been hit near its berth and vertical launch systems.
In late May, Novorossiysk came under a two-day raid by the 1st Separate Drone Centre, led by Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, Commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces. This time, the drones came for the Essen from the side rather than from above, skimming in at the waterline despite the ship's air defences.
In August, a major joint operation brought together Defence Intelligence of Ukraine's Department of Active Operations and Department of Unmanned Systems, the Security Service of Ukraine, the Navy and the State Border Guard Service, working in coordination with the General Staff. The forces deployed Palianytsia long-range jet-powered drones, Neptune cruise missiles, uncrewed surface vessels and other assets.
By the end of the night, four vessels had been confirmed hit: both frigates, a Project 21631 Buyan-M-class small missile ship and a Vasily Bykov-class patrol vessel. The strikes also hit a 30N6E radar station belonging to an S-300 air-defence system, the Grushovaya oil depot and an oil-loading jetty.
The August attack appears to have left the frigates critically damaged.
A through-hole is visible on the satellite image of the Makarov, directly over the eight-cell 3S14 universal launcher that fires Kalibr missiles. Because the missile warheads are not normally kept on board in port, the strike did not trigger a detonation. The launcher silo itself, however, was destroyed. Further damage can be seen on the stern superstructure, where the dome of the Kentavr-NM1 secure satellite communications station has been destroyed, and the nearby antenna mast of the Positiv-M1.2 3D radar system has been damaged.
The Essen has taken a different kind of beating. Multiple fires have left the deck around the missile silos blackened with soot, and the PK-10 passive countermeasure launchers and the TK-25 electronic warfare station have been rendered inoperable. The ship remains afloat, and its main weaponry is most likely intact. Four consecutive strikes have nevertheless compromised its close-in defences and detection systems.
The image shows the extent of the damage, but not how deep it goes. A hole in the deck around the launch system is clearly visible. Satellite imagery cannot reveal whether the launch system module beneath the Makarov's deck has been destroyed or whether the damage is limited to the structures above it. The same uncertainty applies to the Essen's superstructure: it is impossible to tell how extensively its interior has been burnt out. Neither the Russian side nor the Ukrainian authorities has released a detailed damage assessment.
That said, the damaged launch tubes could seriously affect the ships' ability to launch Kalibr missiles on Ukraine. The 3S14 is not a standalone structure that can simply be removed and replaced. It is a module integrated into the hull. On Project 11356R frigates such as the Makarov and the Essen, it is recessed into the bow, between the 100mm A-190 gun mount and the superstructure.
The size of the module gives an idea of just how difficult it could be to repair. The Russian export brochure for the 3S-14E launcher lists its height at 9,580 mm – almost ten metres down into the hull – its length at 3,760 mm, and its width at 1,970 mm. The module weighs 14,000 kg and has eight missile launch positions. In other words, this is not a unit that can simply be lifted out by crane from any quay.
In theory, the module is repairable. The deck above it would first have to be opened up so that the launch system could be accessed from above and the upper-deck structures could be cut through. The module would then have to be removed and replaced using cranes capable of handling its weight. All systems linked to the launch mechanisms would also have to be rebuilt.
It sounds like a complex operation, but one that the Russians are capable of carrying out. The Black Sea Fleet has historically relied on the shipyards of Sevastopol for major repairs. However the port has become too dangerous, which forced the frigates to flee several years ago. Novorossiysk was built as a home port, not a repair centre, and has very limited facilities for dockyard work of this scale. As a result, even a partially damaged ship can be effectively out of action for the long term: there is simply nowhere to carry out the necessary repairs.
Interestingly, the August attack hit more than just the two frigates. The Essen and the Makarov stole the headlines, but a comprehensive analysis of the imagery by the Exilenova+ community shows that the damage in the harbour was far more widespread. Traces of damage were also found on five other vessels, each playing a specific role at the base:
- A minesweeper that ensures safe passage out of the bay and provides mine protection for the navigation channels
- The Priazovye, a medium-sized intelligence-gathering vessel responsible for signals intelligence and air surveillance for the Black Sea Fleet
- A Vasily Bykov-class patrol vessel equipped with a Tor-M2KM containerised air-defence system
- The Viktor Cherokov, a naval arms transport vessel used to carry munitions
- A dry cargo vessel near the outer harbour wall; its type is difficult to determine from the photograph.
The Exilenova+ analysis also pinpoints the home port of the 4th Submarine Brigade, which operates the Varshavyanka-class submarines that carry most of the Black Sea Fleet's Kalibr missiles. There are no visible signs of damage to the submarines in the images. Even so, the fact that the area was targeted suggests that the strike zone encompasses the entire base rather than being limited to individual berths.
The strikes have not stopped – the latest came only a few days ago. On the night of 8–9 September, Ukrainian forces struck the Novorossiysk naval base again. Defence Intelligence of Ukraine said operators from its Department of Active Operations took part in a joint deep-strike operation that targeted the base's infrastructure and the frigate Admiral Essen. A fire broke out on the ship's superstructure. An analysis by Ukrainian military outlet Defense Express found that the strike hit the forward part of the superstructure, destroying the bridge and several control stations for the ship's weapons and equipment.
On the same day, the Ukrainian Navy said the weapon used in the attack was a domestically produced Neptune missile. The following day, it clarified that the missile was the extended-range version, known as the Long Neptune.
The Navy stated: "Satellite imagery confirms that the ship's upper superstructure was hit. The damage sustained prevents the ship from carrying out combat missions. The missile carrier will require lengthy and costly repairs."
Why stay in the line of fire?
The obvious question is: if the ships are attacked so frequently, why not take them out into the open sea? The answer is that leaving the harbour would expose them to Ukrainian unmanned surface vessels and anti-ship missiles.
This was how the Russian Navy lost the cruiser Moskva, the large amphibious assault ship Tsezar Kunikov and several other vessels between 2022 and 2024. While in port, the ships at least had the protection of coastal air defences and access to a nearby repair base. In 2026, however, even the ports have become dangerous: the harbour is fully exposed to Ukrainian strikes.
Russians even captured Kalibr launches directly from the harbour on video. The roofline of a distinctive high-rise building and a lower landmark visible in the footage were identified on a satellite image. Their lines of sight intersect at 44.7072, 37.7798, revealing the filming location on the eastern shore of Tsemeskaya Bay. The military harbour lies directly across the water.
In other words, the Russian missile carriers are firing from berths inside the city harbour, under the cover of residential neighbourhoods, rather than moving out to firing positions in the open sea.
Conclusions
A flagship without a strike capability. The Admiral Makarov has become the de facto flagship of the Black Sea Fleet since the Moskva cruiser was sunk in April 2022. Damage to its 3S14 launch system and the destruction of its satellite communications station have stripped it of both capabilities: it can no longer launch Kalibr missiles or coordinate operations. Restoring these capabilities will require a factory-level repair.
The redeployment to Novorossiysk has failed to provide the safety the Russians were seeking. The ships were moved from Sevastopol to put them beyond the reach of Ukrainian strikes. Yet in 2026, combined attacks have repeatedly reached them at their berths, more than 300 km from the front line – five times in just six months. There is nowhere else for them to retreat to in the Black Sea. It is a closed basin.
The missile carriers have turned into floating batteries. Ships built to operate at sea are now firing from the harbour walls because venturing out is more dangerous than staying moored. This works as long as the harbour remains operational. The Black Sea Fleet's strike capability has become tied to a single point on the map – and that point is already under fire.
This story was produced by the Plitka OSINT community specifically for Ukrainska Pravda.
Translated by Artem Yakymyshyn
Edited by Susan McDonald

articles.title: Why US is pushing a halt to Russia-Ukraine energy strikes in the war's fifth year
articles.body:
Washington, DC — Immediately after US President Donald Trump announced on Monday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt strikes on each other's energy targets — which he claimed were causing a global diesel squeeze — reactions from Moscow and Kiev were swift but measured.
Russia described the proposal as a "good idea", without confirming whether it would halt attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities. Kiev pledged "de-escalatory steps" provided that "our American partners succeed in securing a real readiness from Russia".
Both sides continued to exchange strikes following Trump's announcement, with Russia reportedly attacking petrol stations in Kiev and Ukraine claiming to have struck a Russian oil refinery.
With global oil prices climbing again amid shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and growing risks in the Red Sea, analysts note the US president's announcement is driven more by the oil shock from the fighting in the Middle East than by anything else.
"Yes. This is Trump's motivation," Arkady Moshes, director of the EU's Eastern Neighbourhood and Russia programme at the Finnish Institute of International Affair, tells TRT World.
"But this will have little bearing on Moscow which gains financially from the high energy prices," Moshes argues.
Trump insists that the Russia-Ukraine war and not the US war on Iran, is driving up fuel costs for Americans who vote in crucial midterm elections in November. Opinion polls indicate that the US war on Iran is unpopular. Meanwhile, inflation in the country remains elevated — and the Democratic Party is seeking to capitalise on politically.
Months of Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure have caused domestic fuel rationing and an export ban, further tightening global markets already strained by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
Meanwhile, attacks by the Houthi group near the Bab al Mandab Strait have jeopardised commercial shipping in the southern Red Sea, further exacerbating global oil supply pressures.
However President Trump has claimed that Kiev was "hurting the world" with its strikes on Moscow's diesel facilities.
"The World's Diesel price rise is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War, not Iran," Trump said on Monday as he announced an agreement between Ukraine and Russia to halt strikes on energy infrastructure.
When it comes to the Ukraine-Russia conflict, says Moshes, President Trump's statements "do not correspond to reality."
"But even if this were true, this would be one step down the escalation ladder," he says, but adds the situation would still be nowhere near a lasting truce, noting that since 2014 not a single ceasefire agreement has held even for several days.
Fuel supply crunch
Past US-brokered energy pauses have seen limited success: one in January 2026 lasted only a few days, while another 30-day proposal in 2025 never fully materialised. Reports indicate that Russia remains reluctant to ease winter pressure on Ukraine.
US average retail diesel prices rose above $6 a gallon for the first time last week. Russia has restricted diesel exports after Ukrainian drone strikes damaged its refineries, tightening an already strained global supply that has been squeezed by the war with Iran and recent attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure.
Experts cited by The New York Times say tensions involving Iran drove price rises, with US diesel up 65 per cent, while Russian and Middle Eastern exports fell by roughly 90 and 75 per cent.
An analysis by the Reuters news agency concluded that even a sustained halt to attacks on Russian oil refineries would not promptly reverse the ongoing fuel supply crunch.
According to the International Energy Agency, Ukrainian drones have struck a Russian refinery on average every three days, with repair efforts facing severe logistical obstacles.
