Rachel Ziemba, adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, a Washington-based think tank, told Bloomberg that "the thought here is that a stop in attacking refineries would give Russia time to repair and reduce risk of further outages."
"But if Gulf channels are still blocked it won't help much."
October talks
Trump has been pursuing an end to the Russia-Ukraine war, despite his pledge to halt the conflict on the first day of his term.
Recently, his special envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, met Russian President Vladimir Putin and later Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, but the talks yielded no breakthrough.
The Kremlin described the talks positively, while US officials assessed potential next steps. However, fundamental territorial disputes remain unresolved.
Zelenskyy said US officials presented "decent ideas" for peace, emphasising that diplomatic efforts must deliver tangible results to end the war, now in its fifth year.
Mikhail Alexseev, a political science professor at San Diego State University, tells TRT World that Washington's failure to designate Russia as the "aggressor", expand support for Ukraine, and impose further sanctions on Moscow makes this diplomacy unlikely to succeed.
"Absent those conditions, no diplomacy would succeed, and only the battlefield would decide the war," argues Alexseev, adding, continuing the talks merely for the sake of it may be interpreted by Moscow as a sign of weakness from Washington and its allies.
Moscow insists that Kiev cede claimed territories, particularly in the Donbass, and abandon its ambition to join NATO.
Meanwhile, Kiev rejects formally surrendering territory to Russia and insists that any settlement must safeguard Ukraine's sovereignty and defensive capabilities.
Even as the war continues, both sides have signalled their readiness for US-mediated talks tentatively set for October 2026.
"We are preparing for October," said Kyrylo Budanov, head of Ukraine's Defence Intelligence, last week. "We do not rule out such a possibility. We are talking about the foreseeable future," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov added.
However, a diplomatic breakthrough remains unlikely without a significant shift in strategic leverage.
Europe and US role
Then there is Europe.
In peace negotiations, Moscow does not regard Europe as an autonomous player, believing European involvement would only complicate the process.
Trump — for better or worse — appears to share that perspective, says Moshes of the Finnish Institute of International Affair.
"He [Trump] has achieved what was important for him — Europe paying for American weapons delivered to Ukraine. Europeans may not be happy, but they can hardly do anything about it," argues Moshes.
"The imminent risk is that no one will drive the process: Russia will veto European involvement, whereas Washington may withdraw once more."
Europe remains vital to Ukraine, and vice versa, but alignment between the US and Europe on the conflict is critical. Any strategic divergence between the Western allies ultimately benefits Moscow.
From a European vantage point, security guarantees and mutual trust are paramount to prevent any disadvantageous agreement from being imposed upon Ukraine.
"We already saw this kind of understanding most likely reached at the Alaska summit, and subsequent events demonstrated that Ukrainian resilience combined with European support provides Ukraine with significant safeguards," says Alexseev.
Another indirect safeguard lies in the White House's transactional approach to foreign policy, with the procurement of American armaments serving as an influential incentive, he adds.
Moshes emphasises that confidence in Washington as an impartial mediator has waned over time.
He says Kiev remains wary of potential US-Russia economic compromises, while Moscow expressed dissatisfaction following the Anchorage summit when Washington declined to endorse terms reflecting Russian priorities.
"That occurred prior to the US-Iranian conflict, which continues to consume significant military and diplomatic resources of the United States."

articles.title: What Greece and Israel's defence deal means for the Middle East
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Achilles Shield: What Greece and Israel's defence deal means for the Middle East
Greece's decision to spend roughly €3 billion on an Israeli-built integrated air-defence network is about more than adding another layer of protection to its armed forces.
The proposed “Achilles Shield” comes as Greece’s relationship with Turkey worsens, while Athens deepens ties with Tel Aviv.
Greek proponents see Israeli technology as a way to modernise Greece's defences against drones, aircraft, and missiles. Critics, however, warn that the deal could bind Athens more closely to Israel at a time when Tel Aviv is increasingly isolated worldwide because of its rogue actions in Gaza and elsewhere.
There are also questions to raise about whether systems developed for Israel’s very different geography and security environment are right for Greece.
The result is a major defence purchase with implications well beyond the battlefield. The deal could significantly impact Greece’s relationships with Turkey, Israel, the United States, and fellow European Union (EU) members.
A critical question relates to whether Athens is buying an integrated shield for its territory, or a deeper strategic commitment to Israel.
Turkey the central factor in Greece's defence planning
For all the uncertainty surrounding Greece's security environment, Turkey remains the central reference point in Athens's defence planning. The two NATO members have spent decades at odds over the Aegean, Cyprus, maritime boundaries, and competing territorial claims, even as periods of diplomatic calm have periodically reduced tensions.
Tony Rigopoulos, an Athens-based journalist and political analyst, sees the Greek-Turkish rivalry as the most important explanation for this historic defence deal.
“Greece’s main and long-lasting threat comes from Turkey; even in periods when tensions were low, Greek governments have been using the ‘Turkey card’ to justify expensive defence deals,” he told The New Arab.
“In the case of the Achilles Shield deal, the conservative government of the ‘New Democracy’ party and its friendly media exhibited very low interest in analysing any potential threat from Iran and focused once more on Turkey.”
As Rigopoulos explained, comments from Turkish officials about “taking” Greek islands and the upcoming vote on the “Blue Homeland” law in Turkey’s parliament are, from Athens’ perspective, a grave threat to Greece’s sovereignty.
Dr George Tzogopoulos, a lecturer at the European Institute of Nice (Cife), offers a less exclusively Turkey-focused interpretation. In his view, Greece is modernising its armed forces because its strategic environment has become more unpredictable, rather than because Athens expects an imminent confrontation with Turkey.
That distinction matters. Greece may regard Turkey as its principal long-term military challenge while recognising that the immediate security environment has also changed. The US-Israeli war on Iran, for example, creates risks for Greece even though Athens maintains positive relations with Tehran.
Greece hosts important American military facilities and is closely aligned with Washington, potentially making it vulnerable to conflicts in which it is not a direct participant.
Stavroula Pabst, an independent analyst, similarly cautions against reducing the deal to Greek-Turkish tensions. While Athens is concerned about Turkey’s expanding military capabilities, she points out that both countries have repeatedly expressed an interest in managing their disputes through dialogue.
“Achilles Shield” may therefore be less a preparation for war with Turkey than an attempt by Greece to hedge against a range of threats.
“I am wary of saying this is primarily driven by Turkey but am forced to acknowledge this is a major factor for Athens. I believe Athens feels threatened by Turkey’s advancements in defence as of late, where Turkey is putting significant effort into fielding weapons like ICBMs, and armed drones,” she told The New Arab.
“But even as this occurs, I also want to point out that there are reasons to believe level heads will prevail here: Greece and Turkey have repeatedly made it clear that they would like to work on their grievances with each other [with the Cyprus issue being an example] among themselves. I don't know if these weapons deals will change that,” added Pabst.
Nevertheless, the Turkish question remains unavoidable. The more sophisticated Ankara’s weapons become, the greater the pressure on Athens to ensure its own defence apparatus does not fall behind. “Achilles Shield” can therefore be understood both as a response to Turkey and as part of a broader effort to preserve Greek options in a less predictable regional environment.
Can Israel's air-defence model work across Greece's islands?
Israeli defence companies have been able to market their systems to foreign governments on the basis that they have been used repeatedly in real-world conflicts, including against drones and missiles.
For Greece, which is seeking to rapidly modernise its defences, that experience is potentially a powerful selling point. Dr Tzogopoulos argues that Israel’s technological expertise and battlefield experience are precisely what make its systems attractive, even though many details of “Achilles Shield,” including the precise systems to be deployed and their locations, remain unknown.
Dr Ioannis E. Kotoulas, an adjunct lecturer in geopolitics at the University of Athens, similarly argues that Israel’s battle experiences are particularly valuable for Greece because of limitations within Europe itself.
“Israel’s battlefield experience and technical expertise, especially concerning air and missile defences, is very important for Greece since the EU has not yet managed to develop similar levels of technical assistance and suffers from bureaucratic obstacles. This is a fast way to obtain advanced defence capabilities,” he told The New Arab.
But the meaning of “battle-tested” is worth addressing. Israel’s recent experience against Iran does not necessarily demonstrate that its air-defence architecture could independently withstand a comparable attack.
In Rigopoulos’ assessment, Israeli defences required substantial assistance from the United States and other allies to deal with large numbers of Iranian missiles and drones. He also points to a fundamental difference between Israel and Greece’s environments.
Turkey and Greece share land and maritime borders, while Iran and Israel are separated by thousands of miles and several countries. Turkey’s ability to produce large numbers of relatively inexpensive drones and missiles could therefore present a different challenge from the one for which Israeli systems were designed.
Geography creates another complication. Greece’s territory is dispersed across hundreds of islands, with many in the Aegean and some considerably closer to the Turkish mainland than to mainland Greece. A centralised architecture that makes sense for Israel may require significant adaptation to work across Greece’s fragmented territory. Some Greek defence specialists question whether a network of smaller, geographically distributed systems might be more appropriate.
This highlights the danger of treating combat experience as a guarantee of effectiveness in a different strategic environment. The relevant question is whether Israeli systems can be integrated into Greece's existing defences and adapted to its geography and Turkey’s military capabilities.
Greece has presented the project as an integrated national air-defence network capable of responding to ballistic missiles, aircraft and drones. However, the precise architecture, deployment timetable and relationship between its various systems have not been fully disclosed.
The system’s effectiveness will therefore depend heavily on interoperability. Greece already operates a mixture of American, European and other weapons systems, and the value of a new shield will depend on how effectively those systems can communicate.
Israeli technology can be interoperable, but the details of Greece’s plans have not been made public. The same uncertainty applies to command and control. An integrated network could give Greek commanders a more comprehensive picture of incoming threats and allow different defensive systems to respond in coordination. However, its effectiveness will ultimately depend on how much information can be shared and how quickly decisions can be made.
There is also a more fundamental question about technological sovereignty. Rigopoulos has drawn attention to comments by Moshe Patel, director-general of Israel’s Missile Defence Organisation, concerning Greece’s access to the system’s source code and Israel’s continuing role in support and maintenance.
If Athens lacks full access to the underlying software and remains dependent on Israel for substantial technical support, the meaning of “national” control over the shield becomes more complicated.
Foreign military systems routinely require supplier support, so dependence is not unusual. But the more central “Achilles Shield” becomes to Greece’s national defence, the more significant that dependence could become.
That question also illustrates why the deal is more than a conventional arms purchase. An integrated defence architecture involves software, command systems, training, maintenance, upgrades and long-term technical cooperation.
If “Achilles Shield” becomes deeply embedded in Greece's military infrastructure, Israel could consequently become an indispensable partner in Greek national defence for decades. The strategic significance of the agreement may therefore lie as much in the relationship it creates as in the weapons Greece receives.
Greece faces a growing divide over its ties with Israel
The strategic case for closer cooperation with Israel exists alongside a significant political problem: Greek public opinion toward Israel has deteriorated sharply amid the Gaza genocide.
Polling data from February-May 2026 shows 65 percent of Greeks expressing an unfavourable view of Israel, while there have been hundreds of pro-Palestinian demonstrations across the country since October 2023.
Pabst expects substantial opposition to “Achilles Shield,” arguing that the Greek public has broadly opposed closer cooperation with Israel because of its conduct in Gaza. The contrast between public sentiment and government policy is striking. While Athens has continued to deepen its relationship with Israel, many Greeks appear increasingly uncomfortable with a country whose technology will now play a significant role in their national defence.
Yet, opposition to Israel does not necessarily translate into opposition to the defence relationship. Dr Tzogopoulos makes an important distinction between attitudes toward the current Israeli government and perceptions of Israel as a useful strategic and technological partner.
“Greek citizens are concerned about the future trajectory of Greek-Turkish relations. In that regard, closer collaboration with Israel, which goes beyond the Achilles Shield, is considered important in the context of the national interest,” he told The New Arab.
“The image of the current Israeli government in Greece is being deteriorated because of the Gaza war, but this is different from considering Israel a partner in the process of modernising armed forces - both at the political and public opinion level,” noted Dr Tzogopoulos.
Rigopoulos similarly describes the relationship as something that parts of Greek society may regard as a “necessary evil”, essentially constituting a partnership that is politically uncomfortable but difficult to reject if believed to strengthen Greece’s security.
That tension could become increasingly important as the defence relationship deepens. Arms agreements are unusually durable forms of foreign policy, involving large financial commitments and creating networks of military, technological, and institutional cooperation that can last for decades.
Pabst argues that this could eventually make it more difficult for Greece, or even other European governments, to distance themselves from Israel or hold its government accountable for its actions. The more Greek defence planning depends on Israeli technology, the greater the political cost of disrupting the relationship.
'Achilles Shield' entrenches Greece's partnership with Israel
Domestic politics aside, “Achilles Shield” is the latest step in a Greece-Israel relationship that has deepened for more than a decade, alongside increasingly close ties with Cyprus. Joint military exercises, energy cooperation, and defence links have given the relationship a strategic dimension, while deteriorating Israeli-Turkish relations have made the Greek-Israeli partnership more conspicuous.
From Athens' perspective, cooperation with Israel offers access to advanced military technology while strengthening ties with a regional actor whose interests overlap with Greece’s on several issues. “Achilles Shield” is therefore not an isolated procurement decision but another piece of a broader Eastern Mediterranean security network.
Dr Kotoulas describes that network in more explicitly strategic terms, arguing that “Achilles Shield is an important upgrade of Greek defence capabilities and functions as a factor of deterrence for any Turkish regional aspirations.” He also noted that “the network of Greece-Cyprus-Israel in the Mediterranean creates an important military counterweight to any regional hegemonic attempts”.
It would nevertheless be premature to describe this network as a formal anti-Turkish alliance. Dr Tzogopoulos rejects the idea that regional alliances are necessarily forming, arguing instead that states are building partnerships around overlapping interests.
Israel’s disagreements with Turkey are also different from Greece's: Israel's disputes with Ankara centre heavily on Syria and the Palestinian question, while Greece's concern the Aegean, maritime boundaries and Cyprus.
“Israel will not help Greece in a Greek-Turkish crisis,” he told The New Arab, adding that he will “not be surprised if Israel and Turkey will be able to better manage their relationship in the future”.
Even without a formal alliance, however, defence agreements, exercises, intelligence relationships, and military technology can alter perceptions of the regional balance of power. “Achilles Shield” adds another layer to that process, making Greece and Israel more deeply connected militarily and giving Turkey another reason to watch their relationship closely.
The implications of “Achilles Shield” extend beyond Greece, Israel, and Turkey. For the United States, stronger Greek air defences are broadly compatible with Washington's interest in strengthening the military capabilities of a key ally on NATO's southeastern flank.
At the same time, Washington has its own defence industry to consider, and greater Greek reliance on Israeli systems could mean fewer opportunities for American weapons manufacturers. Greece’s broader modernisation strategy, which also involves military cooperation with the United States, France, and Italy, suggests that Athens is attempting to diversify its partnerships rather than replace one major supplier with another.
Dr Kotoulas sees the strategic relationship from an Israeli perspective as even broader. “Greece along with Cyprus function as the strategic depth of Israel in the Eastern Mediterranean,” he told The New Arab.
For NATO, the equation is similarly complicated. A more capable Greek military could strengthen the alliance's southeastern defences, particularly against drones and missiles. But “Achilles Shield” also raises questions about interoperability and dependence on a non-NATO supplier.
Those questions become more significant if the Israeli system is eventually integrated deeply into Greece's wider command-and-control infrastructure. The system’s value to NATO will depend not only on what it can intercept, but also on how effectively it can communicate with the alliance's existing networks and other weapons systems.
The EU faces a different dilemma. Greece's growing dependence on Israeli defence technology comes at a time when European governments remain divided over Israel's conduct in Gaza. Pabst's concern is that arms agreements can create relationships that are much harder to unwind than ordinary diplomatic partnerships.
If Israeli technology becomes critical to Greek or wider European security, governments seeking to place political or economic pressure on Israel could face an additional constraint: the practical consequences of disrupting an increasingly important defence relationship.
Turkey, meanwhile, is likely to view the deal with suspicion even if it does not regard “Achilles Shield” as evidence of an imminent Greek-Israeli military alliance. The system could contribute to an arms competition in the Eastern Mediterranean if Ankara concludes that Greece is acquiring capabilities specifically intended to offset Turkish military advantages.
Dr Tzogopoulos, however, stresses that conflict is not inevitable. Greek-Turkish communication channels remain open, and both countries have an interest in preventing disputes from escalating into a military confrontation.
The United Arab Emirates and other regional actors will also be watching the Greece-Israel relationship, particularly against the backdrop of the intensifying US-Iran confrontation. But perhaps the most important geopolitical implication is the one that is easiest to overlook, which is the fact that “Achilles Shield” could make Athens’ relationship with Tel Aviv substantially more difficult to reverse.
Once a country relies on another state for critical military technology, maintenance, upgrades, and expertise, the relationship acquires an institutional momentum of its own. Therefore, the significance of the deal may lie in the possibility that Israel is becoming embedded in the architecture of Greek national defence.
What exactly is Greece buying with 'Achilles Shield'?
“Achilles Shield” is ultimately difficult to understand as a response to any single threat. Turkey remains the most important long-term concern in Greek defence planning, but the US-Israeli war on the Islamic Republic has demonstrated broader risks arising from Greece’s position in a volatile region and its close relationship with Washington.
At the same time, the system’s suitability for Greece remains tied to unanswered questions about geography, interoperability, effectiveness, and technological sovereignty.
What is clearer is that the €3 billion project represents more than a conventional arms purchase. It is another step in Greece's military modernisation and toward a deeper, potentially more durable strategic relationship with Israel. That relationship may provide valuable technology and capabilities, but it also creates dependencies with political consequences well beyond the battlefield.
The central question, then, is what kind of security architecture Greece is building, and how much of that architecture is Athens prepared to place in the hands of a foreign partner seen throughout much of the world as a rogue state guilty of genocide?
In an Eastern Mediterranean already defined by overlapping rivalries and shifting partnerships, the answer could prove highly complicated.
Giorgio Cafiero is the CEO of Gulf State Analytics.
Follow him on Twitter: @GiorgioCafiero
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Grossi’s toxic legacy: Greenlighting aggression, smearing Iran
articles.body:
Grossi’s toxic legacy: Greenlighting aggression, smearing Iran
In a brazen violation of diplomatic norms, Austria barred Iran’s nuclear chief from IAEA summit due to US pressure
TEHRAN — The head of the UN nuclear watchdog has once again seized the international stage to smear Iran and advance a hostile agenda dictated by the US, turning an ostensibly technical body into a political instrument of Western coercion.
Addressing the 70th regular session of the General Conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) in Vienna on Monday, Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi used his platform to deliver an alarmist, distorted narrative regarding Tehran’s nuclear activities, conveniently glossing over the blatant military aggression waged by the United States and Israel against Iranian territory.
Grossi sought to depict the disruption of technical cooperation as an arbitrary move by Tehran rather than the natural, security-mandated consequence of unprovoked foreign military attacks against sovereign, safeguarded facilities.
“The situation regarding the Agency’s oversight of Iran’s nuclear programme deteriorated in 2026. There were renewed attacks on that country at the end of February. We had to withdraw our inspectors and apart from an inspection of the Bushehr nuclear power plant in June, we have not conducted any in-field verification activities in Iran for more than six months,” Grossi said.
By framing the halt in inspections without holding the aggressors accountable for striking peaceful nuclear infrastructure, he brazenly inverted the roles of victim and perpetrator. “It is well over a year since the Agency lost continuity of knowledge in relation to the previously declared inventories of LEU and HEU enriched up to 60% U-235 at the declared nuclear facilities affected by the attacks of June 2025.”
Rather than condemning the catastrophic precedent of Washington and Tel Aviv bombing sites under full IAEA safeguards, Grossi predictably weaponized the aftermath of those very airstrikes to manufacture an artificial crisis and heighten international hysteria against Tehran.
Grossi noted, “The Agency’s lack of information about this nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of serious proliferation concern and needs to be addressed with the utmost urgency.”
In an obvious bid to amplify Western talking points and lend unwarranted international legitimacy to coercive measures against Iran’s peaceful civilian nuclear infrastructure, the director general went on to issue sweeping warnings about the erosion of the global non-proliferation framework.
He said, “I warned last year that the global nuclear non-proliferation regime was coming under strain from more than one angle. Discussions about whether to acquire nuclear weapons continue to surface even in countries in good standing with their obligations under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.”
Grossi’s complicity exposed
Grossi’s inflammatory rhetoric in Vienna is not an isolated incident, but part of a systematic, long-standing pattern of subservience to Western geopolitical designs.
Crucially, just one day before the outbreak of the 12-day war in June 2025—in which Israel and the US launched aggressive military strikes against Iran—the IAEA Board of Governors adopted a confrontational, anti-Iran resolution. Grossi’s politically biased reporting and calculated timing served as the catalyst, directly laying the political and diplomatic groundwork for the US-Israeli war of aggression on Iran.
By systematically echoing Washington’s demands, refusing to condemn the bombing of safeguarded nuclear sites, and presenting routine technical matters as acute international threats, Grossi has effectively acted as an accomplice to US-Israeli crimes against the Iranian nation. Analysts widely view Grossi’s desperate drive to appease the White House and European powers as a calculated maneuver to secure Western backing for his personal political ambitions, specifically his campaign to succeed António Guterres as the next United Nations Secretary-General.
US dictates visa ban to silence Iran
Grossi’s diatribe coincided with an overt, orchestrated Western maneuver to silence Iran’s voice at the Vienna gathering. Mohammad Eslami, the Head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI), was barred from attending the IAEA General Conference after the host country, Austria, capitulated to direct pressure from the Trump administration.
US officials made no effort to conceal their heavy-handed meddling in the affairs of an international body. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told reporters in Vienna that Washington had actively opposed the participation of the Iranian delegation.
“He’s a sanctioned individual and we don’t want sanctioned individuals evading their sanctions. He asked for a waiver of the sanctions and it was denied,” Wright said.
Echoing this obstructionist stance, Preston Wells Griffith, the US ambassador to the UN in Vienna, confirmed that Austria’s exemption request was blocked after Washington lodged an objection with the committee.
“While we are focused on a diplomatic solution to the challenges posed by Iran’s nuclear program, we could not allow a UN-designated official to travel … without any meaningful cooperation on nuclear safeguards,” he said.
Eslami had been formally scheduled to address the global gathering to expose Western double standards and clarify Iran’s legal positions before Austria bowed to Washington’s diktat and denied him entry.
Iran condemns host-country violation
The brazen violation of diplomatic norms sparked immediate outrage in Tehran. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmael Baghaei said in his weekly press briefing on Monday that Austria’s move to deny a visa to Eslami for a trip to Vienna was “completely unjustified,” stressing that the Austrian government should have issued entry visas to the Iranian delegation.
He confirmed that Iran’s Foreign Ministry had summoned Austria’s chargé d’affaires to formally convey the Islamic Republic’s strong protest over the decision to the European country.
“They are seeking to prevent Iran’s voice from reaching the world. Austria’s claim that it took this action under US pressure does not absolve the host government of responsibility,” the Iranian spokesperson emphasized.
In Vienna, Reza Najafi, Iran’s ambassador and permanent representative to international organizations, mounted a fierce legal defense against the discriminatory move.
Najafi said preventing the head of the Iranian delegation from attending the conference violated the principle of sovereign equality enshrined in Article IV, Paragraph C of the IAEA Statute. He said the principle guarantees equal rights for all members and their enjoyment of the benefits of membership.
The envoy said the move also undermined Iran’s right to participate in the General Conference through a representative of its own choosing and weakened the privileges required for representatives to perform their duties under the IAEA Statute and the Agreement on the Privileges and Immunities of the IAEA.
Equal representation and participation are treaty-based membership rights that “cannot and must not be undermined,” he said.
Najafi further described the action as a violation of Austria’s obligations as host country under the IAEA Headquarters Agreement between Austria and the Agency.
He said the agreement requires Austria to take all necessary measures to facilitate the entry of representatives of member states into Austrian territory and issue their visas as promptly as possible. The obligation, he stressed, is binding and unconditional for representatives holding valid credentials.
Najafi warned that preventing the head of a delegation from attending the agency’s highest policy-making body undermined the conference itself, stressing that anything short of corrective action would set a dangerous precedent for all IAEA members.
The unlawful maneuver by Vienna and Washington drew sharp condemnation from other international delegations. The Russian ambassador to the UN in Vienna, Mikhail Ulyanov, said Austria had “grossly violated” its obligations as host nation of the IAEA.
Western nations had “unleashed a genuine campaign of visa-related abuses to settle scores with countries they deem to be undesirable,” he said.
Manufactured crises and failed coercion
The theatrical confrontation in Vienna unfolds as the Western bloc rapidly escalates its campaign of maximum pressure. Earlier this month, the UN atomic watchdog’s board adopted a resolution reporting Iran to the UN Security Council for the first time in 20 years because of its failure to cooperate, citing a long-running investigation into uranium traces detected by inspectors at undeclared sites. The hostile resolution was tabled by the UK, France, Germany, and the US.
This dangerous move followed the reckless decision last year by France, Britain, and Germany (the E3) to trigger the so-called snapback mechanism, an unlawful push designed to automatically reinstate expired United Nations sanctions against Iran over its peaceful nuclear program.
In response to the criminal aggression of June 2025, when the US struck Iran’s nuclear sites during the 12-day war, Iran hasn’t given IAEA inspectors access to the affected sites. Tehran maintains that an international agency cannot expect routine access while turning a blind eye to illegal foreign strikes on the very infrastructure it is supposed to safeguard.
The IAEA has also been unable to verify the status of a stockpile of highly-enriched uranium since the June bombing. According to the IAEA, Iran maintains a stockpile of 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60% purity.
Despite relentless Western sanctions, sabotage, and Grossi’s overt collusion with imperialist powers, Tehran has reaffirmed that it will neither surrender its sovereign technological achievements nor bow to foreign dictates, underscoring that the Agency’s subservience to Western capitals has fatally compromised its standing as an impartial global watchdog.

articles.title: The war that changed everything. On historical mistakes, the role of progress and the new world
articles.body:
The war that changed everything. On historical mistakes, the role of progress and the new world
The Russian-Ukrainian war has become the first major war on the territory of Europe, that has no analogues since the Second World War, and it is already part of human history. This is a history not only of events, facts, and the number of victims. This is also the story of the people who stood behind it, people who do not yet realize that they have already entered history. A history that is ruthless toward human feelings because it operates with facts.
However, today this history is only being written. It will be reread and studied much later, in 50 years, when the last witnesses of those events have themselves passed into history, allowing others, people with a cool mind and honesty, to draw conclusions and never repeat the mistakes. To step into history, not get mired in a mess. It was precisely the mistakes that led to this war that prevented it from being brought to a timely end and most importantly failed to predict its consequences.
It is not just a war that has changed so much. In fact, it has changed the most important thing – the world order amidst the applause of absurdity and eccentricity. The world order that our grandfathers built with their own blood over eighty years ago and which we, the generation that still read books, lacked the strength to preserve.
This is a war that, like the Second World War, began due to the cowardice of those who were not being killed at that particular moment. They believed the best course of action was not to disturb the beast.
This is a war that could have ended with far fewer casualties, yet the very people who feared the beast would not sate its appetite and would attack them next simply pretended that these were not their red lines. Because the main thing is to avoid nuclear war.
A war that ultimately became a theater of sympathy for the daily killing of an entire nation choking on its own corruption.
And above all, this is a war that has surrendered itself to marketers and wheeler-dealers – people who, driven by a lack of understanding and strategy, merely stoke the flames of this in pursuit of quick profits, all while increasingly flaunting the rapid pace of technological progress.
A war that came as a surprise, because progress exists not to shape the contours of its conclusion, but precisely to prolong it. For some, it is the conviction that the matter does not concern them, while for others, it is a way of life and a means of earning a living.
A war where strategy and global decisions were left to history while the conflict was still at its peak. And yes, history will not forgive this, because it is people, not machines, who stand behind it all.
This is what the current war means for human history.
However, when speaking specifically about progress as a path to victory and the end of the war, it is necessary to remember: military affairs have their own science, historically developed and still based on established principles, regardless of what content fills TikTok. It is a pity that, due to that very same progress, an understanding of this is increasingly becoming accessible only to a narrow circle of people, and we cannot reach those whose strategy consists solely of social media views and the latest sensational headline.
It was the end of the Second World War that determined two important things that will also characterize the conclusion of this war, which is steadily gaining momentum. The end of the Second World War determined the place and time for the start of the next war, as well as the forms and methods by which that war would begin. And while the first is merely a repetition of mistakes by politicians and their voters, the second undeniably belongs to progress, which will inevitably use these mistakes.
It was precisely this development that lost its intensity with the end of that war and could not lead to anything fundamental. Thus, both the start of the expansion and the restoration of the Russian Empire began as a war in many respects similar to the major conflicts of the 20th century, drawing specifically on the experience of the Second World War. There is nothing surprising or unnatural about this, except for the fact that it was possible to prepare for it at least to avoid it, even if only for a short while.
Then, in the summer of 2023, as military operations within Ukraine intensified and required to survive on the battlefield, the wheel of progress started turning after standing still for nearly 80 years.
My initial thoughts on this in the autumn of 2023 sparked political objections within Ukraine itself and met with absolute incomprehension from representatives of the world's former leading armies.
In Ukraine today, it is politically and financially advantageous to move away from trading in curtains and become a representative for technologies. Those who, just three years ago, formulated their grievances against me now insist that technology is the only right choice for them.
Today, every arms exhibition resembles a scene from science fiction movies and a museum of past wars all at once. Back then, however, everyone thought otherwise. Apart from the progress that was gathering momentum and awaiting the emergence of a new empire to tame it. However, unfortunately, things turned out differently. Progress has become available to our enemies as well, just as it did nearly a century ago, from Verdun and the Somme to Robotyne and Bakhmut. There is nothing wrong with drawing this analogy.
Having gone static, the front brought to life not industrial horrors, but technological ones. And once again, nothing surprising occurred in the evolution of the art of war. The only surprising thing remains that, just as in 2023, using these patterns is still politically disadvantageous here and financially impossible for the world's former leading armies.
This was once the case with cavalry and the famous red trousers worn by the soldiers of one army before the First World War, which were supposed to help against repeating rifles, machine guns, long-range artillery, and the use of smokeless powder, which had been invented there as well, and later against tanks and aircraft. My generation knows how it ended.
And today, the current illusions of collective security, much like that soldier more than a hundred years ago in his dark-blue greatcoat and red trousers, despite being an obvious target on the battlefield, are, regrettably, perceived almost as a symbol of national identity and a source of national pride.
This war has, of course, changed the forms and methods of its conduct, yet it has left its essence unchanged. It is an act of violence, but now violence against the entire country. Violence that, just as in the Second World War, placed on the same level the infantryman physically unable to leave his trench and a newborn baby in another part of the country. Because both of them are constantly in the crosshairs of someone who wants to kill them both. Today's technology of warfare is precisely that it turns an entire country into a vast wasteland, sparing no one – neither those in the trenches nor those in supposedly peaceful places, such as a supermarket. Everything remains the same, yet the bombing process itself has changed, becoming more effective and, consequently, excessively cruel. Do those moving tanks and artillery closer to the crisis zone understand this? Apparently not. The red trousers taught them nothing.
This is no longer a drone war. Someone is about three years behind the times when it comes to drones. They simply no longer exist on their own. They evolved into weapon types more familiar to us, while reducing costs and increasing accessibility and effectiveness.
It is correct to consider that 2026 is a time of war of technologies, and not only technologies. It is also a war of strategies and doctrines that are constantly evolving under the pressure of progress. Therefore, it is a major mistake to focus on individual technologies and their promotion merely as weapons that complement the Soviet strategy and, of course, require specifically Soviet-style executors. Weapons that need to be produced and sold profitably in time and, better yet, used to de-occupy some territory in the process.
It was precisely the desire to liberate the territories and hold them using Soviet methods and strategies, only now with new weapons, that drove mobilisation into a dead end. Mobilization offered only one chance, and fewer and fewer people were willing to take it. But we are not capable of enduring a war of machines against a vast Soviet country, where people are effectively turned into machines and sent to fight against real machines. Damn marketing that kills.
Recognizing technology as a new weapon, it is essential to consider the patterns of the evolution of the art of war and, based on this, invariably shape new forms and methods of its employment. Only then should organizational changes be implemented within the structure of the Armed Forces that employ this new weaponry using new forms and methods of application. This is precisely where mobilisation fits into the new strategy, based on new weapons and specifically on new, rather than Soviet, forms and methods of their employment. Only in this way can we approach the improvement of mobilization and most importantly create systemic pressure and an advantage over the enemy. Of course, this takes time.
These changes are absolutely irreversible and affect the conduct of war at all levels – tactical, operational, and strategic, as well as the development of the military-industrial complex. Logically, all of this inevitably leads to the emergence of a word that some today find rather strange – doctrine. It is doctrine that provides the foundation for systematically influencing the adversary and shapes a strategic vision focused solely on future victory. In whom we observe this systemic influence, and who is closer to victory today – that question remains politically correctly open. However, assessing this in Ukraine through the scale and systematic nature of the strikes and the duration of air-raid alerts is quite straightforward. And a static front certainly cannot reassure those who see it only within the boundaries of operational zones.
It is a pity that many still do not realize or perhaps do not want to realize the scale of these changes. However, this cannot in any way stop scientific and technological progress or the evolution of the art of war.
The old rules no longer apply. The Russian-Ukrainian war demonstrates this daily, and any new major conflicts erupting amidst the reshaping of the old world order will inevitably demonstrate it as well.
The challenges of adapting to new conditions, such as the increased capability and availability of strike assets, the deployment of robotic systems and artificial intelligence, the protection of logistics and ports, effective and uninterrupted communications, space technologies, the digital dimension of security, and the adjustment of personnel training to meet the demands and challenges of modern warfare are challenges that no longer face national armies today, because they should already be prepared for them a priori. These are challenges for governments and alliances, which must unite around technologies that defend their own future.
Modern warfare requires new doctrines. To focus on rapid scientific and technological progress while failing to formulate these doctrines is so shortsighted that it is unlikely to allow us to cast off those same red trousers and see the future. Some still believe it is possible to formulate a truly effective doctrine for the use of drones and robots, while others think it is impossible.
Meanwhile, a war of technologies is already underway, and Ukraine is experiencing systemic pressure resulting from the implementation not only of technologies but also of a new doctrinal approach to their application, including production and research, as an integral part of the strategy. It is precisely this that gives Russia the right to issue us ultimatums through well-known intermediaries. This is precisely what is being targeted, and it could lead to a whole series of crises. Even though some people in a country at war still find it funny, the majority do not need to have it explained to them exactly which crises are involved. Let me remind that a war of attrition involves not only battles but also societal upheavals. The key is who triggers them first.
And if this is obvious, then why do the laws of war once again give way to forecasts, and strategy to marketing? Because capturing general trends for rough forecasts is precisely what curtain marketing requires. Quickly and in large quantities. However, whether this creates systemic pressure on Russia, or increases Russia's systemic pressure on us, remains an unanswered question, even though the ways to understand it are more than obvious.
Thus, to find a way out of this entirely predictable situation, it is necessary to understand the need to seek and implement a systemic response to Russia's systemic pressure. This systemic response must be based on a strategy in which the joint production and implementation of new technological solutions become part of systemic measures both to defend and to impact on Russia's ability to continue the war. For this, of course, the search for resource and technological alliances capable of ensuring this production, including to meet their own defence needs, remains relevant. This production must be doctrinally incorporated into the strategy for victory, where what is produced is not some magic weapon, but the entire new arsenal required, including for civilian purposes, in accordance with the conditions of technological progress.
Ukraine and Russia have turned into real-time testing grounds. Therefore, analyzing and understanding this new logic of war should help not only to shape new doctrines, tactics, and strategies but also, above all, to provide a vision of how peace and people's security can be preserved while we, Ukrainians, are paying for it with our blood.
Valerii Zaluzhnyi, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Ukraine to the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021-2024)

articles.title: 19 Russian defense companies remain outside international sanctions, helping sustain Russia’s war machine
articles.body:
Ukraine's military intelligence agency, HUR, published data on 54 Russian enterprises within KRET, a defense holding under Russia's state-owned Rostec corporation, on 15 September. More than a third of KRET's enterprises face no sanctions from any country in the international sanctions coalition, HUR reported on 15 September.
Russia's defense industry is vast, and sanctions have targeted companies and individuals across the sector in multiple rounds since the full-scale invasion to restrict its ability to produce and finance weapons. But complex networks of state-owned holdings and subsidiaries can leave gaps, allowing some companies involved in military production to remain outside international sanctions. An August report by the anti-corruption organization NAKO found that the EU had sanctioned only 23% of 482 Rostec-linked entities.
What KRET makes for Russia's military
- KRET makes electronic warfare systems, friend-or-foe identification systems and onboard electronics for Russian fighter jets and helicopters, HUR said. Its companies also make other military equipment, including anti-drone systems and remotely operated machine guns.
- KRET also supports Russia’s missile production. The Signal plant in Stavropol makes compact jamming stations for 9M723 Iskander-M missiles, and the Kaluga Research Radio Engineering Institute makes electronic protection systems for 3M22 Zircon missiles.
- KRET’s main organization covers funding shortfalls for state defense contracts carried out by its companies, according to HUR.
Unsanctioned companies make missile and drone parts
HUR also named several of the 19 unsanctioned companies that it says are involved in Russian weapons production.
Among those firms, HUR identified manufacturers of navigation systems for Kh-59M2 and Kh-59M2A guided air-launched missiles and Orion drones, gyroscopes for 9M727 cruise missiles used in the Iskander system, and electric motors for drones.
The enterprises include JSC Inertial Technologies of Technokompleks, JSC Tambov Plant Elektropribor, and JSC Ulan-Ude Instrument-Making Production Association.
HUR calls for broader sanctions
The intelligence agency called for more defense companies to be added to international sanctions lists, better monitoring of compliance, and punishment for violations. KRET is the 10th Rostec holding whose enterprises HUR has published on its War&Sanctions portal. The portal now lists 764 Rostec enterprises, UNN reported.
On 8 September, HUR published data on 155 enterprises belonging to Roselektronika, another Rostec holding. Nearly half were not under international sanctions.

articles.title: The winter that will reach Russia's rear
articles.body:
The winter that will reach Russia's rear
Cars queue at a Gazpromneft gas station in the suburbs of Moscow, in Istra, Russia, on July 10, 2026. (Contributor / Getty Images)
Liubov Tsybulska
Director of Join Ukraine
In late August and early September, it began to look as though Russia was winning the exchange of strikes.
According to Zelensky, in late August, jet-powered drones made up more than half of all unmanned aerial vehicles launched. Ukraine shoots them down at a rate of six in ten, compared with more than nine in ten for propeller-driven ones.
There is almost nothing to shoot down ballistic missiles with: the interception rate was 40% in June and 15% in July; on the night of Aug. 1, Russia launched 27 ballistic missiles at Ukraine, with Kyiv as the main target, and only one was shot down.
According to an estimate by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, U.S. stocks of PAC-3 MSE interceptors have shrunk almost threefold as a result of combat operations against Iran.
In late August, the capital went through 13 air raid alerts in a single day.
The winter ahead may be the hardest of the full-scale war. Russia will once again try to make life in large cities impossible: electricity, water, heating, and food. The calculation is the same as in 2022: to make Ukraine break. Against this backdrop, it is fairly easy to fall into a funk. But the situation is not so one-sided.
On the night of Aug. 12, Novorossiysk was under attack for eight hours. The next day, the Russian regional communities we track published more than 300 posts about it.
In 112 of the 300, the story was about civilian deaths; in 98, about damaged buildings; in 29, about a collapsed overpass. Ships came up in only eight.
The frigates "Admiral Makarov" and "Admiral Essen," whose launchers, according to an analysis of satellite imagery, were likely knocked out of action by the strikes and fires, were not mentioned by anyone at all. Nor does the Russian reader ever hear about the shutdown of three grain terminals that previously handled exports of around 25 million tons of Russian grain.
Why do we bring up this example? Ukraine focuses on targets that matter for stopping the Russian war machine. Russians, meanwhile, see in their information environment almost nothing but what matters to them personally.
Russians feel the hardships of war before analysts do.
In our databases, which cover around a thousand regional Telegram and VKontakte communities, the fuel topic grew by 85% over the four weeks of August: hours-long lines in Perm, purchase limits in Moscow, "gasoline availability maps" as the most in-demand of all digital services.
Despite the large number of successful strikes on facilities in Russia's rear throughout August, practically none of them became a nationwide topic in Russia (as Wildberries did in July).
Russians rally around a topic in the information space only when their own skin is in the game: the most reactions and comments still go to the same Wildberries and Ozon — everyone wants to know what will happen to deliveries and whether their parcels have burned.
The social distance between Russian regions is so great that the explosions in Novorossiysk were of little interest even to residents of relatively nearby Stavropol.
Of course, strikes on Russia's rear provoke anger. But it is not aimed where the Kremlin would like it to be.
Anti-Ukrainian jabs in the comments under posts about the strikes are consistently few: 5–7% in both July and August, and that counts any mention of Ukraine at all, while outright hatred along the lines of "khokhly" (a slur for Ukrainians) is two to three times rarer.
Roughly the same share of comments is addressed to their own authorities and air defenses, and, across individual events, that share ranges from 10–16%.
The most upvoted comment under one of the posts about the already mentioned attack on Novorossiysk: "We hit them, they hit us. And for the sake of protecting facilities, complete disregard for people's safety." The second most popular: "If they can't protect us, let them wrap up this Special Military Operation. Meanwhile, all the air defense and electronic warfare systems around Moscow are lined up several rows deep."
Attention to the other August strikes was distributed the same way.
The strikes on the Syzran oil refinery were discussed almost exclusively in Samara Oblast, and the governor never named the plant.
The plant in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, which makes propellant for "Smerch" and "Tornado-S" multiple rocket launchers, exists in the feeds only as "5 dead in Rostov Oblast."
The strike on the "Sivash" drilling rig in the Black Sea, where Russians had placed surveillance equipment, was not mentioned even once.
The only strike to become a nationwide topic was the one on Koledino, Wildberries' largest warehouse, damaged by a strike and fire on August 16: 38% of reactions under posts about it were the angry emoji, a record for our monitoring.
The result of this systematic work: oil refining in Russia fell in August to an average of 3.8 million barrels per day, the lowest level in 20 years, no matter what Putin said about "only 10% of the oil refineries still left to repair"; the gasoline export ban has been extended to Jan. 31, 2027, and since Sept. 1, gas stations have been allowed to sell Euro-2, a fuel that can damage modern cars.
So let's go back to where we started.
Russia will bet on terror and on making survival in Ukraine's large cities impossible in winter. That means strikes on energy, water supply, warehouses of food, medicine, and essential goods, and gas stations. It is absolutely clear that this winter will be extremely difficult.
But we have been through something like this before. This will be the fourth hard winter, and the country knows roughly what to prepare for. Betting that this time it will not hold out, after three previous attempts, is a dubious investment.
We know a hard winter awaits us. But for the first time in this war, Ukraine can respond at least roughly in kind.
For Russia, however, this will be the first winter in which its rear is this vulnerable. There has never been such depth before, nor such numbers.
As for the depth, in August, Ukrainian drones reached Tobolsk, 1,900 kilometers (1,180 miles) away, and twelve large oil refineries were hit within the month. And on Sept. 9, according to the Special Operations Forces, their drones reached Novy Urengoy and the Purovsky plant in Yamal, more than 3,000 kilometers (1,864 miles) from the border; the previous record, Omsk in July, was 2,500 kilometers (1553 miles).
This is the heart of Russian gas production, which until now was considered a safe rear area.
Now numbers are also hitting records. The Russian Defense Ministry itself claims a record 1,671 drones allegedly shot down in a single day, and the mayor of Moscow reports 8,670 drones in August headed toward the Moscow region, compared with 6,225 in July.
Defending such a vast territory is impossible.
We know a hard winter awaits us. But for the first time in this war, Ukraine can respond at least roughly in kind.
How delighted Russian society will be with its own hard winter remains an open question. Judging by the comments, not very.
On Aug. 18, when more than 600 drones were flying toward Moscow, two comments under a "Moskva 24" post collected more than 800 likes each: "They fly in every day, it's no longer treated as an emergency, it's taken like the rain. Look where it's got us — couldn't just live in peace!"
And: "Are we really getting used to what's happening... or are we just ceasing to notice how our idea of normal life is changing?"
In Samara, where missiles struck on Aug. 15, the most popular reply is shorter: "We've got no damn air defense at all. They only protect Moscow."
Moscow, the Russians will probably manage to defend through the winter. The rest of Russia, they won't.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

articles.title: Ukraine Exposes 54 Russian Firms Behind Iskander and Zircon Missiles
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Exposes 54 Russian Firms Behind Iskander and Zircon Missiles
Ukraine’s military intelligence has disclosed information on 54 Russian companies linked to the production of electronic warfare systems, military aircraft electronics, drones, and components for Iskander-M and Zircon missiles.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) on September 15, the companies are part of or managed by Concern Radio-Electronic Technologies (KRET), a subsidiary of Russia’s state-owned defense conglomerate Rostec. The information was published through HUR’s War&Sanctions database.
KRET companies primarily develop and manufacture electronic warfare equipment, identification friend-or-foe systems, and onboard electronics used by Russian fighter jets and helicopters, HUR said.
Their production also includes electric motors, navigation and control systems for drones, counter-drone equipment, and remotely operated machine-gun platforms.
HUR identified several KRET companies as participants in Russia’s missile supply chain. The Stavropol-based Signal plant manufactures and supplies S200A1 compact jamming stations for 9M723 ballistic missiles used by the Iskander-M system.
The Kaluga Scientific Research Radio Engineering Institute, another company within the KRET network, supplies components for the 3B228 electronic protection system installed on Russia’s 3M22 Zircon missiles, according to Ukrainian intelligence.
HUR also said KRET’s central organization provides financing to cover shortfalls in Russian state defense contracts carried out by companies within the concern.
Of the 54 companies disclosed by Ukrainian intelligence, 19 are currently not sanctioned by any country participating in the international sanctions coalition.
Among them is Inertial Technologies of Technocomplex, which HUR identified as a manufacturer of strapdown inertial navigation systems for Kh-59M2 and Kh-59M2A guided air-launched missiles and Orion unmanned aircraft systems.
The Tambov Elektropribor plant, also not covered by coalition sanctions, supplies gyroscopes for 9M727 cruise missiles used by the Iskander system. The Ulan-Ude Instrument-Making Production Association produces aircraft automation equipment, radio-navigation systems, and electric motors for drones, according to HUR.
KRET is the tenth Rostec holding whose corporate network has been published by Ukrainian intelligence through the War&Sanctions portal. The database now contains information on 764 companies associated with the Russian state corporation.
Earlier, on September 9, Ukraine’s military intelligence said it had breached the Moscow Institute of Thermal Technology, a key Russian missile developer behind the Yars, Bulava, Iskander-M, and Oreshnik systems, obtaining data on the institute’s structure, projects, and 2,648 employees.
