Alex Ahrendtsen, defense spokesperson for the Danish People’s Party, urged calm.
“Of course, we should not go to war with the Russians because of some signal lights that have been sent up,” he said.
Bruus said both the frigate and helicopter had a right to operate in international waters and called the helicopter’s work normal.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats described the incident as serious but unsurprising.
She said it was part of a pattern involving “an increasingly aggressive and assertive Russia” that is testing NATO and conducting hybrid warfare against Europe.
“Russia wants to intimidate and sow discord. Our response is to stand closer together and strengthen the defence of Denmark and Europe,” Frederiksen said.
A citizen proposal seeking tighter controls on untreated wastewater discharges has received the 50,000 signatures required for consideration by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The proposal, titled “Discharge of untreated wastewater into streams, watercourses, fjords and the sea,” was published September 3 and reached the threshold 10 days later, the Folketing said Tuesday.
It will now be submitted to parliament as a motion for a resolution.
The proposal contains four measures. The first would require flow meters at every wastewater overflow in Denmark. Data from the meters would be published on a digital platform, allowing the public to see how much untreated wastewater is discharged.
The second measure would require an authorized analysis company to take regular water samples and test them against 14 European Union requirements for chemical measurements.
The proposal would also introduce a fee for discharging waste substances that are diverted around treatment plants without being treated. Its final measure would require every overflow structure to have a valid permit.
The proposal received attention after Amanda Heitmann, a member of parliament for Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, signed it.
Venstre’s environmental spokesperson, Marie Bjerre, reprimanded Heitmann for supporting the citizen proposal.
“As a political party elected to the Folketing, it is not our job to sign citizen proposals, but to take a position on the content,” Bjerre told Politiken, a Danish newspaper.
Heitmann was also one of five Venstre lawmakers who recently went against the party line and voted against the fertilizer act in parliament.
Russian frigate fires flares near Danish military helicopter in international waters
A Russian frigate fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter in international waters off Gedser on Monday, Denmark’s Armed Forces said.
The Fennec helicopter was taking routine photographs of the ship when the flares were fired. One passed close to the aircraft, according to a military statement.
Flares are pyrotechnic devices normally used as attention signals at sea. No personnel were injured, and the helicopter was not damaged.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats called the incident serious and described Russia’s actions as “very unprofessional seamanship.”
“It is serious. It is an expression of the boundaries having been moved regarding the willingness to take risks from the Russian side,” Bruus said.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen will summon the Russian ambassador to discuss the incident, though the date of the meeting has not been announced. Bruus said he did not expect further action beyond that meeting.
The defense minister said the incident would not change Denmark’s monitoring operations.
“We view it seriously, but it is not the case that we will change our behavior, understood in the sense that we have a completely legitimate task in monitoring what is going on,” Bruus said.
Inger Støjberg, leader of the Denmark Democrats, a Danish right-wing party, said the incident showed that Russian provocations had reached Denmark.
She called for NATO unity and continued support for Ukraine in its war against Russia.
“It is therefore crucial that NATO stands united, and that we continue to support Ukraine,” Støjberg said. She added that she expected a briefing from Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
Danish electricity prices head for most expensive month in years as gas costs rise
September could become the most expensive month for Danish electricity customers in several years, energy company Norlys said.
Halfway through the month, the average electricity price was 1.11 DKK per kilowatt-hour in western Denmark and 1.12 DKK in eastern Denmark.
It is the first time since December 2022 that the monthly average has exceeded 1 DKK per kilowatt-hour, according to Norlys.
“We are halfway through September, so a lot can still change, but with the rising gas prices, we unfortunately have to expect that it will be an expensive month,” said Ellen Trolle, director of Norlys’ energy business.
Electricity prices were set to rise above 7 DKK per kilowatt-hour Monday evening, their highest level in almost two years.
Norlys said the increase was caused by higher gas prices and limited electricity production from wind and solar power. Natural gas plants often supply electricity when the weather does not provide enough wind and sunlight, making power prices more sensitive to gas costs.
Kristian Rune Poulsen, an analyst at Danish energy organization Green Power Denmark, also pointed to gas prices.
“The conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, which doesn’t really want to come to an end, means that a great deal of the liquefied natural gas that we have become so dependent on cannot get out onto the world market,” he said.
Poulsen said prices would continue to fluctuate but were unlikely to fall soon while the conflict continued.
“We expect that the elevated price level will persist throughout the winter, as it looks right now,” he said.
Nearly 12 percent of Danish ninth graders fail to pass Danish or mathematics exams
More than one in 10 Danish ninth-grade students failed to earn a passing grade in Danish or mathematics in this summer’s final exams, new government figures show.
The Ministry of Education said 11.8 percent of students did not receive at least 2, the minimum passing grade, in one or both subjects during the 2025-2026 school year.
“It is too high a proportion. Because it means that they initially will not have the opportunity to move on to youth education programs,” Andreas Rasch-Christensen, a school researcher at VIA University College, a Danish higher education institution, told DR, Denmark’s public broadcaster.
DR reported a failure rate of 10.5 percent, while the ministry listed 11.8 percent. The difference is that the ministry included students whose schools did not register that they sat the exam. DR excluded those students.
The result marks a small decline from the previous school year, when 9.9 percent failed to pass Danish or mathematics. The rate was 10.1 percent in 2023-2024 and 6.9 percent in 2018-2019.
The average final exam grade was 7.3, in line with the previous four years, DR reported.
The figures follow the release of a PISA study showing that Danish students’ performance had declined in reading, mathematics and science.
The government said similar declines were occurring across much of Western Europe. Danish politicians have pointed to mobile phones as a possible cause, saying quick stimulation from phones may make it harder for students to concentrate.
The government wants to introduce a complete ban on mobile phones in schools.
Lower food VAT would cost Danish businesses about 725 million DKK a year to administer
Lowering Denmark’s value-added tax on food would cost businesses about 725 million DKK annually in added administration, according to a parliamentary response.
Tax Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates said Monday that the government wants to lower the general VAT rate on food and remove it from fruit and vegetables as soon as possible. The changes will not take effect this year.
“It is of great importance to the government to make it cheaper for Danes to fill their shopping baskets,” Engel-Schmidt said at a consultation.
The estimate is uncertain because the government has not decided how the new VAT system would work. Shops and other businesses would have to cover the administrative costs.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and Denmark’s main business and employers’ association, said the actual cost would be higher.
“When the VAT rules for food become more complicated, it affects the VAT accounting in virtually all active businesses,” tax policy chief Jacob Bræstrup said.
Bræstrup said the change would affect more than wholesalers, supermarkets and restaurants. He said total administrative costs would be “significantly higher” than the estimated 725 million DKK.
The broader proposal would cost the state 17.4 billion DKK a year, according to the Ministry of Taxation and Growth.
Leading economists have criticized the plan as an expensive and inefficient way to help people. They warn that businesses might not pass the full tax reduction on through lower prices. Some savings could instead pay for administration or increase company earnings.
The government plans to present several possible models in the second half of 2026.
Extensive damage to the overhead wire system near Sorø is expected to disrupt train services between Ringsted and Slagelse until 10 a.m. Tuesday, according to Banedanmark, which manages work on Denmark’s rail network.
One track has reopened after DSB, the Danish passenger train operator, stopped services on the section around midday Monday. Trains are now running on a reduced timetable, with longer travel times and some cancellations.
Tony Bispeskov, DSB’s head of information, said priority would be given to international, InterCityLyn and InterCity trains.
Banedanmark said it received a report of problems with the overhead wire system between Sorø and Slagelse at 12:45 p.m. Monday. Train services were stopped completely while the cause was identified.
“There we can see that we have extensive damage to one of our tracks. At the moment, this means that we only have one passable track to operate on, and that we are running with a reduced timetable,” Banedanmark said.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said Monday that she is “quite optimistic” Denmark, Greenland and the USA can reach an agreement on security and defense in Greenland.
Frederiksen spoke at a news conference in Finland, where she attended a European summit focused on security in the Arctic.
“We have agreed to start a high-level working group on closer cooperation on security and defense, also in Greenland,” Frederiksen said.
“As long as the working group between Greenland, Denmark, and the USA continues its work, it is too early to draw a conclusion. But I am quite optimistic that we will succeed in finding a way,” she said.
Frederiksen visited Greenland last week with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Denmark is among 10 NATO countries conducting a joint military exercise in Greenland. The exercise is intended to show that Denmark and NATO are protecting Greenland and the Arctic.
US President Donald Trump has criticized Denmark for not doing enough to protect Greenland from threats posed by Russia and China.
During the first weeks of September, 400 soldiers from 10 NATO countries are operating on land, at sea and in the air near Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq. They are training to operate in Arctic conditions as part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry surveillance and deterrence mission.
“If one is to be able to operate in the Arctic, one has to train up here,” Søren Andersen, head of Denmark’s Arctic Command, told the Danish news agency Ritzau last week.
Andersen said the temporary Arctic Shield exercise is part of a long-term strategy for Greenland and the Arctic.
“For us, it is about helping to transform NATO’s northern flank into a hard target. Meaning all the way from Alaska across Canada, Greenland, and to the northern part of Norway,” he said.
Denmark and Greenland are also discussing whether to give the USA greater access to Greenland. The New York Times reported in the spring, based on American sources, that the USA wants three bases in Greenland as part of a possible agreement. Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq were reportedly among the possible locations.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats declined to discuss the working group’s talks during a visit to Narsarsuaq last week.
“I cannot comment on that. What goes on in that working group, goes on in that working group,” Bruus told Ritzau.
Bruus said the government wants to extend the operating period of Narsarsuaq Airport by one year if it receives support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“Initially, it is a one-year extension. That gives us the opportunity to extend the playing board,” Bruus said.
Chief of Defense Michael Hyldgaard said Narsarsuaq would be an obvious possible location for an American base because of its position in southern Greenland and its access to transatlantic routes, the Denmark Strait and the GIUK gap.
The GIUK gap is the sea area between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom. It is an important military passage where NATO can monitor and block Russian submarines moving toward the Atlantic.
The USA previously operated a military base in Narsarsuaq from July 1941 to November 1958.
CPH Half will expand to 45,000 runners for its race on September 19, 2027, because of high demand, organizer Sparta Atletik og Løb, a Danish athletics and running organization, said in a news release.
Around 35,000 people are taking part in this year’s half marathon, up from about 32,000 in 2025.
Tickets for the 2027 race will be sold through a lottery instead of on a first-come, first-served basis.
Registration for the lottery opens September 16 and remains open for two weeks. People can register alone or in groups of up to three. Each group will either be selected together or not selected at all.
Selected runners will have 48 hours to buy a ticket. The price is DKK 795 plus a small administration fee.
“When demand is so high, access to the bib numbers must also function in a way where everyone has a fair and equal chance of getting a bib number,” Dorte Vibjerg, CEO of Sparta Atletik og Løb, said in the release.
The organizers also used a lottery to sell tickets for this year’s CPH Half, which is part of the World Athletics Road Running Championships. Similar systems are used for major marathons in Berlin and London.
This year’s race starts Sunday. Elite international runners will begin first, followed by the other participants.
Danish police brought 79 new charges linked to possible crime-for-hire cases from January through the end of July, the Ministry of Justice said Monday.
In total, police brought 316 charges from April 2024 through the end of July this year that may involve crime-for-hire, a practice also known as “Violence as a Service.”
The figures come from NSK, a Danish police unit that handles serious and organized crime. In January, authorities had recorded 237 charges, according to figures released by the ministry in February.
The government disclosed the latest figures as it sent a bill proposing stricter penalties and other measures against gangs and crime-for-hire for consultation. That process allows judges, lawyers, police and other groups to submit concerns or objections before the proposal moves forward.
The bill would increase penalties for crime-for-hire and treat criminal families in the same way as gangs.
“We will not tolerate children and young people being recruited into a life of crime, and residential areas being marked by fear, control, and parallel power structures,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen of the Social Democrats said in a statement.
The proposal would also add a provision to the penal code intended to make it easier to convict people who provide minor services to gang leaders.
Other measures include allowing background checks for dockworkers and increasing the penalty for violating a stay ban. Police have recorded a large increase in such violations.
A stay ban can be imposed on a person who has committed a crime connected to a gang. It prevents that person from entering a specific area, such as part of a town or municipality, for a set period.
Violating a stay ban currently carries a fine of 10,000 DKK. Under the proposed law, a violation would result in 30 days in prison.
Power and diesel prices heading for nearly two-year high
The electricity price on Monday evening is the highest level in almost two years, when the price exceeds seven kroner per kilowatt-hour. The energy company OK writes this in a press release Monday morning.
According to Troels Skipper, commercial director at OK, the high electricity price is due to a combination of rising gas prices and a lack of wind and solar energy.
“Right now, we are in the unfortunate situation where the high gas price pushes the electricity price up along with it. And unfortunately, we do not get enough electricity production from wind turbines and solar cells to push the price the other way,” he said.
The last time the hourly price was at around seven DKK per kilowatt-hour was in December 2024.
Also, Diesel prices in Denmark rose to a record high on Monday, reaching 19.19 kroner per litre after an increase of 20 øre, according to FDM, the Danish motorists’ association. Petrol prices also increased by 40 øre per litre. FDM consumer economist Ilyas Dogru said the increases followed the weekend’s escalation in the war involving the United States, Iran and Israel.
Denmark is set for a week of changing autumn weather, with periods of rain, sunshine and mild temperatures, according to the Danish Meteorological Institute, DMI.
Monday began cool, particularly in central Jutland, where temperatures fell to between 6 and 8 degrees.
“The temperature is down to 6-8 degrees, so if you are going out cycling, you can clearly feel that autumn has arrived,” DMI duty meteorologist Jesper Eriksen told Ritzau.
The rest of Monday is expected to remain dry, with a mix of sunshine and clouds. Temperatures will reach between 15 and 18 degrees, with light to moderate winds from the west.
### Tuesday to be warmest day
Tuesday is expected to be the warmest day of the week.
Winds will turn to the south, bringing slightly warmer air over Denmark and pushing temperatures to between 17 and 21 degrees.
There will be periods of sunshine, although some rain is possible, particularly in Jutland.
More rain is expected to reach Jutland later Tuesday afternoon before moving east during the evening and overnight.
Wednesday will bring some sunshine but also showers.
Temperatures are expected to fall back to between 15 and 18 degrees, while winds will turn west again.
Thursday and Friday are expected to bring periods of rain and showers, with temperatures remaining between 15 and 18 degrees.
Winds from the west and southwest are also expected to strengthen gradually toward the end of the week.
Eriksen said the week would not be particularly cold despite the unsettled weather.
“In the week as a whole, you will not need the really warm clothes, but in periods you will need rainwear and rubber boots,” he said.
It remains unclear whether September will bring another spell of warmer weather later in the month.
“We will have to see what happens, whether the last spasms with some warmth arrive. It is not decided yet,” Eriksen said.
More than half of the Danish schools that were selected for the latest Pisa survey declined to participate. In total, 398 schools were drawn for the survey. Of those, 215 chose not to participate, writes Kristeligt Dagblad.
When a selected school chooses to decline, a reserve school could step in. In advance, two reserve schools had been designated for each of the drawn schools.
Therefore, a total of 283 schools ended up participating in the survey. However, this is significantly fewer than in 2022, when 347 schools participated.
According to Kristeligt Dagblad, the number also remains below the OECD’s “technical minimum requirement”.
According to Monika Klingsbjerg-Besrechel, chief consultant at Statistics Denmark, which was responsible for the practical part of the survey, the many declines have not affected the quality of the survey.
“Fortunately, we reached a higher response rate, but despite that, we were unfortunately still below the minimum requirement from the OECD. If we had not had the reserve schools, we really would have been in serious trouble,” she says to Kristeligt Dagblad.
She points out that it was subsequently investigated whether the many declines had affected the result.

“Here in Søhøjlandet we have a unique setting for both participants and spectators with hilly landscapes, great viewpoints over the Silkeborg lakes, and an exciting city center where urban life and nature merge. I look forward to showcasing that.”
In 2026, the host cities were Randers, Ringkøbing, Middelfart, Helsingør, and Copenhagen/Frederiksberg. This year, Denmark can expect new cities other than Silkeborg to join the Royal Run host club, with a new host city scheduled to be announced every day this week.
The Royal Run offers three distances to run, including 1.6 kilometers (also known as one mile), five kilometers, and ten kilometers.
The event first took place in 2018, when the then Crown Prince turned 50 years old. Since then, it has been held every year on Whit Monday.
Last year, a record 112,450 runners participated.

articles.title: Air Force Stacks Inert Sentinel ICBM Ahead of First Test in 2027
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—The Air Force has erected an inert version of its LGM-35A Sentinel intercontinental ballistic missile at Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif., the service announced Sept. 14.
Officials also confirmed at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference that they still expect to finish restructuring the long-troubled Sentinel program by the end of the year and conduct a first test launch in 2027.
The announcement did not specify when the vertical stacking was completed but said that it showed “the maturity of the missile’s design and verified that all critical subsystems are on track.”
An accompanying image shows the missile with “US AIR FORCE” running vertically down its side, along with the Air Force roundel and the emblems of Air Force Global Strike Command and the Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center.
In its own announcement, contractor Northrop Grumman said the stacking was a four-month test process that involved transporting missile components “on specially designed vehicles from across the U.S.” to Vandenberg, where technicians “rigorously tested mechanical operations including transportation, mobile crane use, and safe vertical integration while validating all interface connections on the test pad.”
The successful stacking “proved the viability of all missile stages, propulsion elements, shroud, and subcomponents to be assembled into a single configuration on the test pad,” both Northrop and the Air Force said in their releases.
The service has tested the different stages of the Sentinel’s solid rocket motor multiple times in recent years, as well as the new reentry vehicle that will sit atop them. But it has yet to put them all together for a single test of the entire system.
The Air Force also said that its 719th Test Squadron used the stacking event to complete its first “flight test design review” of the Sentinel to ensure it meets requirements for “performance, safety, and mission assurance ahead of flight testing.”
This February, officials announced they were targeting 2027 for the first test launch. Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink confirmed in his keynote address at Air, Space & Cyber that the 2027 timeframe still holds.
Holding steady represents a win for the program; in 2024, officials were hoping for a first launch in early 2026. But massive cost and schedule overruns forced the program to restructure and slowed progress, leading the Government Accountability Office in 2025 to project a first launch in March 2028.
Gen. Dale R. White, director of critical major weapons systems, is overseeing Sentinel as the program tries to rebuild momentum from those overruns, which triggered a congressional notification and a Pentagon review under the Nunn-McCurdy Act.
As part of that process, Pentagon leaders rescinded Sentinel’s Milestone B decision, which authorizes officials to work on engineering and manufacturing development. Program leaders were instructed to restructure to manage the cost growth and schedule slip.
White told reporters during a roundtable at the Air, Space & Cyber conference that the restructuring process is nearing completion.
“We’re still on track for Milestone B. … That is going very well,” White said. “That was one of the areas I had concern early on about how you kind of navigate those waters and make sure you get that recertification right.”
Sentinel first received a Milestone B certification in 2020, but officials found over time that some of their baseline assumptions were no longer accurate.
The ground facilities in particular were the source of most of the problems rather than the missile itself. Those led to some “hard conversations” during the restructuring, White acknowledged, but senior leaders have now “pretty much locked down the majority of the design” for the infrastructure.
As part of that process, officials agreed Sentinel will no longer use the same silos as the Minuteman III, which are already around 60 years old. In March, the Air Force and Northrop broke ground on a new prototype silo in Promontory, Utah.
Broadly speaking, White said, the Air Force now has a better handle on the program as it progresses toward Milestone B once more.
“In terms of the cost piece, we’re learning as we go along because of just the sheer amount of data that we have now,” he said. “It’s so much more mature than when we did this [six] years ago, and so it’s been really fantastic, because we’ve integrated both the Air Force Cost Analysis Agency and [the office of Cost Assessment and Program Evaluation] with us, and we’re going through this together.”
White declined to say what the restructured program may cost. The previous baseline from 2020 was $77.7 billion; officials said in 2024 it would be closer to $141 billion. White has said he is treating the latter as a cap on the program’s cost.
“I don’t think we’re anywhere near a number right now,” White said Sept. 14. “I’m very comfortable with what I have seen, though, and I think that we’re certainly within the realm of what we have talked about all along. So I don’t think you’ll see any surprises from a cost perspective.”

articles.title: Ukraine successfully tests interceptor against faster Gerans as Russia floods its skies with drones
articles.body:
Ukraine has successfully tested another interceptor designed to counter Russia’s increasingly common jet-powered Geran attack drones, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 15 September.
The test comes as Russia rapidly expands the use of faster jet-powered Gerans, creating a new problem for Ukraine’s air defenses: these drones give defenders less time to detect and engage them while allowing Russia to maintain large-scale attacks. A successful interceptor could give Ukraine a cheaper, scalable way to counter that threat without relying as heavily on scarce high-end air-defense missiles.
Zelenskyy said Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi reported the successful test, during which the new interceptor struck a Russian Geran drone.
The system still reportedly needs further work, including improvements to some aspects of its control. But the successful test marks another step in Ukraine’s effort to develop a new layer of air defenses against Russia’s faster drones.
Russia is making its drone attacks faster and larger
Russia has sharply expanded its use of jet-powered Gerans in recent months, adding a faster and more difficult-to-intercept threat to its large-scale drone campaign.
Geran is Russia’s designation for its domestically produced Shahed-derived attack drones, with newer jet-powered variants representing a major upgrade over the earlier propeller-driven models.
Zelenskyy recently said Russia launched around 2,100 drones against Ukraine last week, alongside nearly 1,700 guided aerial bombs and 78 missiles. The attacks have increasingly targeted energy facilities, railway infrastructure, businesses, and residential areas.
The newer Gerans are faster than earlier Shahed-derived drones and can reach targets deep inside Ukraine. Their speed gives Ukrainian air defenses less time to detect, track, and engage them.
Russia has also changed how it uses its drones. Rather than concentrating attacks almost exclusively overnight, Russian forces have increasingly launched waves during the day as well, keeping Ukrainian cities under repeated air-raid alerts.
The result is a growing challenge not only of interception, but of scale. Ukraine must defend a large territory against increasingly large drone barrages while preserving more sophisticated air-defense missiles for ballistic missiles and other threats.
Ukraine is building a new layer of air defense
Ukraine has already been racing to develop such systems. In late August, Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said four potential interceptor systems capable of shooting down jet-powered Gerans had undergone field testing. Ukraine was aiming to bring them to the required level and eventually produce thousands of units.
Today’s announcement shows that effort continues to produce concrete results.
Ukraine is also expanding other parts of its counter-drone network. Zelenskyy said the country is increasing purchases of electronic warfare equipment and reorganizing mobile fire groups and air-defense positions.
The goal is to build enough layers to cope with Russia’s evolving drone campaign: electronic warfare, mobile fire teams, traditional air defenses, and increasingly specialized interceptors.
Russia is making its drones faster and launching them at greater scale. Ukraine’s response is now moving beyond adapting existing defenses toward developing weapons specifically designed to catch them.

articles.title: Chinese bank helped Huawei spirit $1B out of London days after US indictment of the tech giant
articles.body:
A little after sunrise on a cloudy Saturday morning, nine bankers returned to their workplace in London’s financial district for an extraordinary meeting. It was Feb. 2, 2019, and the Lunar New Year holiday would soon halt operations at the Beijing headquarters of the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China.
Five thousand miles from the Chinese capital, the bank officers made their way through the lobby of ICBC’s London branch, housed inside an imposing building a short walk from London Bridge. The bank’s managers had called them in on the weekend with a request: Swiftly transfer $1.3 billion for an important client, the Chinese tech giant Huawei.
The company needed to repatriate its “emergency cash,” according to confidential ICBC records reviewed by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists. The bankers suspected that the urgency might have something to do with a recent scandal making international headlines. “[I]t was probably the negative news,” Chenhu Liu, a senior bank officer who attended the meeting, later told an internal auditor.
Five days earlier, the U.S. Justice Department had unsealed an indictment accusing Huawei of fraud, violating sanctions on Iran and other crimes. (Huawei has denied wrongdoing, and the case is being tried in New York.) The company’s chief financial officer — the founder’s daughter — was under house arrest in Canada after being detained at the request of the U.S.
The incident triggered an unprecedented diplomatic spat as Chinese authorities retaliated by detaining two Canadians on spurious espionage charges. And yet, in London, the criminal case did not deter the ICBC officers from fulfilling Huawei’s request within a matter of hours. The transaction, while not illegal, reveals how readily ICBC’s London branch bypassed ordinary banking protocols to satisfy the demands of its Chinese parent, especially when a strategic client — one that had come to symbolize China’s technological advancement — needed a helping hand.
Huawei was not the only politically connected client to benefit from special treatment at ICBC London. A tranche of 4.8 million confidential bank records spanning 20 years shows how ICBC officers ignored red flags and breached internal anti-money laundering policies under pressure from the bank’s Beijing headquarters. At times, the demands of the Chinese parent led to clashes between eager-to-please managers and compliance officers — the bank’s internal watchdogs — who feared risky clients could jeopardize ICBC’s reputation.
The findings are part of China Capital, an ICIJ investigation with 23 media partners that provides an unprecedented look into how China’s domestic priorities and global ambitions dictate the daily operations of one of its most powerful financial arms. The records, including client dossiers, due diligence reports, meeting minutes and internal emails in English and Chinese, expose the inner workings of ICBC’s U.K. subsidiary and London branch, and the crucial role ICBC London has played in propelling Beijing’s favorites onto the world stage.
The years after Xi Jinping became China’s president in 2013 heralded a golden era in the U.K.’s relationship with the Asian superpower. As it enthusiastically courted Chinese investment, the British government eased rules introduced after the 2008 financial crisis to protect the banking system from international shocks. As long as certain foreign banks served big corporate clients, instead of retail customers, they could open branches in London to move vast sums in and out of Europe.
For ICBC, China’s largest state-owned commercial bank, the changes meant its London branch could rapidly expand under the direction of executives in Beijing whose priorities were, and remain, to serve the Chinese Communist Party and push the president’s agenda. At a time when the Xi administration uses financial statecraft to project power worldwide, China Capital raises questions about the ability of regulators in one of the world’s most prominent financial centers to supervise Chinese state banks effectively. ICBC and Huawei did not respond to ICIJ’s repeated requests for comment.
Martin Thorley, who wrote a book about the party-state’s influence in the U.K., described ICBC and other Chinese banks as a “different beast” compared with their international peers because “they have to make sure they operate within the party’s red lines, and that shapes behavior.” This, he said, presents a challenge to the U.K. and other countries’ security and sovereignty.
“If you’re a Chinese entity and you have to choose between following the guidance of British regulators or the party back home, there is only one winner there, and it’s not the British regulator,” said Thorley, who’s also a senior analyst at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime. “It’s an existential question.”
Comrades and bankers
On Dec. 1, 2014, ICBC Chairman Jiang Jianqing and a Chinese Embassy official pressed an oversized red button at a ceremony to declare the bank’s London branch open for business. Gold confetti rained down on guests including the directors of the U.K.’s main banking regulators, who smiled for the cameras as they celebrated the milestone.
ICBC had opened its U.K. subsidiary a decade earlier. But this was the first time it had obtained a branch license under a new supervisory regime. Andrew Bailey, who then helped oversee one of the regulators, the Prudential Regulation Authority, and now serves as Bank of England governor, said publicly at the time that the policy shift was “not a special arrangement for China.” Chinese banks had lobbied for the change, though, which was a boon for ICBC.
Unlike the subsidiary — a legal entity focused solely on retail clients and small firms — ICBC’s London branch could grow rapidly and execute much larger transactions for major corporate clients while remaining under the control of the Chinese parent. A spokesperson for the Prudential Regulation Authority told ICIJ in an email that the agency does “not comment on firms or issues.”
Despite their distinct legal statuses, the two units shared offices a few steps from the famed central bank headquarters, as well as employees, including managers and other staff dispatched from China in addition to locally recruited bankers. The Chinese staff were encouraged to take part in London’s cultural life and promote ICBC’s brand; more than once they joined the Lord Mayor’s Show parade through the city’s streets alongside a pair of panda mascots.
Like most Chinese companies, ICBC has a Communist Party committee, an internal cell that ensures its operations are aligned with — and advance — the party’s interests. Managers at ICBC London, like their peers in China, pledged to implement government policies, the records show. Some Chinese managers appointed to lead the London operations were internally referred to as comrades.
With more than $8 trillion in assets, ICBC is China’s biggest commercial bank, placing it among an elite group of four state-owned financial behemoths so powerful they have become “their own little empires,” according to Daniel Koss, who teaches East Asian politics at Harvard University and has studied Chinese banks. At the same time, the so-called Big Four banks — which also include Bank of China, Agricultural Bank of China and China Construction Bank — adhere to the ruling Communist Party guidelines for two reasons. “There’s the ideological goal, which is to be loyal and understand Xi Jinping’s policy,” Koss said in an interview with ICIJ. “And a more practical one: to get more funding, more credit and approval for politically useful projects.”
When assessing clients, the records show, ICBC London bankers weighed the commercial value of deals against borrowers’ ability to advance Beijing’s economic agenda. This included policies such as Going Global, focused on helping Chinese firms access foreign markets, and the Belt and Road Initiative, a massive infrastructure and influence scheme spearheaded by Xi. In some cases, the bank waived its own anti-money laundering checks.
In 2013, ICBC London saw an attractive client in China Tobacco International, which operates under the State Tobacco Monopoly Administration, according to internal memos. Other banks had shied away from financing unlisted Chinese companies with opaque financial flows. But the state company’s ties to China’s political elite made it particularly appealing to ICBC: The deputy director of the tobacco monopoly was then-Premier Li Keqiang’s younger brother. China Tobacco International could not be reached for comment.
About two years into the relationship — after the branch had financed more than $350 million in trade linked to China Tobacco International — a client review revealed that the branch didn’t have “vital” information on the company’s directors and financials. To renew a loan that promised to yield $3 million of annual income for the bank, ICBC London’s head of commodity and structured finance, Julian Madgett, flew to Raleigh, N.C., to collect one of the missing documents from China Tobacco’s North America office. The company’s U.S. partner, Alliance One International, provided another one. Madgett later described the process as “exhausting” in an email to his colleagues. (Madgett told ICIJ that he no longer works for ICBC and declined to comment.)
ICBC London made an exception to its protocols and signed off on the “recalcitrant” client’s due diligence approvals, despite failing to confirm personal details of two China Tobacco International directors. The deal went through a few weeks later.
Such clashes between compliance staff in London and their managers were common, ICIJ found. Some officers worried that the Chinese headquarters’ more lax standards led their bosses to ignore compliance advice on handling risky clients. But managers warned that the officers’ risk aversion was stifling growth. “Their approach tends to be stricter than necessary, perhaps because they lack a comprehensive understanding of the business,” Xiao Lu, then-deputy general manager of the London subsidiary, said during a 2018 audit. “As a result, they have significantly curtailed the scope of permissible business activities.” (Lu did not respond to ICIJ’s request for comment.)
In reality, the bank’s risk officers had reason for concern. In 2015, along with another bank, ICBC London had approved a $351.5 million loan for a subsidiary of Sanpower, the Chinese real estate conglomerate controlled by Yuan Yafei, a tycoon who was then a member of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, an advisory body. The former government official turned entrepreneur acquired the British department store chain House of Fraser during a buying spree of Western brands, promising to revive the indebted retailer that had once owned Harrods. Instead, the company soon became insolvent, putting thousands of jobs at risk. ICBC faced a loss of more than $125 million, records show. Sanpower did not respond to ICIJ’s requests for comment.
The bank’s London branch recovered at least $29 million in 2019 following a meeting with the client in Nanjing, according to an internal memo. Ruixiang Han, ICBC London’s top executive at the time, explained the reason for the original risky lending decision during an internal meeting: “namely the involvement of a strong Chinese parent, Sanpower.”
‘Strategic customer’
No client tested the relationship between the bank’s compliance officers in London and their managers in Beijing more than Huawei — the symbol of the U.S.-China battle for technological supremacy.
Huawei was founded in 1987 by a former military engineer as a small reseller of imported telephone switches. Within a decade, it prevailed over competitors to supply innovative network equipment to the Chinese army and other government bodies, earning the “national champion” status reserved for firms that bolster Beijing’s strategic aims. The Chinese government backed its international ambitions and used it as a “tool of diplomacy” in developing countries lacking digital infrastructure, according to Antonia Hmaidi, a senior analyst at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies.
But Huawei’s expansion, at home and abroad, was mired in controversy. The company sold cellphones to consumers and network equipment to the world’s largest telecom operators. It also supplied its technology to oppressive regimes in Iraq and Iran, according to U.S. intelligence. Huawei files also showed the company promoted facial recognition technology that was deployed in China’s Xinjiang autonomous region, where Xi’s government has orchestrated a repression campaign against the Muslim Uyghur minority through mass internment, pervasive surveillance and forced labor.
In the summer of 2018, despite mounting U.S. pressure over concerns Huawei’s networks could be used for espionage, the telecom powerhouse was in full expansion mode. The company is known for its “warrior” culture and a refusal to “admit defeat,” Hmaidi said, and it had the government and state banks at its side.
ICBC considered Huawei “a strategic customer” and provided loans, cash management and other services, the records show. At the time, the company’s account with ICBC’s branch in Shenzhen, where Huawei is headquartered, had an average daily balance of about $1.2 billion and “wealth management products” worth $7.3 billion.
When Huawei opened an account for a U.K. subsidiary with ICBC London, it was classified as a “going out” customer, referring to Chinese companies that need financial support to expand overseas. The subsidiary, Huawei Global Finance UK Ltd., provided financial services to other Huawei entities around the world and increased ICBC London’s total client deposits by about 66%, the records show. Then in December 2018, breaking news triggered an alert in the bank’s internal system, according to an operational incident report and other confidential ICBC records.
Around 11 a.m., on Dec. 1, Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s CFO and the founder’s daughter, disembarked from a Cathay Pacific flight at Vancouver International Airport. She was waiting to board her connecting flight to Mexico when Canadian border agents stopped her for questioning. Canadian federal police formally arrested her hours later. Closed-circuit television footage from that morning showed Meng wearing comfortable clothing: a T-shirt, dark pants and white shoes. She had no idea that the U.S. had issued a warrant for her arrest on fraud charges related to violations of sanctions against Iran, her father, Ren Zhengfei, later told Canadian media.
The arrest of such a high-profile executive sent shockwaves around the world. Nine days later, Chinese authorities retaliated by detaining two Canadians in Beijing and Dandong. A Vancouver court soon released Meng under house arrest after payment of her $7.5 million bail. The Canadians — a former diplomat and a consultant — would remain in their prison cells for more than 1,000 days.
In London, ICBC officers closely monitored the news for nearly two months. Then, a day after the U.S. Justice Department indicted Meng and Huawei for sanctions violations, money laundering and other crimes, the bankers called an emergency meeting. ICBC London compliance officers and senior managers agreed to temporarily suspend business with Huawei until it provided information needed to assess whether its deposited funds were associated with the alleged crimes. Instead of supplying the information, Huawei’s U.K. managers demanded an urgent, in-person meeting with the bankers, the bank records show.
Late Friday afternoon, on Feb. 1, 2019, Huawei representatives visited ICBC London’s office on King William Street with a request, according to a memo detailing the events. Huawei wanted to withdraw all of its subsidiary’s deposits — “quickly.”
During the meeting, two of the bank’s senior managers, Chenhu Liu and Xiao Lu, sought “to prevent the transaction from taking place,” the memo said. Huawei was, after all, one of the branch’s largest depositors, and withdrawing the funds would have amounted to a significant loss. But these efforts “proved fruitless.” Huawei’s executives had already asked the bank’s headquarters in Beijing to approve the transfer. The request had been greenlit.
‘Very high risk’
The following day, at 8 a.m. in London, ICBC executives in Beijing held a conference call with the nine London officers called in to facilitate the transfer. The executives told the bankers that ICBC’s headquarters would ensure the branch had enough funds to finance its operations, according to the bank files. That morning, the officers wired $1.3 billion from Huawei’s ICBC account in London to its account in Shenzhen.
The news of the transfer only reached the branch’s compliance team on Monday, raising alarm bells. Eric Guegan, ICBC London’s money laundering reporting officer at the time, launched an internal investigation and interviewed the officers involved in the transaction over the next two weeks. (Guegan did not respond to ICIJ and The Times’ requests for comment.)
“It is unusual to execute payments outside of London business hours[,] and by mobilising a team to come in on a Saturday to execute significant payments increases the possibility for fraud,” Guegan said, according to an internal memo. He believed his colleagues should have completed a thorough investigation before releasing the funds but noted their decision was made “under pressure from Huawei” and Beijing headquarters.
Guegan flagged that the transfer raised ethical issues: ICBC’s China corporate team had ignored the earlier decision to suspend business with Huawei and executed the transfer without checking if the funds were linked to the alleged crimes. And some of those London officers had not challenged ICBC executives’ view that the U.S. government allegations were unsubstantiated and politically motivated, he wrote. He described their eagerness to please the head office as “unorthodox.”
“There is a possibility that Huawei were seeking to repatriate funds in order to avoid asset freezing by US Sanctions investigators,” Guegan concluded. “The relationship with [head office] requires review and we need to think about when to push back.”
There is a possibility that Huawei were seeking to repatriate funds in order to avoid asset freezing by US Sanctions investigators.
— ICBC London’s money laundering reporting officer in an internal memo
He then emailed ICBC London executives recommending “enhanced due diligence” on Huawei — a standard procedure for customers accused of wrongdoing. Within 15 minutes, Han, the CEO, replied, relaying clear instructions from headquarters: “carry on business with Huawei.” The message echoed an earlier one from ICBC’s Shenzhen branch, which had requested that all ICBC overseas subsidiaries “support Huawei in terms of the opening of new accounts and the possible expansion of business,” according to internal emails.
Indeed, the tech giant wanted to partner with ICBC London to open a new cash account to facilitate the group’s payment of suppliers, payroll and other expenses internationally. Later that month, Huawei’s U.K. managers invited Guegan and four other ICBC London officers for a morning meeting at Huawei’s London office, in a modern skyscraper nearby. Huawei’s compliance manager, Nelson Wang, dialed in from Shenzhen.
Wang explained some of the company’s new policies, underscoring the U.K. subsidiary’s independence and renewed focus on compliance. Huawei, he said, was “not a financial institution but a telecoms company” and therefore had less strict regulatory obligations than a bank. He acknowledged that Huawei was still operating in Syria, as well as two other U.S.-sanctioned countries, Iran and Cuba, where he estimated it made $13 million annually — 1.5% of its global revenue. He added that Huawei may do business with some sanctioned Russian entities but, he said, transactions linked to those activities would be flagged internally and would not go through ICBC London.
The meeting lasted less than two hours. Guegan described it as “cordial” and “held in a transparent manner,” in an internal report. But he had reservations about Huawei’s anti-bribery and corruption policy, which “was not explained convincingly,” he wrote.
Other ICBC branches had their own concerns about keeping Huawei as a client because of its murky ownership structure, the report said. Huawei had claimed that the majority of its shares were then owned by about 100,000 employees through an employee shareholding scheme. “As of today, no independent evidence exists that can verify whether or not the information regarding the ownership and the management of Huawei Union and the Chinese Government’s involvement is factual,” said an internal ICBC London memo. Huawei has long insisted that it’s not state owned or controlled, but U.S. officials and international researchers have questioned whether its executives and shareholders are truly independent.
A few weeks after the meeting at Huawei’s London office, an external due diligence firm concluded that Huawei was a “Very high risk” client for ICBC London because of its alleged links to the Chinese government and corruption, fraud and other criminal allegations in multiple countries, from the U.S. to the Solomon Islands and Brazil. But none of that mattered to ICBC’s executives. In his final report, Guegan wrote that senior management had fought a “sustained campaign” to retain the business. By October 2019, he had resigned.
“I’m sure the pressure would be exerted from all sides to make sure the relationship is working as smoothly as possible and push the boundaries of legal requirements to the limit,” said Graham Barrow, an anti-money laundering expert and former consultant for major banks. “Ultimately [Huawei and ICBC] share the same allegiance, which is back to China,” Barrow told ICIJ.
Lessons learned
Only a year after ICBC London accepted Huawei’s U.K. subsidiary as a promising client, the tech giant’s fortunes had changed. While Meng fought extradition to the U.S., the Trump administration had added Huawei and 68 of its non-U.S. affiliates, including Huawei Global Finance UK, to a list of companies heavily restricted from buying U.S. technology. Under pressure from their most powerful ally, the U.K. and several other countries moved to ban local cell providers from buying Huawei 5G equipment, citing national security concerns.
ICBC remained a valuable ally for the besieged company. The bank opened new accounts for Huawei in Sydney and Frankfurt, according to an internal report. And to show its “commitment” to helping Huawei counter U.S. sanctions and diversify its funding, ICBC became one of the main underwriters in the company’s first domestic bond sale, worth about $850 million. The Chinese government came to the rescue and “ensured their survival,” said Hmaidi, the China tech expert. “No one else would have given them a loan in this situation because no one knew what was going to happen.”
In London, the records show, a group of senior officers reviewed the handling of the Huawei transfer during a conference call with headquarters’ senior bankers and dismissed some of the mistakes as past mishaps. “[The] case demonstrated the bad culture the Bank had at the time,” Robert Clark, ICBC London chief risk officer, told his colleagues. Jingtang Xie, who headed the Overseas Anti Money Laundering Division in Beijing, suggested that the bank introduce new rules to ensure compliance officers had to approve large transactions to avoid similar problems in the future. “Lessons should be learned for the Bank to strengthen future controls,” Xie said.
In response to ICIJ’s questions, Clark, who retired last year, said that ICBC London has always complied with U.K. regulations. In a message to ICIJ, he declined to comment on the Huawei case but noted that “for Head Office in Beijing [Huawei] was and no doubt remains a priority client.” He added: “The sensitivities around Huawei were well-understood in 2019 and … we acted to protect ICBC London from any regulatory breaches.”
ICBC London ultimately decided to keep Huawei’s U.K. subsidiary as a client and support the company’s global ambitions. In Africa, records show, the bank leveraged Beijing’s influence and trade ties to help some governments acquire Huawei technology by providing financing in renminbi, the Chinese currency. In 2022, ICBC London helped the bank’s Shenzhen branch provide a loan worth about $3 million to a Nigerian bank that was short of U.S. dollars and planned to finance the acquisition of Huawei equipment by MTN Nigeria Communications, one of the country’s largest mobile operators.
ICBC has bankrolled Huawei projects globally for more than 20 years
That same year, ICBC London happily announced in an internal strategy plan: “We have become the cash management bank for clients such as Huawei UK.” Even so, Huawei continued to rely on ICBC’s Beijing headquarters — instead of the bank managers in London — when it needed favors for its U.K. subsidiary.
Huawei remained on the branch’s list of high-risk clients that required additional screening. But in early 2023, the tech giant complained that due diligence requirements were slowing payments. ICBC Beijing managers urgently asked ICBC London officers to speed up the process. “The further [cooperation] between ICBC head office and Huawei group may be effected if we could not offer a more efficient payment resolution to them,” a Beijing officer told a subordinate in London in an email.
ICBC London officers eventually agreed to let Huawei’s transactions go through the account first and then request related information and documents later — just like other ICBC branches in Europe were doing. A bank officer passed on the usual message to her London colleagues: “Head office also mentioned that Huawei is an very important client to them.”
United States v. Huawei Technologies
Last week, lawyers representing Huawei and the U.S. government gathered in a federal courtroom in New York for the opening statements in the high-profile trial that could decide whether the Chinese company is guilty of violating sanctions laws and other crimes.
“The entire business operated through a pattern of theft, lies and cover-ups,” Justice Department attorney Taylor Stout told the court. “For 20 years, that’s how Huawei … abused the American financial system … to dominate the telecommunication industry around the world.” Brian Heberlig, one of Huawei’s defense lawyers, rejected the accusation. “Huawei earned its success,” he said. “There was no blueprint for crime.”
More than seven years have passed since the Justice Department indicted Huawei. Meng was allowed to return to China in 2021 after reaching an agreement with prosecutors in which she admitted to misleading a global financial institution about Huawei’s business in Iran. The charges against her were later dismissed but prosecutors are still expected to submit her admissions as evidence.
The start of the Huawei trial comes ahead of Xi’s scheduled visit to Washington, D.C., to meet with U.S. President Donald Trump to discuss trade and other sensitive topics. Experts told ICIJ that the verdict will not change the fact that Huawei is one of the world’s most influential tech companies.
Since the indictment, the tech giant has provided critical — and cheap — technology to large parts of the world and become a leading firm in the emerging artificial intelligence industry, according to Tim Rühlig, a senior China analyst at the European Union Institute for Security Studies. “Today, these dependencies are giving China leverage,” Rühlig told ICIJ. “There is a vital interest of the party-state that Huawei stays technologically on top, that it is competitive, that it prospers.”
ICIJ’s Denise Ajiri, Agustin Armendariz, Jelena Cosic, Delphine Reuter and Jacob Silverman contributed reporting.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Russian Refinery, Aircraft Plant and Ozon Facility in Massive Overnight Attack
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces launched a massive drone and missile attack on several Russian regions early Tuesday morning, Sept. 15, hitting a Rosneft-owned oil refinery in the Samara region and other industrial facilities.
The Samara region was targeted by more than 40 drones, according to regional Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Damage was sustained by one of the industrial facilities as well as several residential buildings,” he wrote on Telegram, adding that there were no casualties.
According to the Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+, the Rosneft-owned Syzran Oil Refinery was among the targets.
The facility has an annual crude oil processing capacity of about 8.5 million tons and produces approximately 800,000 tons of gasoline and 1.5 million tons of diesel fuel annually.
Following the attack, storage tanks containing petroleum products caught fire at the facility. The refinery was previously struck by drones on Aug. 4.
Later, the General Staff of Ukraine confirmed the strike on the Syzran Oil Refinery.
“Units of the Ukrainian Defense Forces struck the Syzran Oil Refinery (JSC) in Russia’s Samara region and the ‘Atlant Aero’ facility in Taganrog, Rostov region.”
An impact followed by a fire was recorded at the Syzran Oil Refinery. The AVT-6 primary oil processing unit and the tank farm were hit, the report states.
The plant produces gasoline, diesel and aviation fuel, as well as other petroleum products. The facility supplies the needs of the Russian armed forces, the General Staff added.
Intel Reveals 19 Russian Missile, Drone Firms Still Outside International Sanctions
Russian facilities reportedly hit
In the Rostov Oblast, a massive missile attack resulted in “multiple impacts on the ground” and several fires, Oblast Governor Yuri Slyusar reported.
According to Slyusar, two apartment buildings and three private homes, an educational institution, commercial buildings, agricultural warehouses, a grocery store and an Ozon logistics center were damaged.
“Preliminary information indicates there are no fatalities or injuries,” Slyusar wrote.
Exilenova+ also reported that the Beriev Taganrog Aviation Scientific-Technical Complex was among the targets of the missile strike.
The Beriev TANTK aircraft plant in Taganrog is a key Russian aircraft repair and maintenance facility. OSINT analysts reported that Russian military aircraft were undergoing repairs there at the time of the strike, although the specific types and number of aircraft could not be independently confirmed.
Later, the General Staff clarified that explosions and a fire were recorded at the “Atlant Aero” facility, although earlier reports indicated that the Beriev plant had been hit.
“Atlant Aero” specializes in the manufacture of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and their components. Specifically, the enterprise produces “Molniya” strike-reconnaissance UAVs and components for “Orion” UAVs.
The company is involved in meeting the Russian armed forces’ requirements for unmanned systems, the General Staff added.
Strikes come amid energy truce talks
The attack came amid uncertainty over a proposed agreement to halt strikes on energy infrastructure.
US President Donald Trump recently said that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop attacking each other’s energy facilities.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv was prepared to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries if its partners could guarantee that Russia would also stop attacking Ukraine’s energy sector. He emphasized that any such agreement would need to be reliable and long-lasting.
However, according to sources cited by the Financial Times (FT), Russian President Vladimir Putin is unwilling to agree to a mutual halt to strikes on energy infrastructure before winter.
The sources said Putin believes continued attacks on Ukraine’s energy sector could increase pressure on Kyiv and force it to make concessions.
At the same time, sources told the publication that Moscow and Kyiv have resumed negotiations over a possible halt to strikes on energy facilities, although no final agreement has been reached.
In a morning update on Telegram, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Russia continues its strikes on Ukraine’s energy sector, logistics networks and critical infrastructure.
“And our responses to them are significant. There are new results from Ukraine’s Defense Forces regarding the oil refinery in Syzran; there were also hits on a drone manufacturing plant in Taganrog and a drone training and launch site in the Oryol region.”

articles.title: Estonian minister: Lithuania drone downing a first for NATO Baltic mission
articles.body:
Estonian minister: Lithuania drone downing a first for NATO Baltic mission
NATO fighter jets downing a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace overnight was a first of a kind for the newly upgraded Baltic Air Defense mission, Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said.
Tsahkna said the response showed NATO's readiness to defend allied territory, and linked the incident to the wider threat Russia poses to the alliance's eastern flank.
Italian Eurofighters shot down the drone near Pratkūnai, about 60 miles west of Vilnius, after it entered from Belarus and loitered roughly half an hour in Lithuanian airspace.
Tsahkna said the drone was detected and shot down, ensuring the security of Lithuanian airspace and its people. "Today once again demonstrated that NATO acts in accordance with established plans to defend Allied territory, doing so decisively and successfully," the minister said via a press release.
NATO acted swiftly and decisively after a drone entered Lithuanian airspace overnight, with NATO fighter jets detecting and shooting it down.
This is a clear demonstration of Allied readiness to defend NATO territory and a reminder that Russia's war against Ukraine directly…
The intercept was the first time fighter jets on NATO's Baltic Air Defense mission had shot down a drone over Lithuania, following its announcement. The mission is an upgrade of the preceding air policing mission, in place for 20 years now.
Tsahkna added the incident underlined the importance of the Baltic air defense mission and of strengthening allied deterrence. He added that Russia's war in Ukraine has a direct impact on the security of NATO members.
"Russia's aggression against Ukraine is not only Ukraine's problem. Its effects and risks extend to our own borders, and it is therefore in our own interests to help achieve a just and lasting peace," Tsahkna continued via a press release.
Lithuanian officials said the drone likely came from Belarus. The incident follows the recent firing signal flares by a Russian frigate towards a Danish military helicopter, and a drone strike which hit the Ukraine-Poland border zone shortly after a train full of high-level European leaders, including from Estonia, passed through.
LRT reported the drone intercepted in Lithuania was brought down near the village of Pratkūnai in the Kaišiadorys district, about 60 miles west of Vilnius, after entering from Belarus and spending roughly half an hour in Lithuanian airspace. Italian Eurofighters based at the Šiauliai air base carried out the intercept. Lithuanian officials said the wreckage is being examined and would not draw conclusions before the investigation is complete, though one Lithuanian official said there was a high probability the drone carried an explosive charge.
Italian Eurofighters are currently leading the mission in Šiauliai, while F-16s in Turkish Air Force service and Spanish Air Force F-18s hold the Ämari deployment.

articles.title: Pentagon report puts Iran war cost at $33.4 billion, cites US weapons shortfalls and extensive base
articles.body:
Pentagon report puts Iran war cost at $33.4 billion, cites US weapons shortfalls and extensive base
TEHRAN- A newly released US government report has shed further light on the financial and military costs of Washington’s war with Iran, estimating that the conflict had cost the United States $33.4 billion by June 29, while Iranian strikes damaged or destroyed hundreds of structures and dozens of American aircraft across US military facilities in the Middle East.
The figures are contained in the latest Lead Inspector General report to Congress, issued by the US Department of Defense and covering the conflict through the end of June. The assessment highlights not only the scale of material damage sustained by US forces but also mounting pressure on American weapons stockpiles and the defense-industrial base responsible for replenishing them.
Billions spent as US munitions stocks come under pressure
According to the report, $22.3 billion of the $33.4 billion total was spent on munitions, while equipment losses accounted for another $3.7 billion and other expenses for approximately $7.4 billion. The heavy consumption of American weapons during the campaign, the report said, “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply.”
The assessment is significant because the United States entered the conflict with one of the world’s largest and most sophisticated military arsenals, yet the pace of weapons expenditure exposed limitations in its ability to rapidly replenish key systems during a sustained high-intensity conflict.
The report also puts the direct physical damage to US diplomatic facilities in Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates at $184 million because of Iranian attacks. Separate emergency response and evacuation operations added substantially to the overall cost of the conflict.
The findings contrast with repeated assurances from US President Donald Trump that American weapons production remains exceptionally strong. Ahead of the report’s release, Trump said the United States was producing more “Exquisite and Elite Weapons” than at any point in its history.
Iranian strikes damage US aircraft and military infrastructure
The Pentagon assessment also documents the impact of Iranian attacks on US military installations across the region. Hundreds of buildings and other structures were damaged or destroyed, while dozens of aircraft were lost or damaged by the end of June.
Among the aircraft affected was an F-35A Lightning II, which sustained damage from Iranian fire. The incident was particularly notable because it represented the first reported combat damage to an F-35A, one of the most advanced and expensive aircraft in the US inventory.
The report also recorded the destruction of four F-15E Strike Eagle fighters and one A-10 Thunderbolt II, while seven KC-135 Stratotanker aerial-refueling aircraft were damaged or destroyed. In addition, seven helicopters and more than 30 unmanned aircraft were lost.
Earlier Congressional Research Service assessments had already identified at least 42 US aircraft lost or damaged during Operation Epic Fury, although the CRS cautioned that its figures were based on publicly available information and could be revised as additional information emerged. 
 
 Continuing losses underline the cost of the campaign
The military costs have continued to accumulate beyond the period covered by the Pentagon report. In early September, an Iranian ballistic-missile attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan damaged an A-10 and approximately eight F-15 aircraft, according to US officials. The A-10 reportedly suffered severe damage to one wing, while the F-15s were assessed as serviceable after sustaining lighter damage.
The attack also required US forces to launch roughly 30 Patriot interceptors, adding to concerns over the availability of expensive air-defense munitions. Reuters reported that US officials and analysts have warned of pressure on interceptor inventories after months of sustained operations.
The emerging picture is therefore one of a conflict imposing costs well beyond the battlefield itself. In addition to the billions of dollars spent on combat operations, the United States has faced damage to bases and aircraft, depletion of high-value munitions and growing demands on its defense-industrial supply chain.
For Washington, the report offers a rare official accounting of the price of the Iran war and highlights a central challenge of prolonged high-intensity warfare: maintaining the pace of weapons consumption while simultaneously replacing sophisticated systems that are costly, technologically complex, and difficult to produce at scale.

articles.title: Russian regions report Ukrainian strikes as Rostov governor cites 'massive' missile attack
articles.body:
Elena Teslova
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
Ukrainian missile and drone strikes hit several Russian regions early Tuesday, with Kyiv confirming attacks on an oil refinery and a drone production plant as Russian authorities reported damage to residential, industrial and commercial sites.
Rostov Governor Yury Slyusar said the region was subjected to a “massive missile attack,” with damage reported in the city of Taganrog.
An educational institution, commercial building, gas pipeline, agricultural warehouses, grocery store and Ozon warehouse were damaged, Slyusar said on Telegram. Taganrog Mayor Svetlana Kambaeva said five apartment buildings were also damaged, but reported no casualties.
Reports also indicated damage near the Taganrog Aviation Scientific and Technical Complex, although the extent and circumstances were not immediately confirmed by regional authorities.
Ukraine's General Staff said its forces struck the Atlant Aero plant in Taganrog, which it said manufactures drones.
In the Samara region, more than 40 drones were shot down overnight, Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said. An industrial facility and several residential buildings were damaged, but no deaths were reported, he added.
Ukraine's General Staff said its forces struck the Syzran oil refinery, reporting a fire and damage to a crude oil distillation unit and storage tanks.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also confirmed strikes on the Syzran refinery and a drone production facility in Taganrog. He said Ukrainian forces had also struck a drone preparation and launch site in the Oryol region and targets in the Black Sea.
In the Voronezh region, Governor Alexander Gusev said the attack damaged windows at a municipal building as well as the roofs and facades of four private houses. No casualties were reported, he said.
Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry said its forces carried out group strikes with attack drones on logistics centers and ports in Ukraine, as well as vessels it said were used by the Ukrainian armed forces.
In the Odesa region, the ministry said a logistics center used to store and distribute military cargo arriving in Ukraine from abroad was hit in the settlement of Velyka Balka.
At the port of Chornomorsk, a dry cargo vessel and a ferry that the ministry said had delivered cargo intended for the Ukrainian armed forces were also hit, it added.
Russian forces also continued strikes on railway infrastructure in western Ukraine used to transport military cargo from European countries, the ministry said.

articles.title: Gas Stations Hit, Explosions Rock Kyiv as Russia Launches 200-Drone Attack
articles.body:
Russian forces attacked Kyiv with drones early Tuesday, Sept. 15, killing one person and injuring at least seven others, while UAV strikes and falling debris damaged buildings and gas stations across the capital, according to Ukrainian officials.
The Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) announced an air raid alert at 5:25 a.m.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
At the same time, the Ukrainian Air Force tracked jet-powered drones entering the Kyiv region and heading toward the capital before subsequently appearing over the city itself.
Explosions were heard in Kyiv at approximately 5:34 a.m. and again at 5:42 a.m.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko later reported on Telegram that a Russian drone had struck a gas station in the city’s Darnytskyi district, injuring one person.
“Medics hospitalized one wounded person. The man is in critical condition,” he wrote.
He also said that, according to preliminary information, a warehouse facility in the Obolonskyi district had been hit.
A drone threat was announced in Kyiv again at 7:49 a.m. At around 8 a.m., Kyiv Post reporters heard a very loud explosion.
Klitschko subsequently confirmed that a UAV had apparently struck a non-residential area in the Solomianskyi district.
“Emergency services are en route to the scene,” he added.
In an 8:51 a.m. report, Klitschko said heavy smoke was reported in the Holosiivskyi district following a drone strike on a gas station.
NATO Jets Shoot Down Drone Over Lithuania
“Two people have already been wounded in the morning attack on the capital. Medics have hospitalized both of the wounded,” the mayor said.
Klitschko later clarified that the number of casualties had risen to four. All four are being treated in city hospitals, with two in critical condition.
The State Emergency Service (DSNS) later reported that eight people in Kyiv had been injured by Russian strikes since the start of the day.
“Solomianskyi district: a non-residential building was hit; no fire broke out. Six people were injured,” the report said.
Rescuers also confirmed that a gas station in the Darnytskyi district had been hit, injuring one person. The resulting fire was minor and was extinguished with fire extinguishers.
“Holosiivskyi district: a strike occurred at a gas station. One person was injured. The fire has been extinguished. Obolonskyi district: a non-residential building caught fire. Firefighters have brought the blaze under control,” the DSNS added.
In a 10:35 a.m. report, Klitschko announced that one of the people injured in the morning attack on the capital had died in hospital.
“The man had been hospitalized in critical condition,” he added.
187 drones downed or suppressed
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russia launched 200 strike UAVs against Ukraine starting at 6 p.m. on Sept. 14. The attack included Shahed-type drones, including jet-powered variants, as well as Gerbera and “Parodiya” (Parody) decoy drones.
The attack was repelled by Ukrainian aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups.
“According to preliminary data, as of 8:00 a.m., air defense forces had shot down or suppressed 187 enemy UAVs,” the Air Force said.
Russian drones were recorded striking seven locations, while debris from downed targets fell at three other sites.
This story will be updated as new details become available.

articles.title: Poland Scrambles Jets as Russia Attacks Western Ukraine With Jet-Powered Drones
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Poland Scrambles Jets as Russia Attacks Western Ukraine With Jet-Powered Drones
Poland scrambled fighter jets overnight on September 15 in response to renewed Russian attacks on western Ukraine involving jet-powered strike drones, Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command reported.
At around 4 a.m., the Operational Command said Polish and allied aircraft had been deployed as Russian jet-powered drones carried out strikes against targets in Ukraine. Ground-based air defense and radar systems were also placed on heightened readiness.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The measures were taken as a precaution to protect Polish airspace and “aimed at securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions.”
At around 6:30 a.m., the Operational Command announced that the potential threat had passed and that the forces and systems activated during the alert were returning to standard operational status.
“No violations of Polish airspace were recorded,” the Operational Command said.
The heightened readiness in Poland came as NATO responded to another aerial incident elsewhere on its eastern flank. Earlier the same night, NATO aircraft intercepted and destroyed an unidentified drone that entered Lithuanian airspace, with preliminary information indicating that it had arrived from Belarus, according to Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT.
The drone crossed into Lithuania shortly after midnight, triggering air alerts in several areas. About 30 minutes later, NATO fighter jets operating from the Šiauliai Air Base intercepted and shot down the aircraft over the Kaunas region.
Lithuania’s military said Italian fighter jets carried out the interception. The drone’s wreckage was subsequently found in a rural area, where police cordoned off and secured the site.
The incidents follow another recent airspace breach involving a NATO member. On September 8, Romania deployed two F-18 fighter jets after military radar detected an aerial object entering Romanian airspace at around 4:47 p.m., roughly 18 kilometers north of Roman.
The detection prompted air raid warnings in several nearby communities. Shortly beforehand, at approximately 4:20 p.m., neighboring Moldova reported that a drone, preliminarily identified as a Shahed, had entered its territory.
