articles.title: Zaluzhny: desire to de-occupy territories using Soviet methods drove mobilization into deadlock
articles.body:
Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Ukraine to the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021–24) Valeriy Zaluzhny has noted that the Russian-Ukrainian war has become not only a war of technologies, but also a war of strategies and doctrines that change under the pressure of progress, and therefore it is a major mistake to obsess over individual technologies and their PR, which complements Soviet strategy and requires Soviet-type executors.
"It was precisely the desire to de-occupy territories and hold them using Soviet methods and strategies, only with new weapons, that drove mobilization into a deadlock. Mobilization provided only one chance, and there were fewer and fewer willing to take it. For we are unable to endure a war of machines against a huge Soviet country where people are essentially turned into machines and thrown to fight against real machines... It is necessary, while recognizing technologies as a new weapon, to remember the patterns of the development of military art and invariably form new forms and methods of their application based on this. And only after that should organizational changes be carried out in the structure of the Armed Forces that apply this new weapon in new forms and methods. It is precisely in this place that mobilization is located as part of a new strategy based on new weapons and precisely new, rather than Soviet, forms and methods of application," Zaluzhny wrote in his article published in Ukrainska Pravda on Tuesday.
He emphasized that between Ukraine and Russia it is no longer a war of drones, since drones "have transformed into forms of weaponry more familiar to us from the past, lowering costs and availability while increasing effectiveness."
According to the diplomat, the old rules no longer apply, and therefore modern warfare requires new doctrines, while Ukraine is already experiencing the pressure of "known intermediaries" on itself due to the introduction of a new approach to waging war, without specifying who is meant. "Meanwhile, a war of technologies is already underway, and Ukraine is already experiencing systemic pressure, which is the result of implementing not only technologies, but also a new doctrinal approach to their application, including production and research as an integral part of strategy. This very thing gives Russia the right to issue ultimatums to us through known intermediaries. This is precisely what is directed at and can lead to a whole series of crises," Zaluzhny writes.
He stressed that a war of attrition "is not only battles, but also societal breakdowns, the main thing being who causes them first."
"To find a way out of an entirely natural situation, an understanding of the search for and implementation of precisely a systemic response to Russia's pressure is needed. This systemic response must be based on building such a strategy where joint production and the implementation of new technological solutions must become part of systemic steps both for defense and for influencing Russia's ability to continue the war. For this, of course, the search remains urgent for precisely resource and technological alliances capable of ensuring this production, including to satisfy our own defense needs. This production must be doctrinally included as part of the victory strategy, where it is not a magical model of weaponry that is produced, but the entire necessary new arsenal, including civilian-purpose items in accordance with the conditions of progress," Zaluzhny summarized.

articles.title: Ukraine to Boost Protection of Railways, Fuel Stations
articles.body:
Ukraine will strengthen protection for railways, gas stations and other critical enterprises against Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday, Sept. 15.
Zelensky made the announcement after a meeting of Ukraine’s top military command, where officials discussed contracts for systems protecting critical infrastructure and logistics.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine to expand electronic warfare and air defense
Officials reviewed the security needs of Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s national railway operator, fuel station networks and other facilities identified as priority targets for Russian strikes.
“Solutions for protection exist,” Zelensky said. “In particular, we will significantly strengthen the electronic warfare component and increase procurement volumes. The contracts have been confirmed.”
The president said mobile fire groups and air-defense lines protecting designated facilities would also be reorganized. He did not disclose details of the protection plans.
The meeting came amid continued Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy and logistics infrastructure, including strikes on fuel stations in Kyiv. Kyiv has said that Russia’s campaign against critical infrastructure is continuing despite discussions about a possible pause in energy strikes. Previously, Moscow and Kyiv had not agreed on formal terms for such a truce.
Backup logistics routes planned for frontline regions
Zelensky instructed the Finance Ministry to provide additional resources for logistics needs and thanked international partners helping maintain uninterrupted railway operations.
Russian Forces Use Artificial Intelligence to Show Artificial Victory
Officials also discussed railway security in border areas near European Union countries and Moldova, as well as support for Ukrzaliznytsia’s rolling-stock repairs and equipment supplies.
The government is preparing backup logistics routes for frontline regions, including plans to combine rail and bus transport when necessary.
“Details are not public,” Zelensky said of updated measures to protect critical infrastructure.

articles.title: Israeli official calls for int'l coalition against Houthis
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israeli official calls for coalition against Yemen's Houthis as military advises against direct action
An Israeli official has called for an international coalition to confront Yemen's Houthis, warning that failure to form one could lead to chaos in the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, according to Israel's public broadcaster Kan.
The call comes as Israel grows increasingly concerned over Houthi advances around Bab al-Mandab, while the Israeli military has advised the government against launching direct attacks on the group or placing Israel at the forefront of military action.
The unnamed official said that "an international coalition must be formed against the Houthis", adding that without one, "chaos could erupt in one of the world's most important vital shipping routes".
Israel believes there may be no alternative to forming an international coalition to act against the Houthis after the group announced its control of Bab al-Mandab last week, Kan reported.
Hundreds of ships pass through the strait each day between Asia, Africa and the Middle East, including vessels bound for Israel.
Houthi control of the strait could allow the group to disrupt shipping using relatively simple means such as missiles or explosive-laden boats, potentially closing the waterway without the need for coastal defence radar or missile systems.
Israel currently leans towards avoiding direct intervention in the Yemen conflict, Kan reported, while continuing to discuss the issue with regional partners led by the United States.
The Israeli military has separately recommended treating the Houthi threat as an international and regional concern rather than a confrontation led by Israel, according to Haaretz.
Senior Israeli security officials said the recommendation was made during closed discussions in recent days following the Houthi capture of the strategic port city of Mokha and other positions near Bab al-Mandab.
The Houthis have also seized Perim Island and the Hanish Islands in the southern Red Sea after hundreds of Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces reportedly withdrew.
The advances have given the Iran-aligned group an increasingly powerful position around Bab al-Mandab, the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and one of the world's most important maritime trade routes.
Israeli security officials reportedly see an international coalition as a means of keeping international attention focused on Iran over its support for the Houthis.
The approach would allow Israel to avoid taking the lead in another regional military confrontation while encouraging Saudi Arabia, Egypt and other states with interests in Red Sea shipping to take a greater role against the Houthis.
Israeli military officials reportedly assess that Egypt and Saudi Arabia are increasingly alarmed by the Houthi advances.
Egypt is particularly concerned about the economic consequences of further disruption to Red Sea shipping and traffic through the Suez Canal, while Israeli officials believe Saudi Arabia increasingly feels it lacks sufficient US support against renewed Houthi attacks.
Washington has so far resisted Saudi requests for direct US military intervention against the Houthis, according to Reuters, although the US continues to provide intelligence assistance to Riyadh.
The Houthis have meanwhile renewed attacks on Saudi territory, including strikes targeting Saudi Aramco facilities and King Khalid Air Base at Khamis Mushait.
Israel has itself repeatedly attacked Yemen since the outbreak of the Gaza war, carrying out strikes on Houthi-controlled ports, energy infrastructure and other sites that have caused civilian casualties.
The Houthis began targeting Israel and vessels they said were linked to it during Israel's war on Gaza, framing their Red Sea campaign as an attempt to impose a maritime blockade on Israel and force an end to the assault and siege of the Palestinian territory.
Despite Israel maintaining a relatively low public profile over the latest fighting, Haaretz reported that the military continues to prepare for a scenario in which Iran encourages the Houthis to intensify attacks on Israel amid escalating regional tensions.
Israeli security officials reportedly believe, however, that individual military strikes would not provide a long-term solution to the Houthi threat, which they view as deriving partly from the group's ability to disrupt maritime trade and expand the number of fronts confronting Israel.
The coalition call comes days after reports suggested Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had offered Israeli participation with Saudi Arabia in a broader campaign against the Houthis.
The apparent caution within the military does not necessarily indicate opposition to action against the group, but suggests Israeli security officials favour a multinational campaign in which Israel would not assume the leading military role.

articles.title: Pentagon confirms F-35 fighter jet hit by Iran during war
articles.body:
The Iran war has cost $33.4 billion so far, according to a new Pentagon watchdog report. It also confirms a historic first: an F-35A took combat damage
A Pentagon inspector general report found the Iran conflict has cost $33.4 billion through late June, detailing the loss of multiple fighter jets, helicopters and drones alongside severe munitions shortfalls. The report also confirms an F-35A sustained combat damage for the first time in the aircraft's operational history.
American aviation assets also sustained notable combat operational losses throughout the campaign. The findings detail the loss of four F-15E fighter jets, an A-10 ground attack aircraft, seven KC-135 refueling planes, seven helicopters, and over thirty unmanned aerial vehicles. Additionally, a fifth-generation F-35A stealth fighter suffered damage from enemy fire, marking the first time an aircraft of its model sustained combat damage in operational history.
The operational expenditure of advanced precision weaponry has strained national inventory levels, prompting defense procurement officials to seek streamlined supply chain frameworks and accelerated manufacturing timelines.
In response to the documented equipment losses and stockpile drawdowns, executive leadership has emphasized that national defense production remains at historic levels.
MNA

articles.title: Parliament approves CHF3.4 billion for Swiss Armed Forces
articles.body:
Parliament approves CHF3.4 billion for Swiss Armed Forces
The priorities set by the government for the modernisation of the Swiss Armed Forces have been well received by parliament. Following the Senate, the House of Representatives has also approved the Armed Forces Message without amendment – including the supplementary credit for the procurement of F-35 fighter jets.
In total, the government requested commitment credits of around CHF3.4 billion for the armed forces from parliament. It has earmarked around CHF2.4 billion for defence procurement, CHF562 million for property projects and CHF394 million as a supplementary credit for the procurement of F-35 fighter jets.
On Tuesday, the House of Representatives approved the aforementioned credits. Contrary to the proposal of its Security Policy Committee, it decided against a CHF500 million increase for air defence munitions. This decision was passed by 104 votes to 91, with one abstention. The Social Democratic Party, Centre Party, Green Party and Liberal Green Party voted against the additional CHF500 million.
No majority for a ‘rushed exercise’
These funds were to be used for ammunition for ground-based air defence systems of long and medium range, as well as for systems providing indirect fire support at medium range. This was intended to enhance the army’s sustainability.
For the Swiss People’s Party and the Radical-Liberal Party, it would have been imperative to replenish ammunition reserves as quickly as possible. The defeated majority on the committee argued that, due to high demand, ammunition procurement was taking ever longer and costing ever more.
The centre-left warned that the funding for these additional resources was unclear. Linda De Ventura from the Social Democrats warned against a “rush job”.
More
F-35 jets: fixed-price scandal will have no immediate consequences
Additional F-35 credit despite ‘fixed-price fiasco’
All other motions for increases and cuts were also rejected in the House of Representatives. Consequently, following approval by both chambers of parliament, the credits are now a done deal.
A particular point of contention in the debate was the CHF394 million supplementary credit requested by the government for the procurement of F-35 fighter jets. A majority in the House of Representatives wished to proceed with this, even though the parliamentary oversight body had established last week that the fixed price for the purchase of the fighter jets – which had been repeatedly communicated – had never actually existed.
Spokespersons for the centre-right parliamentary groups emphasised that there was no alternative to the F-35 procurement. The left criticised the fact that the report by the House of Representatives’ Committee on the Examination of Public Accounts had undermined confidence in the procurement process. There was repeated talk of a “fixed-price fiasco”.
Eroded trust
Defence Minister Martin Pfister commented on the report for the first time during the debate. The government would issue a statement on the matter “very soon, and not just in December”. He described the report as “nuanced, objective and interesting”. It formed a “good basis for improvements to processes within the defence ministry”.
At the same time, Pfister noted that the criticism contained in the report placed a “heavy strain on the work of the defence ministry and its staff to build trust”. He appealed to the committee members to conduct the discussion on the report in an objective manner. “I sometimes find that lacking.” For Switzerland’s security, it is important to procure the maximum possible number of new fighter jets, he said.
Pfister has now been given the go-ahead to do so. The army can press ahead with the forthcoming air defence procurements. Further funding requests will be on the agenda during the winter session. Owing to the improved outlook for the federal budget, the government is requesting an additional CHF1 billion or so. Once this has been approved, the government will be able to make the down payments for the new procurements.

articles.title: Jaguar Land Rover in talks to sell Defender to Nato countries
articles.body:
Jaguar Land Rover is in talks with Nato countries about selling them the newly revamped Defender military vehicle, as the UK-based carmaker seeks to tap into Europe’s defence spending boom.
It is also among carmakers bidding for a UK defence ministry contract worth £900m to replace an ageing fleet of Land Rovers that have been out of production since 2016, competing with General Motors and the UK’s Ineos Automotive, which builds the Grenadier 4x4 for the civilian market.
JLR, owned by India’s Tata Motors, has set up a new Defender defence division to explore new partnerships to supply vehicles for people and equipment transportation to defence sectors around the world.
The carmaker is trying to expand beyond its relationship with the British armed forces to exploit a spending boom by Nato countries racing to rearm, as it faces weaker demand elsewhere coupled with higher costs.
JLR insisted that the move, which was first reported by the Financial Times, was not related to its planned 4,000 job cuts globally, as part of an effort to save £1.7bn. It is slashing costs as it struggles with tough trading conditions, Donald Trump’s tariff wars and the fallout from a damaging cyber-attack last year.
As he unveiled three new variants of the Defender Wolf Series II, the next-generation military vehicle, Patrick McGillycuddy, the Defender managing director, said: “Through our newly established Defender defence division, we will offer Defender Wolf Series II to defence organisations worldwide, while also bidding for the UK Ministry of Defence light mobility vehicle tender.”
He said the new 4x4s were “exceptionally robust and versatile”, and added that their lightweight aluminium monocoque (French for “single shell”) construction, with a stiffer body structure, means they can be adapted to the “wide range of roles and operational requirements demanded by military organisations”.
He said: “It is a modern successor to the world-famous Defender Wolf and Land Rovers that have served the British armed forces for more than 70 years.” The new Defender series is designed and engineered in the UK, with engines built in Wolverhampton.
JLR also wants to break into the $80bn (£59bn) US pickup truck market with a local version of its Defender vehicle. The Defender pickup will be built in the US through a joint venture with the Chrysler carmaker, Stellantis, the Sunday Times reported at the weekend. JLR declined to comment on this.
It is the most high-profile UK carmaker to pivot the newly booming defence sector as manufacturers grapple with a transition to electric vehicles and rising competition from Chinese rivals.
Last week, Volkswagen struck a deal to sell its Osnabrück factory to Israel’s Aurelius Capital and VW’s second-biggest shareholder, its home state of Lower Saxony, in a move labour officials said could save about 1,400 of the site’s 1,800 jobs. The site would switch production from cars to heavy-duty trucks that carry anti-missile systems for the maker of Israel’s Iron Dome, Arrow and David’s Sling air and missile defence systems.
“These plans involve the potential manufacture of systems and components for air defence systems for Germany and Europe,” Volkswagen said, adding the cooperation could pave the way for further such deals.
Renault is repurposing part of its Le Mans chassis plant in western France to make up to 600 drones a month for the French ministry of defence.

articles.title: About the China Capital investigation
articles.body:
About the China Capital investigation
A global investigation by ICIJ lays bare the hidden playbook of one of China’s most powerful banks.
China Capital is a cross-border investigation led by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists that exposes how the world’s biggest bank, the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, maneuvers behind closed doors to help Beijing achieve its geopolitical goals.
Based on a trove of 4.8 million ICBC records, the investigation reveals that ICBC used its London operations as a financing hub for companies linked to sanctioned Russian and Belarusian business owners, autocrats publicly accused of corruption, debt-ridden states and China’s political establishment. At times, the records show, the bank breached its own sanctions and anti-money laundering policies.
ICIJ’s investigation found ICBC officers in London acted at the direction of the bank’s Beijing headquarters to pursue explicitly political objectives for its majority shareholder, the Chinese state: cement alliances, acquire natural resources and expand control over communications, energy and transportation infrastructure globally. ICBC is the world’s largest bank by asset size.
Among the findings, China Capital reveals that with Russia’s war in Ukraine raging, ICBC stepped up to help Russian mining giant Norilsk Nickel, aka Nornickel, a company partly owned by four sanctioned oligarchs aligned with the Kremlin. Documents show ICBC bankers discussing ways to finance the firm in renminbi, the Chinese currency, to avoid U.S. dollar transactions, and applauding Nornickel’s idea of building a smelting plant in China to label their products Chinese.
The confidential documents, while offering only a glimpse into the lender’s operations, reveal the bank served a surprising number of clients linked to autocrats, oligarchs and Chinese companies with political connections. Among the clients: a bank owned by the daughters of Ilham Aliyev, Azerbaijan’s longtime authoritarian ruler; Angola’s state oil company, then controlled by cronies of dictator José Eduardo dos Santos; and a Chinese company that partnered with a Belarusian firm sanctioned by the European Union for its ties to Alexander Lukashenko’s regime.
The investigation found that ICBC London continued to bank — and make exceptions for — high-risk clients even after authorities in more than a dozen countries expressed concerns about ICBC’s compliance and anti-money laundering practices.
China Capital reveals that in early 2019, not long after the U.S. Justice Department indicted Huawei for allegedly violating sanctions on Iran and other crimes, ICBC bankers moved with remarkable speed, transferring a staggering $1.3 billion in “emergency cash” for the tech giant. The transaction, while not illegal, triggered a wave of recriminations and infighting at the bank, particularly from its own financial crime prevention unit, which was not told about the move ahead of time.
Beyond the bank’s walls, ICBC has also had its share of run-ins with governments and courts for not following banking rules, including monitoring potentially illicit flows. An ICIJ analysis shows that since 2014 courts and regulators in eight jurisdictions have hit the bank and its overseas branches and subsidiaries with adverse court rulings and penalties totalling at least $96 million. The confidential records also show that ICBC executives were aware of compliance issues at its units in the U.K. and other countries.
An ICIJ-led investigation in collaboration with media partners in 24 countries, China Capital also lays bare what experts describe as the bank’s “muscular” lending tactics, which have burdened some of Africa’s most economically vulnerable states.
In 2011, the bank signed a loan with ZESCO, the Zambian state-owned power company, for $285 million. Seven years later, as the drought-stricken nation of 18 million was barreling toward sovereign default, ICBC came for its first payment of $20 million. This was just after ZESCO had paid the bank $15 million in “management fees” for a separate loan that “put some pressure on the company’s financial situation.” But the utility had little recourse; Zesco had already set up an account at ICBC London for the $285 million loan. Keen to collect the first payment, ICBC headquarters pushed officers in the U.K. to take the money out of Zesco’s account and send it to Beijing before ICBC London had completed the necessary checks on the client, as required by the bank’s compliance policy.
Meanwhile, few outside the bank and the government knew the extent of Zambia’s indebtedness to ICBC and other Chinese banks. The lack of transparency paralyzed debt relief efforts, triggering a financial crisis in 2020 that tanked the value of its currency and made daily staples unaffordable for an already impoverished population.
China Capital’s rare view of ICBC’s inner workings comes from the confidential archives of the bank’s London branch and a U.K. subsidiary, dated between 2005 and 2024 — a span when China ascended on the world stage and President Xi Jinping rose to power.
The trove includes reports marked as trade secrets; internal emails in English and Chinese; confidential dossiers and lists on more than 4,000 corporate clients; meeting minutes; suspicious transaction logs; and directives from the bank’s Communist Party committee, an internal cell that facilitates party activities and advances government policies.
ICIJ also analyzed agreements related to about 200 loans which ICBC London committed to provide — alone or in coordination with other banks — to nearly 200 borrowers. Among them were the Zambian government and companies headquartered or operating in about 30 countries — including the U.K., South Africa, Luxembourg and some offshore financial centers. The ICBC London loan amounts found in the data ranged from about $3 million to $400 million and were mostly for firms in commodity trading, energy and financial services.
The records highlight the hybrid nature of ICBC, a commercial bank that often appears to act like a development bank, contributing to China’s rise as the largest nondemocratic actor in global finance. The bank helped Chinese state firms secure lucrative contracts overseas, financing the acquisition of key transportation, energy and telecommunications infrastructure in foreign countries. Its clientele included companies and individuals accused of corruption, environmental violations, theft of trade secrets and harmful market practices by courts or regulators in other countries. ICBC also loaned millions to foreign state entities as a way to boost China’s alliances and economic power. As is the case for many other Chinese banks, though, ICBC’s lending activities have remained opaque.
Through a spokesperson, the Chinese government said it rejects “false narratives” of “opaque lending.” A representative of China’s Embassy in Zambia told ICIJ in a statement that China “strictly” follows market rules and international norms and “never forces borrowing, presses for repayment, attaches political conditions to loan agreements, or seeks political interests.”
ICBC did not respond to ICIJ’s repeated requests for comment. A Times reporter personally delivered media partners’ questions to the bank’s London office as well but didn’t receive any response.
China Capital provides an unprecedented look at how Beijing has used one of its most powerful financial arms to fulfill its global ambitions.

articles.title: US government watchdog confirms hit to weapons stockpiles
articles.body:
The joint assessment, compiled by inspectors general from the Defense Department, State Department and USAID, offers Washington’s first official accounting of critical munitions depletion alongside extensive physical damage to American assets across the West Asia region, Al Jazeera reported.
According to expert estimates cited in the report, it will take defence contractors up to three years to restore advanced missile and interceptor stockpiles to pre-war levels.
The report also details widespread physical losses, revealing that Iranian strikes damaged or destroyed hundreds of structures across US bases in eight countries: Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan. Dozens of American aircraft and drones were also damaged or destroyed in the strikes.

articles.title: US confirms for first time it has deployed weapons in space
articles.body:
The US has deployed weapons in space, the US military has confirmed, in an extraordinary public announcement that analysts warn will accelerate a high-risk arms race with Russia and China in Earth’s orbit.
The US secretary of the air force, Troy Meink, said Washington had active “on-orbit” weapons, meaning they had been deployed and were circling the globe.
“Today, we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenges of evolving threats wherever they exist,” Meink said on Monday at the annual Air, Space, Cyber conference. “This is why the United States now has, on-orbit, space-control weapons.”
Meink said he would not go into the “specifics” of the weapons. However, a US Space Force spokesperson said space control could refer to “employing kinetic [combat] and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities”.
The statement added that “these capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes”.
Responding to the US announcement, China’s foreign ministry said Washington was “preparing for war in outer space”, and warned against turning space “into a battlefield, as well as an arms race there”. In Moscow, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, told reporters that Russia believed “that space must be free of any weapon” and called for “the complete demilitarisation of space”.
It has been an open secret that the US, Russia and China are working on space weapons, which could include signal jammers to disable other satellites or more “kinetic” options including those that fire projectiles.
Still, space experts warn a public confirmation of such capabilities in orbit for the first time could accelerate a risky arms race.
The astronomer Jonathan McDowell, who has spent decades compiling a list of rocket launches, told the Guardian it was reasonable to assume Washington had such weapons in space, probably jammers, as it had already deployed several satellites with secret payloads.
He said that after the announcement, Russia and China would now “respond in kind” and deploy their own weapons.
“In the long run, I find it questionable whether this is in the US national interest, and for sure we will see comparable systems from China, if they don’t already have them,” he said.
Even radio jamming would be a big escalation of military activity in space, said McDowell, who worked at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics until he retired this year.
Victoria Samson, the Secure World Foundation’s chief director of space security and stability, told the Defence One website that the US now had to accept that the Chinese and Russians would do the same. “Well, that’s huge, because I don’t think any US government official has ever said that before,” she said.
While the militarisation of space began in the 1950s with both Washington and Moscow exploring ways to destroy satellites, there have been attempts over the decades to preserve the emptiness around Earth for peaceful means.
In 1967, superpowers and other countries signed the outer space treaty, which banned weapons of mass destruction in orbit, although the text does not contain a general prohibition on placing conventional weapons in Earth orbit.
The end of the cold war in 1989 brought a moment of cooperation – including the in-orbit assembly of the International Space Station by multiple nations – but in the 21st century space has gradually become a potential battlefield.
Russia sparked international criticism in 2021 when it struck one of its defunct satellites in orbit in a test of a ground-based anti-satellite missile. The blast created thousands of pieces of orbital debris.
As satellites zip around the Earth at thousands of miles an hour, the fear is that an orbital confrontation will lead to a domino effect where the space near Earth becomes cluttered with tiny, high-speed bits of metal.
McDowell said that in the US, the mentality of working towards the solely peaceful use of space was changing. “The US sees conflict in space as something that is conceptually normalised, whereas 20 years ago it was ‘no, we will never want to do that’,” he said.
“I think this is wrong,” he added. “I also think it is still not too late to change course on this. To work mainly with China, because they are the real competitors in space now. I hope the US establishment takes a step back and rethinks some of this.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with 200 drones: Air Defense destroyed 187 targets
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with 200 drones: Air Defense destroyed 187 targets
Kyiv • UNN
Overnight, Russia launched 200 attack and decoy drones at Ukraine. Air Defense destroyed or suppressed 187 of them; hits were recorded at seven locations.
During the night of September 15, Russian occupiers attacked Ukraine with 200 Shahed-type attack UAVs (including jet-powered ones), Gerbera drones, and Parody-type decoy drones. This is reported by the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, reports UNN.
Details
The enemy launched them from the Russian cities of Orel, Kursk, and Millerovo, as well as from occupied Crimea and Donetsk.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
As of 08:00, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 187 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and drones of other types.
Hits by the enemy’s air attack weapons were recorded at 7 locations, as well as the سقوط of downed targets (debris) at 3 locations.

articles.title: Russian Forces Use Artificial Intelligence to Show Artificial Victory
articles.body:
Russian sources are increasingly using AI-generated and AI-altered videos to falsely portray Russian forces as capturing Ukrainian territory they do not control, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW)
ISW said the practice does not yet appear to be centralized across the Russian military. Instead, several Russian units and milbloggers appear to be producing or amplifying AI-altered footage, potentially to conceal battlefield failures or create the impression that units have met Kremlin-set objectives.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Russian sources use AI to fake territorial gains
Russian sources began posting AI-altered flag-raising videos at scale in June 2026, according to ISW. The footage typically shows Russian servicemembers raising flags in settlements that Russian forces have not actually captured.
ISW identified at least 35 videos suspected of being AI-altered between June 1 and Aug. 30. Commercially available AI-detection software assessed with high confidence that at least 10 had been manipulated using AI models.
The actual number is likely higher, according to the report, because existing detection tools don’t consistently identify AI manipulation.
The videos often contain distorted soldiers, inconsistent shadows, unnatural movements and flags that appear to disappear or deform. Russian sources also use camera movements, zooms and jump cuts to make the anomalies harder to spot.
ISW said accurate geolocation does not prove that such footage is authentic, as Russian sources may record real footage of settlements and use it as reference material for AI-generated scenes.
‘You’re Simply Forced to Sit Within These Four Walls’: Kyiv Residents Living Under Constant Drone Attacks
For instance, on July 27, milblogger DIVGEN published a video showing a Russian soldier waving a flag, with the caption: “Own sources. Soldiers of the 3rd Motorized Rifle Battalion of the 127th Regiment, together with ‘Storm-V’ detachments, have completed the liberation of the urban-type settlement of Bely Kolodez [in the Kharkiv region].”
According to the ISW, the video was an AI-generated fake. It was exposed by several visual anomalies, including the soldier’s implausible body proportions and his sudden disappearance from the bushes when the drone camera zoomed out to show the supposedly captured settlement.
Another video, posted by the “Yuzhny Rubezh” (Southern Frontier) Telegram channel on Aug. 20, showed a Russian flag apparently “growing” out of the roof of a house before disappearing back into it.
The channel claimed that the village of Mykolaipillia in the Donetsk region had been “liberated as a result of active and decisive actions by a unit of the Southern Group of Forces.”
One of the most prominent examples involved Sviatohirsk, a town guarding the northern flank of the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk “fortress belt” in the Donetsk region.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin and the Russian Defense Ministry announced in early September that Russian forces had captured the town.
However, Sviatohirsk remained behind Ukrainian lines, a fact underscored by Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi, commander of Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps, who published a video address from the town center.
The claims were also challenged by some Russian pro-war “Z-channels.” The “Voenny Osvedomitel” (Military Informant) channel posted two videos purportedly showing the Russian “liberation” of Sviatohirsk but later said the footage had been generated by a neural network.
The pro-war Rybar channel also criticized the use of AI-generated footage, saying such “deliberately false” reports could expose serious problems in Russia’s battlefield reporting. It noted that Ukrainian footage showing Biletskyi walking around the Sviatohirsk Lavra contradicted the Russian claims of control.
Rybar also warned that the consequences could go beyond propaganda. False reports about captured settlements could distort commanders’ understanding of the battlefield, potentially leading to military operations being planned based on an inaccurate tactical picture.
AI fakes used to exaggerate Russian advances
ISW said the fabricated footage is particularly useful for Russian units that have struggled to make battlefield progress.
Russian milblogger Voin DV, for example, repeatedly attributed territorial gains to Russia’s 36th Motorized Rifle Brigade using footage that ISW assessed or suspected was AI-altered.
Russian sources have also used AI-generated footage to claim advances in the Donetsk region, including along the Fortress Belt, where Russian forces have made slow and costly progress.
The campaign has also targeted Ukrainian gains. After President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukrainian forces had liberated 26 settlements in the Oleksandrivka direction in August, Russian sources posted footage purportedly showing Russian troops still occupying several of those settlements. ISW assessed that some of the footage had been altered using AI.
Russia’s AI campaign targets the information war
ISW said the fabricated videos are intended not only for Russian audiences but also to shape perceptions of the war abroad.
Russian officials have repeatedly made exaggerated claims about territorial gains. AI-generated footage can provide visual material to make those claims appear more credible and reinforce the Kremlin’s narrative that Russia maintains the battlefield initiative.
Most settlements claimed by Russian sources using suspected or assessed AI-altered footage remained under Ukrainian control as of Aug. 31, ISW said.
The think tank expects Russian sources to expand their use of AI-generated material as video-generation technology becomes more accessible. It also warned that Russian sources could eventually use AI-generated satellite imagery to fabricate evidence of military activity or territorial control.
Despite improving technology, ISW said visual anomalies remain common and that open-source researchers will need to continually refine methods for distinguishing authentic battlefield footage from AI-generated material.
You can also highlight the text and press Ctrl + Enter

articles.title: Daily Code Drops at 30,000 Feet: How New Software Rules Could Help Munitions
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Defense industry leaders say the Air Force needs to be able to update the software on its munitions multiple times a day, not every few months, and a new Pentagon instruction released last week could enable that.
The instruction, titled “Accelerated Mission Software,” went into effect Sept. 8 and mandates that Pentagon acquisition offices use agile models for software acquisition and testing like development, security, and operations, or DevSecOps.
Speaking Sept. 14 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference, Rise8 CEO Bryon Kroger said the war in Ukraine have shown that the current model, where munitions technicians might wait months or longer to update software, doesn’t work on the modern battlefield.
“I don’t think that it’s a foreign concept to anybody in this room, but when it comes to software, we’ve just historically been bad at this,” said Kroger, a former USAF intelligence officer and cofounder of Kessel Run, the service’s first software factory. “In some cases, we’re fielding software slower than hardware.”
That slowness has often been the result of software not being prioritized during a weapon’s development, testing, and deployment—creating a challenge for Airmen in the field.
“You wouldn’t think about not establishing a refueling apparatus for aircraft that need it across long distances, but we haven’t really thought about, from an enterprise IT perspective, how to create a similar refueling apparatus, right?” Kroger said.
Pointing to Ukraine’s defense against Russia’s invasion, he called static software “dangerous at this point.”
“We end up talking a lot about hardware and stockpiling everything from munitions to rockets,” Kroger said. “But the question I’d add in the mix is whether the systems can change after we field them.”
The new Pentagon instruction could set the stage for faster software updates. It modernizes software practices such as built-in cybersecurity features, zero trust architecture, continuous testing, and software reuse before introducing new code.
The instruction bolsters software’s prominence by making its development and deployment a strategic asset across the DOD and establishes continuous monitoring across industry to manage supply chain risk.
It also sets rules to manage AI integration and maintain various validations for AI-generated code to protect government data.
The new rules for software development and deployment are based around how the commercial tech industry operates. Kroger made the case that the Pentagon and defense contractors need to follow commercial tech’s lead by decoupling software development cycles from hardware cycles—like how smartphone makers release software updates in between new phone models.
“And we need to set the bar high” Kroger said. “I hear people talking about, ‘Oh, it’d be really nice to get monthly software updates.’” Instead, he argued for updates multiple times a day to “get an update to the field on demand as soon as we need.”
Kroger said the software is critical to the service’s goal of growing its stockpile of munitions, which could become obsolete if the weapons don’ have the proper software to evolve with changing threats.
“The thing the commander actually needs to know isn’t just inventory,” Kroger said. “It’s those effects and both knowing the effects and producing them.”
Ursa Major CEO Chris Spagnoletti echoed Kroger’s comments on speeding up the software update and integration process with munitions hardware.
“When you mentioned software updates, I used to be an avionics guy years ago. The hairs on my back, my neck went up just because it’s so painful,” Spagnoletti said. “… When you make a software change, you have to do this battery of massive testing to make sure that you didn’t screw something else up.”
What’s key, he said, is to push boundaries on how to do the software work faster, while still maintaining the safety and rigor of the current process.

articles.title: Russia to respond accordingly if Lithuania moves to field nuclear weapons — MFA
articles.body:
YEKATERINBURG, September 15. /TASS/. Russia will respond accordingly if Lithuania moves to deploy nuclear weapons on its territory, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said at a briefing on the sidelines of the International Youth Festival.
"Everything they come up with there that threatens us will be taken into due account," the Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman stressed.
"As for the autumn session of the Lithuanian Seimas [on amending legislation to allow the deployment of foreign nuclear weapons - TASS], this is a completely irresponsible act, and I can't say what will come of it. These steps are in line with the extremely provocative and destabilizing anti-Russian policy of NATO countries, which does not take into account what the people of Lithuania want at all, but simply treats Lithuania as a bridgehead, as another platform for possible provocations, because all this involves the escalation and development of various schemes and machinations of so-called extended nuclear deterrence. This leads to the buildup and expansion of the combined NATO-wide nuclear potential, which will, of course, pose a challenge to our country," the diplomat said. "We directly responded to this policy by placing Russian non-strategic nuclear weapons in Belarus, which we now regard as an integral element of ensuring the security and strengthening the defense capability of the Union State."

articles.title: Ukraine says it's open to halting attacks on Russian energy after Trump's claims of deal
articles.body:
Ukraine is willing to halt attacks on Russian energy targets if Russia agrees to a deal to do the same, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday.
But "Ukraine is not convinced that Russia is willing to abide by any agreement," Zelenskyy said in an X post.
Zelenskyy's conditional statement undercut a claim about an hour earlier by President Donald Trump, who in a Truth Social post said: "Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!"
Trump also claimed, "The World's Diesel price rise is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War, not Iran."
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Zelenskyy's post.
Trump on Sunday had urged Zelenskyy to "stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia."
"Let him go after targets but not diesel fuel because he's causing a shortage of diesel," Trump said during his visit to Ireland.
Moscow welcomed Trump's comment.
But Ukraine has insisted that energy sites are legitimate military targets as it continues resisting Russian forces that invaded the country more than four years ago.
Ukraine most recently struck two Russian oil refineries, Zelenskyy announced last week as he accused Moscow of using its oil revenues "to finance the war and the killing of Ukrainians."
In his post on Monday, Zelenskyy said, "If our partners are ready to ensure that Russia genuinely refrains from striking our electricity system, other energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and food supply routes, then, of course, we are ready to ensure a corresponding halt to our strikes."
"So that it is reliable, long-term, has a real impact on people's lives, and does not fall apart after the Russians hold their 'elections' and get an easing of pressure on gasoline and diesel precisely for that period," Zelenskyy wrote.
"The war must be brought to an end. And a de-escalatory step regarding critical infrastructure could be the first step toward peace," he said. "We expect specifics from our partners."
Meanwhile, global energy prices continue to rapidly rise. The average U.S. price of diesel, an important energy source for industrial and other heavy-duty machinery, hit $6 per gallon for the first time Friday.
The sharp price hikes have coincided with an escalation in the Iran war, including a recent drone attack on Saudi Arabia's critical East-West oil pipeline.
The pipeline was used to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, the vital oil shipping route that continues to experience highly throttled commercial traffic since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February.

articles.title: Russian drones started 17 fires in Chernihiv Oblast, adding forest to the list of things the war destroys without aiming
articles.body:
Falling Russian drone debris started 17 forest fires in Chernihiv Oblast between 7 and 13 September, burning 10.8 hectares, Ukraine's state forestry enterprise Forests of Ukraine said.
Russia's drone campaign is causing damage beyond its immediate targets, as falling debris can start fires in forests and other open areas. Forest fires linked to military activity have become a recurring problem across Ukraine. The previous week, 56 forest fires covering 84 hectares were recorded nationwide, with 95% attributed to hostilities, according to the state forestry enterprise.
Drone wreckage also started fires in eight other oblasts during the same period. Kherson Oblast recorded 3.7 hectares burned, Odesa 2 hectares, and Sumy 1.91 hectares. Smaller areas were affected in Zaporizhzhia (0.7 hectares), Dnipropetrovsk (0.5 hectares), Kyiv and Zhytomyr (0.12 hectares each), and Mykolaiv (0.1 hectares), according to Forests of Ukraine.
Russia kept up the daily barrages all week. Between 7 and 13 September, it launched more than 2,000 strike drones at Ukraine, by the Air Force's daily counts, and air defense downed or suppressed about 1,800 of them. The heaviest came on the night of 13 September, when 453 drones and S8000 Banderol munitions flew in from six directions and 405 drones and four Banderols were brought down. Twice that week, Russia also attacked in daylight, sending 410 drones on 12 September and 323 on 13 September between 06:30 and 18:00.
About 165,000 hectares of Ukrainian forest have burned since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, with most of the damage linked to fires caused by shelling and combat.
In total, 46 forest fires covering 25.7 hectares were recorded across the enterprise's territory that week, with about 72% linked to military activity, according to Forests of Ukraine.
The wider environmental toll
The fires are part of a wider environmental toll from Russia's war. The Initiative on Greenhouse Gas Accounting of War, working with the NGO Ecodiya and Ukraine's environment ministry, put emissions from war-driven landscape fires over the first four years at 70 million tons of CO2 equivalent, in an assessment reported by the Ukraine War Environmental Consequences Work Group.
The same review recorded 2,643 environmental incidents monitored by Ecodiya, with 2025 accounting for 931 of them.

articles.title: Two Russian oblasts come under drone attack, with oil refinery and factory hit – photo, video
articles.body:
Two Russian oblasts come under drone attack, with oil refinery and factory hit – photo, video
Drones attacked Russia's Volgograd and Samara oblasts on the night of 14-15 September. The Sebryakovcement Mikhaylovka Cement Plant and Syzran oil refinery may have been among the targets.
Source: Exilenova+ and Supernova+ Telegram channels
Details: A fire broke out at the local oil refinery in Syzran, Samara Oblast. Storage tanks containing petroleum products may have caught fire. An air-raid warning had been issued in the oblast shortly beforehand.
Explosions were also heard at the Sebryakovcement plant in the city of Mikhaylovka, Volgograd Oblast. A missile and drone threat warning had also been issued in the oblast shortly beforehand.
The explosion occurred near cement kiln No. 5, after which firefighters were sent to the plant. Footage posted on social media shows heavy smoke rising over the factory grounds.
There are also reports of a possible missile strike on the Taganrog Aviation Scientific-Technical Complex named after G.M. Beriev. Among other things, the facility repairs and modernises Russian military aircraft.

articles.title: Who Is Umar Kremlev? The Russian Businessman With Ties to Putin Who Partly Funded Trump Jr.’s Wedding Celebrations
articles.body:
A Russian businessman with ties to the country’s President Vladimir Putin footed the bill for celebrations following the wedding of President Donald Trump’s son, Donald Trump Jr., Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina, have confirmed.
Oligarch Umar Kremlev’s contributions to the wedding festivities were first reported by ProPublica, which wrote that the Russian businessman spent hundreds of thousands of dollars to rent out a private island in the Bahamas and a fireworks show. The outlet reported that the guest list included roughly 50 guests, including family members, close friends, and Kremlev, who according to ProPublica was part of a larger group of Russian guests whose presence was a source of confusion for other attendees.
Trump Jr. and Bettina Trump shared a statement on social media in response to criticism over his financial involvement in the event, defending what she described as an “extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend” and denying any political motive behind Kremlev’s attendance.
“Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding,” they wrote in a post on Bettina Trump’s Instagram on Monday in a caption that accompanied a series of photos from the evenings in question showing the couple partying with other guests, performances, and the beach-side venue. “It’s unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from. Friendship doesn’t require a political motive.”
The Trumps’ connection to a figure closely tied to the leadership in Russia—and his apparently lavish financial contribution to the wedding celebrations—has however drawn concerns from Democratic politicians and experts in ethics and intelligence, who have raised questions about what might be expected in return for the "gift" and warned that Russian intelligence services may seek to weaponize such a relationship.
Here’s what to know about Kremlev and his ties to Putin and the Trump family.
Who is Umar Kremlev?
Kremlev, 43, is a native of Tajikistan. He was previously known by his surname at birth, Lutfulloyev, which he changed to Kremlev in 2010 when he was in his late twenties, according to the independent Russian news organization Proekt. Prior to that name change, Kremlev was convicted of extortion in 2004 and battery in 2007.
He went on to join a notorious biker gang, the Night Wolves, not long after changing his name, according to Russian news reports. Outlets reported that during his time in the group, which was the first official biker community in the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR), Kremlev met Alexei Rubezhnoi, who currently leads Putin’s presidential security service. The Washington Post reported that Putin himself is considered an honorary member of the Night Wolves.
In 2015, Kremlev, who had boxed since he was a child, founded a company, Patriot, that promoted boxing matches. Two years later, he became the secretary general of the International Boxing Association (IBA) after a shake-up led to Rubezhnoi becoming the chairman of its supervisory board. Rubezhnoi then nominated Kremlev to the secretary general position; from there, Kremlev went on to be elected as president of the IBA in 2020.
In 2024, Kremlev acquired Rolf, Russia’s largest car dealership group, which had previously been state-owned.
“These services,” Triplett says in reference to the Kremlin, “are exceptional at finding pain points and then and then manipulating them, and you can get people into difficult positions.”
What are Kremlev’s ties to Putin?
Kremlev has been connected with Putin for years, as has been documented through public appearances and business dealings.
During Kremlev’s time as IBA president, Gazprom, a state-owned energy company and one of the largest companies in Russia, became a financial backer of the boxing federation.
That same year, Kremlev stood alongside Putin during the opening of the International Boxing Center in Moscow.
Under Putin, many Russian government officials or oligarchs serve in supervisory positions for sports organizations in the country.
“Umar is guided by Putin. It was using the sport for soft political power,” an ex-IBA board member told ProPublica of Kremlev’s leadership of the organization. “It’s geopolitics. That it’s boxing is just happenstance.”
Following Kremlev’s acquisition of Rolf in 2024, meanwhile, Putin repealed the company’s federal ownership, which he had established through a presidential decree in 2023.
He was also honored by Putin with the Order of Friendship, according to the IBA, a state accolade that celebrates those who have helped to improve the Russian Federation in various sectors. And earlier this year, Kremlev accompanied Putin on a visit to China, according to Chinese state media. Kremlev’s press office told ProPublica in a statement that he was not part of the Russian President’s “official delegation” during the trip.
What are Kremlev’s ties to the Trump family?
Kremlev has been publicly linked to President Trump and Trump Jr. through the IBA in recent months. It’s unclear how else he may be connected with the Trump family.
After President Trump returned to the White House last year, Kremlev and the CEO of the boxing organization sent him an open letter congratulating him on his re-election and expressing the IBA’s “sincere gratitude for your strong and principled stance regarding the inadmissibility in the participation of ineligible athletes in women’s boxing competition,” in reference to Trump’s stance against the participation of transgender women in women’s sports.
The letter then nodded towards the 2028 Olympic Games, which will be hosted by the U.S. in Los Angeles, saying that the IBA looks ahead “with great optimism to the possibility of working together to make the Olympic movement great again, advance the sport of boxing and to champion the rights of athletes globally.”
Last September, Trump Jr. sat on a panel discussion hosted by the IBA in Istanbul, during which he also critiqued the participation of transgender women in women’s sports while onstage with Kremlev.
Kremlev’s press office said in its statement to ProPublica that he and Trump Jr. initially met “a couple years ago” and that the two men “have a friendly relationship.” It added that Kremlev “has never discussed political matters with any of his American friends and acquaintances,” Trump Jr. included.
A spokesperson for Trump Jr. told the New York Times that the two men bonded over boxing and hunting after meeting through a mutual friend, and that they are not in business with one another.
The President, who did not attend Trump Jr.’s wedding or the following celebrations, said in a statement provided to the Times on Monday that “I have no idea who Umar is, never heard of him, and he didn’t pay for Don and Bettina’s wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day.”
A spokeswoman for Eric Trump, Trump Jr.’s brother, meanwhile told the Times and ProPublica, “Eric has absolutely no clue who this person is.”
Intelligence experts raise concerns
“If the allegations are true, then it certainly reflects poor judgment on Donald Trump Jr.’s part,” Dan Hoffman, an intelligence expert with over 30 years of experience working in the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), U.S. military, Department of State, and Department of Commerce, tells TIME. “It is highly unlikely Umar Kremlev would have any interaction with any member of the Trump family without the Kremlin knowing about it beforehand.”
Holden Triplett, who served nearly 15 years with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and was previously the Director for Counterintelligence at the National Security Council at the White House during Trump’s first Administration, says that any kind of relationship between an individual with ties to the President and someone linked to the Kremlin can pose a risk to the U.S.—though he says he doesn’t find the Trumps’ apparent relationship with Kremlev to be particularly alarming.
“Even the most above-board, non-threatening-nefarious relationship could be weaponized by intelligence services,” he tells TIME. “Russians commonly try to use, as a lot of intel agencies do, business relationships as a non-alarming way to establish connection with someone … It is one that the Russians have used with lots of, or attempts at least, with lots of other individuals in politics.”
This isn’t the first time Trump Jr. has drawn controversy over interactions related to Russia. During the 2016 presidential campaign, Trump Jr. met with a Russian lawyer who claimed she could provide information that would hurt his father’s Democratic opponent Hillary Clinton’s campaign. That meeting later became a point in the investigation special counsel Robert Mueller conducted into President Trump’s campaign and its ties to Russia, though Trump Jr. was never accused of wrongdoing in the probe.

articles.title: Massive missile attack on Taganrog, 222 downed drones: Ukrainian strikes' aftermath
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 15. /TASS/. Air defenses destroyed 222 Ukrainian drones over Russia overnight, the Defense Ministry reported.
Several residential buildings and one industrial facility were damaged in the Samara Region as a result of the drone attack. In addition, Rostov Region’s Taganrog was hit by a massive missile attack overnight. Warehouses belonging to the Ozon company and agricultural enterprises were damaged, as were the windows of residential buildings and an educational institution.
TASS has compiled the key details on the attacks’ aftermath.
Scale
- On-duty air defenses intercepted and destroyed 222 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over Russia overnight, the Defense Ministry reported.
- According to the ministry, the drones were downed over the Oryol, Belgorod, Voronezh, Tula, Tambov, Bryansk, Rostov, Kursk, Lipetsk, Ryazan, Saratov, Samara, Kaluga, Ulyanovsk Regions, over Tatarstan and Crimea, as well as over the Black Sea.
- More than 30 drones and missiles were destroyed in Taganrog and nine districts of the Rostov Region, Governor Yury Slyusar reported on his Telegram channel.
- Sixteen drones were shot down over the Voronezh Region overnight, Governor Alexander Gusev said on his Max channel.
- Air defenses destroyed 11 drones over the Oryol Region in the past 24 hours, Governor Andrey Klychkov noted in a post on his Max channel.
Massive attack on Taganrog
- Taganrog came under a massive missile attack overnight, Rostov Region Governor Yury Slyusar said on his Telegram channel.
- According to preliminary reports, there were no fatalities or injuries.
- As a result of the missile attack, windows were damaged in two apartment buildings and three private homes, as well as at an educational institution, a commercial building, a gas pipeline, agricultural enterprise warehouses, a grocery store, and an Ozon warehouse, the governor noted.
- Emergency services are working at the scenes of the incidents.
- Three fires broke out as a result of a massive attack on Taganrog, Mayor Svetlana Kambulova reported on her Max channel.
- She specified that the windows of five apartment buildings and three private homes were damaged.
- Ozon later reported that the delivery hub of its logistics partner was evacuated due to the missile threat.
- No one was injured at the logistics partner’s warehouse.
- The company noted that the attack caused a fire in one section of the building; emergency services are on the scene.
- Ozon will redistribute the goods that were headed there to other facilities.
Other regions
- Several residential buildings and one industrial facility were damaged in the Samara Region due to a drone attack, Governor Vyacheslav Fyodorishchev said on his Max channel.
- There were no fatalities.
- An emergency response team is on the scene gathering information on the aftermath of the attack.
- Windows, roofs, and facades of four private homes were damaged by falling drone debris in the Voronezh Region, Governor Alexander Gusev reported on his Max channel.
- According to preliminary reports, there were no casualties.

articles.title: NATO fighter jets shoot down drone over Lithuania for the first time
articles.body:
NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace overnight on September 15, marking the first time a drone has been downed in the country’s history, according to the Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT. The aircraft that carried out the strike were Italian fighter jets based at an air base in the city of Šiauliai.
The drone was detected in Lithuanian airspace around midnight, prompting authorities to declare an air raid alert in the Vilnius, Trakai, Elektrėnai, and Kaunas districts. It also disrupted airport operations, delaying several international flights.
The drone was shot down between Kaunas and Kaišiadorys, about 100 kilometers (62 miles) northwest of Vilnius.
According to preliminary information, the drone may have been carrying explosives. Authorities are still working to determine who owned it.
Lithuania has repeatedly declared air raid alerts in various parts of the country over drones entering its airspace — including Ukrainian drones that Russian electronic warfare systems knocked off course.

articles.title: There were 225 clashes at the front; Ukrainian forces eliminated 62 occupiers in the Pokrovsk direction, the General Staff reported.
articles.body:
There were 225 clashes at the front; Ukrainian forces eliminated 62 occupiers in the Pokrovsk direction, the General Staff reported.
Kyiv • UNN
Russian forces launched 225 attacks, carried out 55 airstrikes, and used more than 6,000 drones. In the Pokrovsk direction, 62 occupiers were destroyed.
Since the beginning of the day, there have been 225 combat engagements at the front; Ukrainian forces eliminated 62 occupiers in the Pokrovsk direction, with another 15 wounded, reports UNN, citing the General Staff’s update.
In total, since the beginning of this day, 225 combat engagements have taken place. The aggressor launched 55 air strikes using 190 guided aerial bombs, deployed 6,183 kamikaze drones for attacks, and carried out 1,724 shelling attacks on the positions of our troops and settlements
In the North-Slobozhanskyi and Kursk directions, two enemy assault operations have been recorded since the beginning of the day. The enemy carried out one air strike using one guided aerial bomb and shelled the positions of our troops and settlements 50 times.
In the South-Slobozhanskyi direction, the enemy attacked the positions of our units three times toward the settlements of Kozacha Lopan, Lyman and Obukhivka.
In the Kupiansk direction, the enemy attempted to improve its positions eight times, conducting assault operations toward Radkivka, Tyshchenkivka, Monachynivka and Kindrashivka. Five of these attacks are still ongoing.
Six attempts by the invaders to advance were repelled in the Lyman direction near the settlements of Novoiehorivka, Novoselivka, Drobysheve, Lyman and Yampil.
In the Sloviansk direction, the Defense Forces stopped seven attempts by the invaders to advance near the settlements of Ozerne, Kryva Luka and Mykolaivka. Two battles are ongoing.
In the Kramatorsk direction, the Russian invaders did not conduct any assault operations.
In the Kostiantynivka direction, the Defense Forces repelled 27 enemy assaults near the settlement of Kostiantynivka and toward Novoselivka, Illinivka, Dovha Balka, Rusyn Yar, Toretsk, Vilne and Stepove. Two attacks are ongoing.
The enemy carried out 22 attacks in the Pokrovsk direction. The occupiers attempted to advance toward the settlements of Hannivka, Bilytske, Dobropillia, Svitle, Matiiasheve, Serhiivka, Udachne, Molodetske and Novopidhorodne. One assault operation is still ongoing.
According to preliminary estimates, 62 occupiers were eliminated here today and 15 were wounded; six vehicles, a special-purpose piece of equipment, two UAV command posts, a fuel and lubricants depot, and 36 personnel shelters were destroyed. Five vehicles, nine UAV command posts and 123 personnel shelters were damaged. A total of 298 unmanned aerial vehicles of various types were destroyed or suppressed.
In the Oleksandrivka direction, the enemy did not conduct any assault operations.
In the Huliaipole direction, the Defense Forces repelled five enemy attacks near the settlements of Rizdvianka, Dobropillia and Charivne. One of these assaults is still ongoing.
In the Orikhiv direction, the enemy attempted to advance toward Shcherbaky and Stepnohirsk.
In the Prydniprovske direction, the occupiers did not conduct any offensive operations.
There were no significant changes in the situation in the other directions, the General Staff concluded.

articles.title: US hosts Lebanon, Israel envoys for talks in Washington
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Lebanon, Israel envoys to meet in Washington as south burns
Lebanon's and Israel's ambassadors to Washington are expected to meet at the US State Department on Tuesday, as Israel continues its attacks and occupation in southern Lebanon and questions grow in Beirut over the value of negotiations that have so far failed to secure an Israeli withdrawal.
Lebanese Ambassador Nada Mouawad and Israeli Ambassador Yechiel Leiter are expected to discuss recent developments and the implementation of a US-sponsored framework agreed between Lebanon and Israel in June.
Lebanese official sources told The New Arab that the meeting was intended to keep communication between the two sides open following recent setbacks in negotiations. They said no decisions or agreements were expected to emerge from the talks.
Lebanon will reiterate its demand for an end to Israeli attacks and military operations, including the bulldozing, destruction, demolition and booby-trapping of areas in the south, the sources said.
Beirut is also expected to push for agreement on a second "pilot zone" to be handed over to the Lebanese army.
The meeting comes despite growing doubts in Lebanon over negotiations with Israel, which has continued military operations inside the country while refusing to fully withdraw from Lebanese territory.
A US State Department official said earlier that the ambassadors would discuss "current developments" and the continued implementation of the trilateral framework, describing it as the only viable mechanism for restoring Lebanese sovereignty and Israeli security.
The next round of formal negotiations is due to take place in Rome in October. The eighth round of negotiations between Lebanon and Israel had been scheduled for September but was postponed until October.
A Lebanese government source told TNA that Israel had shown little enthusiasm for negotiations and continued to favour military action in southern Lebanon.
"Israel refuses to withdraw from Lebanon and insists on remaining in the south," the source said, adding that Israel sought to maintain its presence for as long as possible as part of a wider regional project.
US ambassador visits southern Lebanon
Against this backdrop, US Ambassador to Beirut Michel Issa visited southern Lebanon on Tuesday accompanied by representatives from the Lebanese government's Council for Development and Reconstruction.
Arriving under heavy security, Issa visited the Our Lady of the Annunciation Monastery in Zawtar al-Gharbiya in Nabatiyeh district. An Israeli drone reportedly flew overhead during the visit.
Issa later stopped in Qaaqaaiyat al-Jisr, where he inspected a newly constructed bridge replacing one destroyed in an Israeli airstrike.
The visit comes as Washington seeks an expanded role in shaping post-war security arrangements in southern Lebanon while continuing to back Israel, whose forces remain inside Lebanese territory.
Issa, who is of Lebanese origin, recently met Lebanon's vice president of the Supreme Islamic Shia Council, Sheikh Ali Al-Khatib. The meeting was viewed by some as an attempt by Washington to engage Lebanon's Shia community while maintaining its campaign against Hezbollah and pressing for the group's full disarmament.
Hezbollah is designated a terrorist organisation by the United States. The group has rejected demands to surrender its weapons while Israeli forces continue to occupy Lebanese territory and carry out attacks.
Zawtar al-Gharbiya is among three villages where the Lebanese army deployed this summer under the June framework agreement. The US-sponsored plan calls for Israel to hand over designated "pilot zones" to the Lebanese army, which is then expected to ensure they have been cleared of Hezbollah weapons and military infrastructure.
Implementation has proceeded slowly amid continued Israeli attacks and occupation. Beirut has repeatedly demanded that Israel halt its military operations and withdraw from Lebanese territory.
Israeli attacks continue
The diplomatic activity comes as Israeli forces continue attacks across southern Lebanon.
Since midnight on Tuesday, Israel has carried out artillery shelling in Wadi Zibqin, al-Mansouri and Kfar Tibnit, as well as detonations in Kounine, Baraachit and al-Mansouri. Israeli operations have remained concentrated around Nabatiyeh despite the Lebanese army reinforcing its deployment in the area.
Fears have also grown over a possible Israeli push towards Nabatiyeh after Israeli forces captured the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge overlooking the city.
Israel's military currently occupies a border zone extending several kilometres into Lebanon, which it calls the "Yellow Line". Dozens of Lebanese towns and villages in the area have been destroyed, preventing large numbers of displaced residents from returning home.
In al-Bayyada in the Tyre district, Israeli forces have been burning what remains of homes, according to Lebanon's state-run National News Agency, while the nearby village of al-Mansouri has faced months of attacks.
On Monday, a resident of Baraachit was killed after Israeli forces opened fire with machine guns in the area.
According to Lebanon's Health Ministry, more than 4,300 people have been killed since all-out fighting between Israel and Hezbollah resumed on 2 March. Since the conflict began in October 2023, close to 9,000 people have been killed in Lebanon and more than 30,000 wounded.

articles.title: Lavrov: Had US not backed away from Anchorage, we would have lived without war for a year
articles.body:
Lavrov: Had US not backed away from Anchorage, we would have lived without war for a year
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov has claimed that Russia "would have been living without war for a year" had the US "not backed away from the agreements" reached in August 2025 in Alaska.
Source: Lavrov at a round table on the Russia-Ukraine war, quoted by Russian propaganda agencies TASS, RIA Novosti and RBC
Quote from Lavrov: "If the Americans had not backed away from the Anchorage agreements, if Europe had not dragged those agreements out, we would have already been living without war for a year. That is a clear fact, so draw your own conclusions."
Details: Meanwhile, he reiterated the claim that Russia has allegedly "never refused negotiations."
"We have never refused negotiations. And all those negotiations that took place were halted not on our initiative. Therefore, if our colleagues are ready, I believe they can certainly be resumed. We have something to say," Lavrov stated.
He also insisted that Moscow has allegedly "never, not once, changed its position" since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and is supposedly "ready to seek compromises".
"Under this heading, we are prepared to search for reasonable compromises, but we have fundamentally not altered our objectives to guarantee our security, prevent NATO's presence on our borders, secure the legitimate rights of Russians and Russian-speaking people who have lived on these lands for centuries, and free them from the threats of Nazification, militarisation, and so forth," the Russian minister said.
He added that Moscow is allegedly prepared for both bilateral and trilateral negotiations.
However, the Russian official stated that the Russian Federation would not halt its aggression against Ukraine during any potential talks.
Background:
- On 15 June, Lavrov stated that Russia was awaiting a renewed visit from special envoys of the US president and wished to hear from them how America intends to implement the agreements on ending the Russian war against Ukraine, which were reached between Russian leader Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Anchorage in the summer of 2025.
- Following this, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio informed journalists that no agreements concerning Ukraine were made during the previous year's summit between US President Donald Trump and Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
- He subsequently added that the approach proposed by the Russians in Anchorage the previous year had failed, as it was unacceptable to Ukraine.
- Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met on 15 August 2025 at a military base in Anchorage, Alaska. The meeting ended without any agreements being reached or any ceasefire in Ukraine being announced, despite claims of "significant progress".
- On 16 August 2025, after talks with Putin, Trump first spoke with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and later with Zelenskyy and European leaders.
- Bloomberg reported that during the call with European leaders and Zelenskyy, Trump said Putin continued to demand the withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from the entire territory of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts in Ukraine's east.
